state_program_name: Health Care Service Firm (HCSF) registration with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs (N.J.S.A. 34:8-45.1; N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13 and 13:45B-14), staffed by Board of Nursing-certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs); Medicaid personal care through NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and the Personal Preference Program (PPP); private-pay home care

front_matter.purpose:
## Purpose

This Policy & Procedure Manual sets out how **[AGENCY NAME]** operates as a New Jersey Health Care Service Firm (HCSF) that places Board of Nursing-certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs). It covers three lines of service:

- Private-pay home care
- Medicaid personal care through NJ FamilyCare PCA, Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) and the Personal Preference Program (PPP)
- Placement and supervision of aides under the HCSF registration issued by the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs

The manual is meant to:

- Turn the legal requirements in the Regulatory Framework section into everyday procedures for staff.
- Protect clients by setting consistent standards for assessment, plan of care, supervision, aide identification and client information.
- Give owners, managers, nurses, schedulers and aides a single reference for registration, renewal, financial reporting, supervision, billing and prohibited practices.
- Support survey, audit and accreditation readiness by recording what **[AGENCY NAME]** does and who is responsible for it.

### Customization, adoption, maintenance and training

This manual is a template and is **not ready for use as written**. Before use, **[AGENCY NAME]** must:

1. **Customize it.** Replace every [AGENCY NAME] placeholder and any other bracketed text. Insert the agency's actual registration details, locations, officers, managing agents, supervising nurse, accrediting body, EVV and billing systems, and service lines. Delete or revise any procedure that does not match how the agency operates.
2. **Have it adopted by the governing body.** The owner, board of directors or other governing authority must formally review and adopt the manual. The adoption date and the signature of the authorized officer should be recorded in the agency's records.
3. **Keep it current.** Review the manual at least annually. Also review it whenever a rule, statute, payer contract, accreditation standard or agency practice changes. Record revision dates and retain superseded versions. Several items in the Regulatory Framework are flagged for confirmation with the issuing agency, and those must be checked before the manual is relied on.
4. **Train staff on it.** Every employee must be trained on the manual at hire and again whenever it is revised. Training must be documented, with the date, the content covered and the employee's acknowledgment. Aides, supervising nurses, office staff and managing agents must each be trained on the sections that apply to their roles.

This manual is an operational guide and is not legal advice. Consult qualified counsel and the regulators listed below on questions of interpretation.
front_matter.how_to_use:
## How to Use This Manual

**Who should use it.** All **[AGENCY NAME]** owners, managing agents, supervising registered nurses, intake and scheduling staff, billing staff and CHHAs. Each person is responsible for knowing the sections that apply to their role.

**How it is organized.**
- This front matter explains the purpose of the manual and the governing rules, and lists the regulators.
- The policy sections that follow should each name the requirement they implement by its exact citation, such as N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9. Staff can then trace any procedure back to its source.
- Forms, checklists and logs belong in the appendices.

**Working with the manual.**
1. **Start with the Regulatory Framework.** Find the rule that governs your task, then go to the matching procedure.
2. **Follow the procedure as written.** If a procedure cannot be followed in a particular situation, tell the supervising nurse or managing agent. Do not improvise on client care, supervision, documentation or billing.
3. **Document.** Where a procedure requires a record (a signed plan of care, a delegation entry, a 30-day inquiry, a waiver, a training record), complete it at the time of the event and file it in the proper record.
4. **Know the payer.** Different rules apply depending on whether a client is private-pay, in NJ FamilyCare PCA, in MLTSS through a managed care organization, or in the Personal Preference Program. Check the client's payer before applying a procedure.
5. **Watch for flagged items.** Items marked "confirm" in the Regulatory Framework rest on secondary sources or on text that was not re-read. Verify them with the named regulator and record the result before relying on them.
6. **Report problems.** Report any suspected violation, client safety concern or manual error to **[COMPLIANCE CONTACT / TITLE]** promptly.

**Customization and control.** Replace all [AGENCY NAME] placeholders before use. The governing body must adopt the manual. It must be kept current through documented review and revision, and all staff must be trained on it and on each revision. Keep a version log with the adoption date, revision dates and the names of the approvers.
front_matter.regulatory_framework:
## Regulatory Framework

The rules below come from the research supplied for this manual. Where the source notes that text was not re-read or comes from a secondary source, the item is marked **confirm**. Verify it with the regulator before relying on it. This list is not a complete statement of all laws that apply to **[AGENCY NAME]**.

### A. HCSF registration and operation (NJ Division of Consumer Affairs)

- **N.J.S.A. 34:8-45.1** defines a health care service firm as an agency that places or arranges placement of personnel for health care, companion or personal care services. A firm that does this must register with the Division of Consumer Affairs. (The statute text was not fetched in this pass. **Confirm.**)
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.2** defines the terms used in the HCSF subchapter and is used to confirm that the firm is in scope. (The rule text was not re-read. **Confirm.**)
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3** sets initial registration requirements:
  - Register on Director-provided forms. The package includes firm and trade names, each primary location, officers, directors and principals, owners of 10% or more, and managing agents.
  - It also includes a criminal-conviction certification from each officer, director, principal or owner (N.J.S.A. 34:8-44), a $10,000 bond, and a list of licenses held in other states with any actions taken. The Director may waive the bond for an entity with a net worth of $100,000 or more, shown by a CPA or licensed-accountant certified financial report.
  - Give owner and managing-agent information before any change in ownership or management.
  - Report any change to application information to the Section in writing within 30 calendar days.
  - If an officer, director, principal or owner is convicted after filing, obtain a new affidavit and file it within 30 days of the conviction.
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5** governs renewal. Renewal requires evidence of accreditation (in effect from May 21, 2019). Financial statements and audits under 13.5A are submitted with the renewal. (Taken from 50 N.J.R. 1299. Full current text was not re-read. **Confirm.**)
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A** governs financial statements, audits and reports:
  - Submit a financial statement for the prior calendar year by July 1 each year. It must match the firm's State tax filing and be filed with the renewal. It must show assets, liabilities, gross income, operating expenses, and money received for NJ Medicaid PCA services.
  - A firm that received more than $250,000 in NJ Medicaid PCA revenue in the relevant year must file a periodic audit.
  - A firm with $10 million or more in gross income must file an audit.
  - A firm with less than $250,000 in PCA revenue and $1 million to under $10 million in gross income must file a report that includes a review by a NJ-licensed CPA.
  - Audits must have an unqualified opinion plus compliance and financial components.
  - A law-firm summary in the research reports subsections (b)-(e) as suspended. **Confirm the current status with DCA.**
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6** lists prohibited acts. An HCSF shall not:
  1. Recruit or advertise for staff, offer services, or contract with a facility before obtaining registration.
  2. Charge a fee or liquidated damages to an employee or in connection with employment, unless it also holds an employment agency license under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-2.
  3. Prevent an employee by contract from working for others. Any fee charged on that basis also requires an employment agency license.
  4. Knowingly send employees to, or keep serving, a facility not under NLRB jurisdiction where a strike or lockout is in progress, to replace strikers.
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7** governs information for patients and employers:
  - Every certified HHA or regulated professional must wear an ID tag at all times while giving care. The tag shows first name or initial, full surname, the certification or licensure level and a photograph. Letters must be equal in size and at least 1/4 inch. The tag must be at least as large as any other ID worn.
  - Give each patient/employer the Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides at least 24 hours before services.
  - The patient may waive the 24-hour timing in writing. The firm keeps the waiver for at least 2 years and must still provide the guide before services begin.
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7** governs homemaker-home health aides and agencies:
  - An agency must be licensed as an HCSF to place certified HHAs.
  - It may refer or place only actively certified HHAs it employs.
  - An HHA may perform only tasks delegated by, or directed by, the health care practitioner supervisor.
  - The supervisor must ensure the HHA demonstrates competence in each delegated task.
  - The supervisor must document in the patient's record every task delegated.
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9** governs duties relating to placements in home care settings:
  - Before placement, an appropriately licensed person must evaluate the patient's needs and write a plan of care. The preparer signs it with their license designation.
  - Placements must match the level of care in the plan.
  - At least once in every 30-day period of service, the supervisor inquires whether the plan is adequate and whether it is being carried out, and records the responses.
  - If the plan needs revision, a licensed person must reassess it immediately. If it is not being carried out properly, the agency must take corrective action immediately.
  - The supervisor makes an on-site, in-home evaluation of the plan at least once in every 60-day period.
  - The agency keeps the original and any revised plan and gives copies to the patient or representative.
- **P.L. 2014, c.29** requires an HCSF to obtain accreditation from a NJ Department of Human Services-recognized accrediting body within 12 months of registration.
- **P.L. 2018, c.48** reinforces the accreditation requirement. Evidence of accreditation is required at renewal.
- **P.L. 2026, c.45** (signed July 22, 2026) moves the annual registration expiration from June 30 to September 30. Registrations that had already renewed for 2026-2027 are extended to Sept. 30, 2027. DCA implementation guidance was pending, and the source is a secondary law-firm summary. **Confirm with DCA.**
- **N.J.A.C. 13:45B-7.1** is cited by a secondary source for an annual registration fee of $500 per primary location. The rule text was not read. **Confirm the current fee on the DCA portal.**

### B. Homemaker-Home Health Aide certification and training (NJ Board of Nursing)

- **N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.2** defines the homemaker-home health aide (as quoted in the Training Book). An HHA is employed by a home care services agency. Under RN supervision, the HHA follows a delegated nursing regimen or performs delegated tasks consistent with N.J.A.C. 13:37-6.2. A NJ RN must supervise the certified HHA and the program of care delivered.
- **N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.4** governs the HHA training program (as reproduced in the Board of Nursing Training Book, rev. 6/13/19):
  - Training is at least 76 hours: 60 classroom plus 16 clinical in a skills lab or patient care setting.
  - Class size is at most 30 students per instructor. Clinical supervision is by an RN at no more than 10 aides per RN.
  - Board of Nursing written approval is required before the program starts.
  - The Board will not certify an applicant until a criminal history check clears.
  - **Confirm** that the current code version is unchanged from the 2019 Training Book.
- **N.J.S.A. 45:11-24.3 et seq.** (as cited in the Training Book) requires all initial HHA applicants to undergo a criminal history background check. The Board will not certify an applicant until it determines that no disqualifying criminal history record exists in FBI or NJ State Police files.
- **N.J.A.C. 13:37-5.5** is the Board of Nursing fee schedule, including the HHA certification application fee. The research cites $50, nonrefundable. **Confirm on current Board pages.**

### C. Medicaid personal care (NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS, Personal Preference Program)

- **N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.4** requires a physician or practitioner to certify the need for PCA services in writing, at the initial application and annually. (The full text was not re-read. **Confirm.**)
- **N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5** sets the duties of the registered professional nurse:
  - The RN assesses the beneficiary and prepares the plan of care consistent with the physician/practitioner certification. This is done at the start of service and never later than 48 hours after it.
  - The plan lists tasks, hours, goals and the beneficiary's strengths and family needs. It is dated and signed by the PCA and the RN.
  - The RN directly supervises the PCA in the home during the PCA's assigned time. The minimum is one visit every 60 days, with the first initiated within 48 hours of the start of service.
  - Extra visits are made for a new PCA, nurse delegation or changed needs. With multiple PCAs, visits rotate until all staff are assessed on each covered shift.
  - For beneficiaries in a managed care plan, the plan completes the State PCA Assessment tool and authorizes hours.
- **N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8** sets limitations on PCA services:
  - No reimbursement in listed settings, including assisted living, nursing facilities, hospitals and adult day health.
  - PCA services by a family member are not covered, except under the Personal Preference Program. There are no exceptions for a spouse, legal guardian or parent of a minor. Other relatives may get case-by-case exceptions requested by the agency. In that case the PCA must be a currently certified HHA, an employee of the requesting agency, and directly supervised by that agency's RN.
  - PCA is not authorized for respite, stand-alone supervision, companionship, child care, parenting tasks, mental-health service needs, non-functional diagnoses, acute short-term conditions or non-hands-on-only needs.
  - No reimbursement if the PCA lives in the beneficiary's home.
  - Maximum of 40 hours per calendar work week, prior authorized.
  - For two or more beneficiaries in one residence, combine individual hands-on hours with group hours for household tasks.
  - Unused units cannot be carried over.
- **NJ SPA 24-0013** sets the fee-for-service PCA rate of $26.68/hour (T1019, 15-minute unit), effective 7/1/2024. MCO rates are contracted and not public.
- **NJ SPA 22-0005** sets the payment methodology for self-directed PCA services (Personal Preference Program, 1915(j)).
- **21st Century Cures Act §12006(a)** requires Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) for Medicaid personal care and home health services delivered in the home. NJ's EVV aggregator is HHAeXchange (per the research).

### D. Regulators and contacts

| Regulator | Role | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **NJ Division of Consumer Affairs, Regulated Business Section** | Registers and regulates HCSFs. Receives applications through the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal. | Phone (973) 504-6370. Email regulatedbusiness@dca.njoag.gov. https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov. Portal: https://rgbportal.dca.njoag.gov/ |
| **NJ Board of Nursing (Division of Consumer Affairs)** | Certifies and regulates CHHAs and approves CHHA training programs. | Call Center 973-504-6430 (Mon-Fri 8:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m.). https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov/hhh/Pages/General-Questions.aspx |
| **NJ Department of Human Services, Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services (DMAHS)** | Administers NJ FamilyCare, including PCA, the Personal Preference Program and MLTSS through managed care organizations. | https://www.nj.gov/humanservices/dmahs/individuals-families/familycare/mltss/ (no phone or email in the source; use the website) |
| **County Area Agency on Aging - Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC)** | Intake and screening for adults 21+ seeking MLTSS. | https://www.nj.gov/humanservices/dmahs/individuals-families/familycare/mltss/ (contact your county ADRC through this page) |
| **NJ Department of Labor and Workforce Development** | Employer unemployment, disability and family leave contributions; state minimum wage. | https://www.nj.gov/labor/ea/employer-services/rate-info |

### E. Keeping this section current

This framework reflects the citations supplied and does not claim to be complete. **[AGENCY NAME]** must designate a responsible person to confirm the flagged items with the regulators, monitor rule and payer changes, and update this manual. After adoption by the governing body, each update must be followed by documented staff training.

policies.title: Organization, Governing Body and Health Care Practitioner Supervisor Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Owners, governing body, administrator, health care practitioner supervisor and all office staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define how [AGENCY NAME] is organized and governed as a Health Care Service Firm (HCSF) registered with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs (DCA), and to set out the duties of the health care practitioner supervisor who directs the Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs) the firm employs and places.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a DCA-registered HCSF under N.J.S.A. 34:8-45.1. It is not a Department of Health-licensed agency. The DCA Regulated Business Section regulates the firm. The NJ Board of Nursing separately certifies the aides. The governing body keeps a current organizational chart that names every owner of 10% or more and the managing agent. It reports changes in ownership or management to DCA as N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3 requires. The governing body designates an administrator and a health care practitioner supervisor who is a New Jersey-licensed registered nurse or physician. The supervisor directs the aides, and no aide performs a task the supervisor has not delegated or directed (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). No state rule was found that sets administrator qualifications, supervisor hours or caseload, or caregiver-to-client staffing ratios. The agency therefore sets its own written standards in this manual and records what DCA and the accreditor confirm.

definitions.definition: An agency that places or arranges placement of personnel for health care, companion or personal care services and must register with DCA (N.J.S.A. 34:8-45.1).
The New Jersey-licensed registered nurse or physician designated by the firm to delegate tasks to, direct and supervise aides.
The person who manages the firm's operations and is reported to DCA with the registration application and any later change.
A Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide certified by the NJ Board of Nursing.

procedures: The governing body adopts a written organizational chart at its first meeting and re-adopts it each year. The chart shows the governing body, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the health care practitioner supervisor, office staff and the aide workforce.
The administrator lists every owner of 10% or more, each officer, director and principal, and the managing agent on the chart and in a separate ownership register kept with the registration file.

Before any change in ownership or management takes effect, the administrator gives DCA the owner and managing-agent information for the incoming person (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(b)). The administrator records the date sent and the DCA acknowledgment.
For any other change to application information, the administrator sends DCA a written report within 30 calendar days. GOV-03 gives the detailed procedure.

The governing body appoints the administrator in writing. It sets and documents the administrator's qualifications and duties as an agency standard, because no state rule sets them. The administrator reports to the governing body.

The governing body designates the health care practitioner supervisor in writing. Before designation, the administrator verifies on the NJ licensing board's online verification that the license is active and in good standing and prints the result.

The administrator keeps a copy of the supervisor's current license and the written designation in the registration file. The designation is a registration document under DCA's FAQ of 7/24/2025, so it is included in the DCA registration materials and updated when it changes.

The supervisor delegates or directs aide tasks, ensures each aide demonstrates competence in each delegated task, and documents every delegated task in the client's record (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(c)-(e)). SVC-03 and REC-03 give the procedures.

The governing body names a back-up supervisor who meets the same licensing requirements. The back-up covers absences so that supervision, 30-day contacts and 60-day in-home evaluations are not missed.
The administrator confirms that only actively certified CHHAs who are agency employees are referred or placed (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(b)). PER-01 and PER-02 give the verification steps.

Because no state rule sets supervisor hours, caseload or staffing ratios, the governing body sets an internal workload standard that allows every supervisory contact to be completed on time. It reviews that standard each quarter against the on-time rates reported under GOV-06.

If the supervisor leaves or the license lapses, the administrator names a replacement or the back-up in writing the same day. The administrator stops new placements that need a supervisor until coverage is in place and reports the change to DCA within 30 calendar days.

The governing body meets at least quarterly. The agenda includes compliance calendar status, QA results, complaints and incidents, and registration and accreditation status. The secretary keeps minutes.

The administrator asks DCA and the chosen accreditor whether they have written expectations for administrator qualifications, supervisor workload or staffing. The administrator files their answers in the registration file and updates this manual as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Adopt the organizational chart, appoint the administrator and supervisor, set internal workload standards and review compliance each quarter.
Keep ownership and management information current, report changes to DCA, verify licenses and keep the registration file.
Delegate and direct aide tasks, confirm competence, document delegation and supervise aides.
Cover supervisory duties during absences.

documentation: Signed organizational chart and ownership register
Written appointments of administrator and supervisor
Supervisor license copy and primary-source verification printout
DCA correspondence and acknowledgments of change reports
Governing body minutes
Written responses from DCA or the accreditor on qualifications and workload

policies.title: HCSF Registration, Service Area and Advertising Requirements
policies.applies_to: Owners, administrator, marketing and recruiting staff, and intake staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] is registered with DCA before it recruits, advertises, offers services or contracts with any facility, and that its advertising and service-area statements are accurate.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not recruit or advertise for staff, offer services or contract with a facility until DCA has issued its HCSF registration (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6(a)(1)). A firm that places certified homemaker-home health aides must be licensed as an HCSF (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(a)). All advertising and public statements are accurate. The firm states accreditation only after it actually holds it. DCA reports an average processing time of 30 to 60 days. That figure is not a rule deadline and the firm does not rely on it for launch dates.

definitions.definition: The DCA approval that allows an entity that places health care, companion or personal care personnel to operate as an HCSF.
Each principal place of business of the firm that is reported to DCA on the registration application.
Any website, social media post, brochure, job posting, directory listing, sign, referral-source material or other communication that offers services or seeks staff.

procedures: The administrator confirms that [AGENCY NAME] is within scope as an agency that places or arranges placement of personnel for health care, companion or personal care services (N.J.S.A. 34:8-45.1; N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.2) and documents that finding in the registration file.

The administrator files the initial application online through the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal (https://rgbportal.dca.njoag.gov/). Questions go to the DCA Regulated Business Section at (973) 504-6370 or regulatedbusiness@dca.njoag.gov.

The application package includes the items listed in N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(a). These are the firm and trade names, each primary location, officers, directors, principals, 10% or greater owners and managing agents, a criminal-conviction certification from each officer, director, principal or owner, the $10,000 bond or a waiver request, and a list of licenses held in other states with any actions taken. The administrator also includes the supervisor designation and the other documents DCA's current instructions require.
The administrator prepares a checklist and has a second person (the owner or counsel) review the package for completeness before filing.

Until DCA issues the registration, no one at [AGENCY NAME] may post job advertisements, recruit aides, accept clients, quote rates, sign a service agreement or contract with a facility. The administrator issues a written 'no-launch' notice to all staff and owners and keeps it on file.
The administrator tracks the application status weekly and logs every contact with DCA. If DCA asks for more information, the administrator answers within the time DCA gives.

When the registration is issued, the administrator files the certificate, records the registration number and effective date, and gives the written 'go-live' notice. The registration is displayed or available as DCA requires.

The administrator approves all advertising and outreach before use. The approver checks that the firm's registered name and any trade name match DCA records, and that no statement is false or misleading.

The firm states accreditation in advertising only after it holds accreditation from a recognized body. Before that, advertising carries no claim of accreditation, 'pending' status or equivalent. GOV-04 covers accreditation.

The administrator defines the firm's service area by county and municipality in a written statement. Intake staff accept clients only within that area unless the administrator approves an exception, and the statement is updated when the area changes.
The firm places only actively certified CHHAs it employs, and advertising does not describe any caregiver as a 'certified aide' unless the caregiver's certification has been verified under PER-01.
The firm adds any new primary location to the registration through DCA before it operates from that location, and reports it under the 30-day change rule in GOV-03.

The administrator reviews all active advertising, the website and online directory listings every quarter and removes or corrects outdated or inaccurate statements. The review is recorded in the advertising log.

responsibilities.duty: File and track the application, issue the no-launch and go-live notices, approve all advertising and define the service area.
Ensure no business activity before registration and sign the criminal-conviction certifications.
Use only approved materials and make no offer of services or staff recruitment before registration.
Accept referrals only within the defined service area and only after go-live.

documentation: Application package, filing receipt and portal confirmations
DCA correspondence log
Registration certificate and number
No-launch and go-live notices
Advertising approval log and copies of approved materials
Service-area statement
Quarterly advertising review record

policies.title: Registration Maintenance: Bond, Insurance, 30-Day Change Reporting and Annual Renewal
policies.applies_to: Owners, administrator, the compliance calendar owner and bookkeeping staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep [AGENCY NAME]'s HCSF registration in good standing by maintaining the required bond and insurance, reporting changes to DCA on time, and renewing on time each year.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains the $10,000 bond required by N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(a), unless the DCA Director has waived it for an entity with a net worth of $100,000 or more shown by a certified financial report from a CPA or licensed accountant. The firm also maintains a certificate of general professional liability insurance of at least $1,000,000, as listed in the DCA FAQ of 7/24/2025. The governing rule subsection was not confirmed, so the administrator treats it as a DCA requirement and checks it with DCA. The firm reports any change to application information to DCA in writing within 30 calendar days. It obtains and files a new criminal-conviction affidavit within 30 days of any later conviction of an officer, director, principal or owner. It renews annually, with evidence of accreditation and the financial statements and audits that DCA requires. One named person owns the compliance calendar.

definitions.definition: Any change to the firm or trade name, primary locations, officers, directors, principals, owners of 10% or more, managing agents, or other facts reported in the registration application.
The $10,000 bond that secures the firm's compliance with the HCSF law.
The written schedule of every registration, bond, insurance, report and renewal due date, with the owner and lead time for each.

procedures: The governing body names a compliance calendar owner in writing ([COMPLIANCE CALENDAR OWNER]). The owner builds the calendar within 30 days of registration and reviews it at every governing body meeting.

The calendar lists the bond expiration, insurance policy expiration, annual registration expiration, accreditation dates, financial statement dates, supervisor license expiration and each owner's conviction-certification status. It assigns each item an owner and a due date and sets a 60-day reminder for the registration renewal.

Bond: The administrator keeps the original bond or the Director's waiver order. If the firm relies on a waiver, the administrator keeps the CPA or licensed-accountant certified financial report that supported it and confirms with DCA when a new report is needed.

Insurance: The administrator obtains a certificate showing general professional liability coverage of at least $1,000,000. The administrator calls DCA to confirm the current requirement and files the certificate. The administrator renews coverage at least 30 days before expiration and replaces the certificate in the file.

Change reporting: When any application information changes, the administrator completes a written change report that day. The report states the old and new information and the effective date. The administrator sends it to DCA within 30 calendar days of the change and keeps proof of delivery.
For a change of owner or managing agent, the administrator follows GOV-01 and sends the new person's information before the change takes effect.

Conviction after filing: If an officer, director, principal or owner is convicted of a crime after filing, that person must notify the administrator immediately. The administrator obtains a new criminal-conviction affidavit and files it with DCA within 30 days of the conviction.

Annual renewal: Registration was moved from a June 30 to a September 30 annual expiration by P.L. 2026, c.45. The administrator confirms with DCA, in writing, the exact expiration date that applies to [AGENCY NAME], the portal steps and any grace period. The administrator records the answer on the calendar.

At least 60 days before the confirmed expiration date, the administrator starts the renewal on the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal and gathers the renewal fee, evidence of accreditation, and the financial statements and audits required under GOV-08.

The annual registration fee is $500 per primary location according to the secondary source relied on for N.J.A.C. 13:45B-7.1. The administrator confirms the current fee on the DCA portal before payment and pays it by the due date.
The administrator submits the renewal at least 30 days before expiration, saves the confirmation and files the renewed certificate when it is issued.

If the registration or the accreditation evidence is not ready 30 days before expiration, the administrator informs the owners and escalates to the governing body the same day. The firm does not operate on an expired registration.
The compliance calendar owner reports status at each quarterly governing body meeting, including any item due within 90 days.
The administrator re-verifies renewal rules after any DCA implementation guidance on P.L. 2026, c.45 and updates this policy under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the calendar, send reminders and report status quarterly.
Maintain bond and insurance, file change reports, prepare and submit renewal.
Report any conviction or change in information to the administrator immediately and sign required affidavits.
Review calendar status each quarter and authorize payment of fees, bond premiums and insurance.

documentation: Bond or waiver order and supporting certified financial report
Insurance certificates
Change reports and delivery proof
Conviction affidavits (if any)
Compliance calendar and quarterly status reports
DCA written confirmation of expiration date and renewal steps
Renewal submission, fee receipt and renewed certificate

policies.title: Accreditation Maintenance and Loss-of-Accreditation Reporting
policies.applies_to: Owners, administrator, health care practitioner supervisor and quality staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] obtains accreditation within 12 months of registration, maintains it, and reports any loss of accreditation to DCA promptly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] obtains accreditation from an accrediting body recognized by the NJ Department of Human Services within 12 months of its initial HCSF registration (P.L. 2014, c.29). Evidence of accreditation is required at each registration renewal (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5; P.L. 2018, c.48). The firm reports any loss of accreditation to DCA within 10 days. That deadline comes from a law-firm summary of the law, so the administrator verifies it with DCA and uses the shorter of the verified deadline and 10 days. The firm's policies and practices are written and kept to meet its accreditor's standards.

definitions.definition: An accrediting organization recognized by the NJ Department of Human Services for HCSF accreditation.
The current accreditation certificate or letter from the accrediting body, submitted at each renewal.
A written plan, with responsible persons and dates, to fix any deficiency found in an accreditation survey.

procedures: Within 30 days of DCA registration, the administrator asks DCA for the current list of recognized accrediting bodies and records the date and answer. The administrator does not rely on an outdated list.

The administrator compares at least two recognized accreditors by standards, cost, timeline and survey process, and presents a written comparison to the governing body. The governing body selects an accreditor in writing within 90 days of registration.

The administrator enters the 12-month accreditation deadline on the compliance calendar, counted from the DCA registration date, with working deadlines at months 3, 6 and 9 and a target to complete accreditation by month 10.
The administrator submits the accreditor's application and fees and keeps copies of all submissions and correspondence.

Before the survey, the administrator and supervisor compare this manual with the accreditor's standards, make needed edits under GOV-05, and run a mock review of ten sample client files and five personnel files.
During the survey, the administrator and supervisor are available to the surveyor. The administrator records every finding at the exit conference.

Within the accreditor's deadline, the administrator writes a corrective action plan for each finding. It names a responsible person and due date and the evidence that will show correction. The administrator submits the plan and follows it to completion.
The administrator files the accreditation decision letter and certificate in the registration file and states accreditation in advertising only after the decision. GOV-02 applies.
The administrator enters the accreditation expiration and any interim report dates on the compliance calendar and begins re-accreditation work at least 6 months before expiration.
At each renewal, the administrator attaches the current evidence of accreditation to the DCA renewal. GOV-03 applies.
If accreditation is denied, suspended, withdrawn, revoked or allowed to lapse, the administrator tells the owners the same day and calls DCA at (973) 504-6370 to confirm the reporting requirements.

The administrator sends DCA written notice of the loss within 10 days, or sooner if DCA's verified deadline is shorter. The notice states the reason, the date and the corrective steps. The administrator keeps proof of delivery.
The governing body meets within 5 business days of any loss to approve a recovery plan. The administrator stops advertising accreditation immediately and corrects any materials that state it.
The administrator reports the accreditation status, open corrective actions and the next survey date to the governing body each quarter.

responsibilities.duty: Select the accreditor, approve costs and oversee corrective and recovery plans.
Manage the accreditation process, report any loss to DCA and keep evidence for renewal.
Help prepare for surveys and carry out clinical corrective actions.
Track the 12-month deadline and re-accreditation dates.

documentation: DCA recognized-accreditor list and date obtained
Accreditor comparison and governing body selection
Application, survey report and findings
Corrective action plans and completion evidence
Accreditation certificate or decision letter
Loss-of-accreditation notice to DCA and proof of delivery (if applicable)
Quarterly accreditation status reports

policies.title: Policy Review and Document Control
policies.applies_to: Administrator, health care practitioner supervisor, governing body and all staff who use the manual at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep the Policy and Procedure Manual current, accurate and controlled so that staff follow the right version, the governing body approves changes, and the manual matches current New Jersey requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reviews every policy at least annually. No HCSF rule sets a review frequency, so annual review is an agency standard. At each review the administrator re-verifies every cited rule against the live New Jersey Administrative Code and statutes, because P.L. 2026, c.45 implementation and any rule revisions may change content. Where the firm's privacy policies change, it revises them as 45 CFR 164.530(i) requires and keeps them current. The administrator and the health care practitioner supervisor sign off on each new version. Regulatory references in this manual, including N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7 and 13:45B-13.3, are tied to the clinical and registration practices that depend on them.

definitions.definition: A policy or form that has an identifier, version number, effective date and approval signatures and is distributed under this policy.
The record of each change to a policy: version, date, summary of change, reason and approvers.
Reading the current text of each cited rule from the official NJ source and recording the date checked.

procedures: The administrator assigns each policy an identifier, version number and effective date and prints them in the header. The same data goes into the master index of policies.
The administrator keeps one master copy of the manual, in electronic form with a locked read-only copy, and controls who may edit it.
Each policy gets a named owner, such as the administrator or the supervisor, who is responsible for its content and annual review.
The administrator sets an annual review schedule so that every policy is reviewed within 12 months of its last review. The review dates go on the compliance calendar.
At each review, the owner performs a live code check. The owner reads every cited rule on the official NJ source, compares it with the policy and records the date and the reviewer's initials.

The owner also checks DCA's website and the portal for new guidance, including implementation guidance on P.L. 2026, c.45, and checks for any rule proposals or adoptions that affect health care service firms.

The owner also reviews changes in the firm's practice, QA results under GOV-06, incident trends, accreditor standards and surveyor findings, and edits the policy where practice or findings call for it.
The owner makes edits in draft, marks changes and sends the draft to the administrator and the health care practitioner supervisor.

The administrator and the supervisor sign and date the final version. The governing body approves any change that affects governance, client rights, scope of services or safety, and the minutes record the approval.
The administrator enters the change in the version log, updates the master index and replaces the old version in the master copy. Superseded versions are archived and kept for at least 6 years.

Within 7 days of approval, the administrator distributes the new version to staff and collects signed or electronic acknowledgments. Staff receive training on material changes before the effective date.
The administrator removes retired copies from office binders and shared drives so that only the current version is in use.

When a regulation changes in a way that needs immediate action, the administrator issues an interim written directive within 5 business days. The directive is incorporated into the manual at the next revision and logged.
The administrator reports the review status and open revisions to the governing body each quarter.
If the firm's privacy practices change, the administrator updates the notice of privacy practices and related policies before the change takes effect, as described in CR-03.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the master manual, index, version log and distribution, and schedule reviews.
Review and sign off on clinical and supervision policies.
Perform the annual live code check and prepare revisions.
Approve material changes and review review-status reports.
Use only the current version and acknowledge new versions.

documentation: Master index of policies
Version log
Live code check records with dates and initials
Signed approval pages
Governing body minutes approving material changes
Staff acknowledgments of new versions
Archive of superseded versions

policies.title: Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement
policies.applies_to: Administrator, health care practitioner supervisor, quality staff and governing body of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To monitor and improve the quality and safety of services and to confirm that [AGENCY NAME] meets New Jersey requirements for aide certification, delegation, plans of care and supervision.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates a written quality assurance and performance improvement (QAPI) program. Each quarter the administrator audits client and personnel files and reviews complaints, incidents, missed visits and electronic visit verification (EVV) exceptions. The audit checks that every record shows the tasks delegated and documented by the supervisor (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(e)), that only actively certified aides are scheduled (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(b)), and that the supervisor completed the 30-day contacts and 60-day in-home evaluations on time (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9). For Medicaid clients, the audit also checks that the physician or practitioner certification of need is current and that the registered nurse completed the 60-day supervisory visit (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5). Results go to the owners and the accreditor, and the firm corrects problems under a written plan. Accreditation evidence and the accreditor's standards support this program (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5).

definitions.definition: The firm's ongoing process of measuring performance, finding problems, correcting them and checking that the correction worked.
A visit record that is missing, edited, late, or not matching the schedule or authorization in the electronic visit verification system.
The physician or practitioner certification that supports a Medicaid PCA client's need for personal care services.
A documented step with a responsible person and due date to fix a problem found in an audit or review.

procedures: The governing body adopts an annual QAPI plan that names the measures, audit sample sizes, reporting dates and persons responsible, and reviews it each year.

Each quarter, the administrator draws a random sample of at least 10% of active client records, with a minimum of 10 records or all records if fewer, and at least 10% of active aide personnel files, with a minimum of 5 files.

Delegation audit: For each sampled client record, the reviewer confirms that the supervisor documented every delegated task (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(e)) and that the aide's competence in each delegated task was demonstrated and recorded.

Certification audit: For each aide scheduled in the quarter, the reviewer confirms that the NJ Board of Nursing certification was verified as active and is on file, and that the aide is an agency employee. The reviewer compares the schedule to the verification dates.
Plan of care audit: The reviewer confirms that a signed, licensed-person plan of care preceded placement and matches the placed level of care (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9).

Supervision audit: The reviewer confirms that the supervisor made a 30-day inquiry in every 30-day period of service and recorded the responses, and that the on-site in-home evaluation was done in every 60-day period.

Medicaid audit: For Medicaid PCA clients, the reviewer confirms that the current certification of need is on file, that the RN's plan of care was written no later than 48 hours after service start, that the first RN supervisory visit started within 48 hours of start, and that RN visits occur at least once every 60 days (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5).
The administrator logs and trends each complaint, incident, missed visit and EVV exception for the quarter by client, aide, shift and cause, and compares the totals with the last quarter.

For every finding, the administrator opens a corrective action entry the same day. Findings that put a client at risk are reported to the supervisor immediately and corrected within 24 hours. Other findings are corrected within 30 days.
The administrator checks that each correction has worked, by re-auditing the same item the next quarter, and keeps the entry open until the check passes.

The administrator writes a quarterly QAPI report with the audit results, trend data, open corrective actions and recommended changes. The report goes to the governing body at its next meeting, and the minutes record the discussion.
The administrator shares results with the accreditor as the accreditor requires and uses the accreditor's feedback to revise the QAPI plan.

Where a pattern calls for it, the governing body starts a performance improvement project with a goal, measures, owner and timeline. Examples are missed visits, late supervisory contacts and EVV exceptions.
The administrator feeds audit findings into training under PER-04 and into policy revisions under GOV-05.
The firm keeps audit tools, samples and reports for at least 6 years.

responsibilities.duty: Adopt the QAPI plan, review quarterly reports and direct improvement projects.
Run the audits, track findings and corrective actions and write the quarterly report.
Correct clinical findings, including late contacts and delegation gaps, and support Medicaid audits.
Supply schedule, missed-visit and EVV data and correct exceptions.

documentation: Annual QAPI plan
Quarterly audit tools and completed sample sheets
Complaint, incident, missed-visit and EVV exception logs
Corrective action log with re-audit results
Quarterly QAPI reports and governing body minutes
Accreditor correspondence about QAPI
Performance improvement project files

policies.title: Corporate Compliance, Fraud and Billing Integrity
policies.applies_to: Owners, administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, billing and scheduling staff, and all Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs) of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] bills Medicaid and private payers only for services that were authorized and actually delivered, and to prevent, detect and correct fraud, waste and abuse.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] bills NJ FamilyCare PCA and MLTSS payers only for hands-on personal care services that were prior authorized, delivered by a qualified employee and verified electronically. We do not bill for companionship, respite, stand-alone supervision, child care or parenting tasks, or for services delivered by a PCA who lives in the beneficiary's home (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(c),(d)). We do not bill for services in settings where PCA is not reimbursable (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(a)). We bill only visits captured through Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) as required by 21st Century Cures Act §12006(a) and 42 USC 1396b(l). Unused authorized units are not carried over and are never billed (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(i)). We screen employees against federal and state Medicaid exclusion lists. No New Jersey rule section was verified for this practice, so it is agency policy and will be checked against each MCO contract. Reporting of Medicaid PCA revenue and the annual financial statement are handled under GOV-08. Staff who report a concern in good faith are protected from retaliation.

definitions.definition: Direct physical personal care (such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, feeding) provided to a beneficiary under an authorized plan of care.

Electronic Visit Verification, the electronic record of service type, recipient, caregiver, date, and start and end times required for Medicaid personal care visits. New Jersey uses the HHAeXchange aggregator.
Knowingly billing for services not delivered, not authorized or not allowed, billing inflated time or units, or other misuse of Medicaid or client funds.
A federal or state list of individuals and entities barred from participating in Medicaid or federal health care programs.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Compliance Officer ([COMPLIANCE OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]) in writing. The Compliance Officer reports to the governing body at least quarterly and documents each report in the compliance file.

Before the first Medicaid claim for any client, billing staff obtain the prior authorization or MCO service authorization. They enter the authorized service type, hours, units and dates into the billing system and check that the plan of care matches them.

Before accepting a Medicaid PCA referral, the intake staff member confirms the client's residence is not a setting where PCA is non-reimbursable (such as an assisted living facility, nursing facility, hospital or adult day health). Intake also confirms the request is for hands-on care and not for respite, stand-alone supervision, companionship, child care or parenting tasks. Any referral that fails this check is declined or referred back to the payer and the reason is documented.
The scheduler does not assign any caregiver who lives in the client's home to a Medicaid PCA shift. Any such arrangement is referred to the Compliance Officer before it starts.

The scheduler does not schedule or bill more than the authorized hours. Total hours for one caregiver and one beneficiary may not exceed 40 hours in a calendar work week, and the 40 hours must be prior authorized (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(g)).

For two or more beneficiaries in one residence, billing staff combine each person's individual hands-on hours with group hours for household tasks as the authorization specifies (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(h)).

Billing staff submit a claim only when an EVV record exists with matching caregiver, client, date, service and start and end times. Visits with missing or mismatched EVV data are held, corrected through the documented EVV exception process in SVC-08, and billed only if the visit is verified.
Billing staff track authorized units against used units weekly. Unused units expire and are not carried over or billed in a later period (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(i)).

Before hire, and then monthly, the Compliance Officer or designee checks every employee, contractor and owner against the HHS-OIG exclusion list, the federal SAM exclusion list, and the New Jersey Medicaid exclusion and debarment list. The check date and result are recorded. Any hit results in immediate removal from Medicaid-billable work pending review.

Each month the Compliance Officer reviews a sample of at least [NUMBER] paid claims per payer. The review compares the claim to the authorization, plan of care, EVV record, caregiver timesheet and the client's care notes. Findings are written and corrected.

Any suspected overbilling, billing for non-covered services or falsified time is reported to the Compliance Officer immediately. The Compliance Officer investigates within [NUMBER] business days and keeps all evidence.

When an overpayment is confirmed, billing staff stop billing the affected claims, and the Compliance Officer repays or corrects them with the payer promptly and in line with the payer contract and applicable law. The Compliance Officer records the amount, cause and fix.

All billing staff, schedulers, Supervisors and aides receive compliance training at hire and annually. Training covers the non-covered services listed above, EVV, false claims, and how to report concerns. Attendance is recorded.

Staff may report concerns to the Compliance Officer or anonymously through [HOTLINE OR PROCESS]. Retaliation against a person who reports in good faith is prohibited and results in discipline up to termination.
Employees who knowingly submit false time, falsify EVV data or bill for non-covered services are disciplined up to termination, and the matter is referred to the payer or authorities when required.
The Compliance Officer reviews this policy and the compliance work plan each year, and whenever an MCO contract or payer rule changes.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints the Compliance Officer, reviews quarterly compliance reports, and makes sure resources are available to correct problems.
Runs the compliance program, exclusion screening, claim audits, investigations, training and overpayment repayment.
Bill only authorized, delivered and EVV-verified services and track units.
Schedule within authorizations and the 40-hour limit, and never assign live-in PCA arrangements to Medicaid shifts.
Confirm that the plan of care and services delivered are hands-on and consistent with the authorization.
Record time accurately through EVV and report any pressure to record inaccurate time.

documentation: Compliance Officer designation and quarterly reports to the governing body
Exclusion screening log with dates and results
Prior authorizations and unit tracking records
Monthly claim audit worksheets and corrective actions
EVV exception and correction logs
Investigation files and overpayment repayment records
Compliance training rosters
Non-retaliation acknowledgments

policies.title: Annual Financial Statement, Audit and Report Compliance
policies.applies_to: Owners, administrator, the person responsible for finance and renewal filings at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] files the required annual financial statement, audit or CPA review report with its Health Care Service Firm registration renewal, accurately and on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] submits a financial statement for the prior calendar year by July 1 each year, filed with the registration renewal (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A(a)). The statement shows assets, liabilities, gross income, operating expenses and money received for NJ Medicaid PCA services, and is consistent with the firm's State tax filing. Each year we determine whether our Medicaid PCA revenue exceeds $250,000 or our gross income reaches $1 million or $10 million, because those thresholds trigger an audit or a CPA review report under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A(b)-(f). Audits must include an unqualified opinion plus compliance and financial components (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A(j)). One law-firm summary reports that subsections (b)-(e) are suspended, and the July 1 filing date and the September 30 registration expiration date appear to conflict. We therefore confirm current status and due dates in writing with the Division of Consumer Affairs, Regulated Business Section each year before relying on either date. Financial statements and audits are submitted with the renewal, together with evidence of accreditation (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5).

definitions.definition: The annual statement for the prior calendar year showing assets, liabilities, gross income, operating expenses and Medicaid PCA receipts.
Money the agency received for NJ Medicaid Personal Care Assistant services in the relevant year, from the State or from managed care organizations.
A CPA audit with an unqualified opinion and compliance and financial components, required for firms meeting the thresholds in the rule.
A report that includes a review by a New Jersey-licensed CPA, required for firms below $250,000 in PCA revenue with gross income of $1 million to under $10 million.

procedures: The Administrator names a Filing Coordinator ([FILING COORDINATOR NAME], [PHONE]) to own the annual financial filing, and records the assignment.
By January 31 each year, the Filing Coordinator creates a compliance calendar with internal deadlines for the year-end close, tax filing, CPA engagement, draft statements and the renewal submission.
By January 31, the Filing Coordinator engages a New Jersey-licensed CPA in writing. The engagement letter states the scope (financial statement, review report or audit) and the deadline.
After year-end close, the finance staff calculate for the prior calendar year: total Medicaid PCA revenue (FFS and MCO), gross income, and the amount of each category in the statement.

The Filing Coordinator compares those figures to the thresholds: Medicaid PCA revenue over $250,000; gross income of $1 million to under $10 million with PCA revenue under $250,000; and gross income of $10 million or more. The result and the required filing type are recorded on a threshold worksheet.

Before relying on the July 1 date or on any suspension of subsections (b)-(e), the Filing Coordinator contacts DCA Regulated Business Section at (973) 504-6370 or regulatedbusiness@dca.njoag.gov. The Coordinator asks which filing is currently required and the due date given the September 30 registration expiration date. The answer is saved in the file with the date and the name of the person consulted.
Finance staff prepare the financial statement so it matches the firm's State tax filing. The CPA or the Filing Coordinator reconciles gross income to the tax return and documents any difference.

Where an audit is required, the CPA performs it so that it includes an unqualified opinion and compliance and financial components. If the opinion is qualified, the Filing Coordinator tells the Administrator and the governing body within [NUMBER] business days and prepares a corrective plan.
The Administrator reviews and signs the final financial statement or report at least [NUMBER] days before the filing date. The owner or an authorized officer certifies accuracy.

The Filing Coordinator files the financial statement and any audit or CPA review report with the renewal through the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal, together with the evidence of accreditation, and saves the submission confirmation.
If the filing cannot be completed by the due date, the Filing Coordinator tells DCA in writing before the deadline and documents the response.
The CPA engagement letter, working papers received from the CPA and supporting schedules are kept in the financial compliance file for at least [RETENTION PERIOD] years.
The Filing Coordinator reports the status of the filing to the governing body at its next meeting after submission and at each meeting until it is accepted.
The Compliance Officer and Filing Coordinator review this policy each year after the filing, and update it when DCA changes the rule, due dates or suspension status.

responsibilities.duty: Provides funds for the CPA work, signs the statement and ensures the filing is made.
Reviews, signs and oversees timely submission.
Maintains the calendar, threshold worksheet, DCA confirmations and portal submission.
Prepare year-end figures, including Medicaid PCA receipts and gross income, and reconcile them to the tax filing.
Prepares the review report or audit and delivers working papers.

policies.title: Prohibited Acts: Employee Fees, Restrictive Covenants and Strike Replacement
policies.applies_to: Owners, administrator, human resources, recruiting and scheduling staff, and Health Care Practitioner Supervisors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] does not engage in acts prohibited to Health Care Service Firms under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not charge any employee a fee or liquidated damages in connection with employment, including training or placement fees, unless it also holds an employment agency license under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-2. We do not use contracts that prevent an employee from working for another person, and any fee charged on that basis would also require the employment agency license. We do not knowingly send employees to, or keep serving, a facility not under NLRB jurisdiction where a strike or lockout is in progress to replace strikers. We also do not recruit or advertise for staff, offer services or contract with a facility before our registration is in place (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6). [AGENCY NAME] does not hold an employment agency license, so these prohibitions apply to us without exception.

definitions.definition: Any charge to an employee or applicant in connection with employment, such as an application, training, placement, uniform, background check or orientation fee, or liquidated damages for leaving.
A contract term that prevents an employee from working for others, including exclusivity clauses and non-compete terms.
A labor dispute at a facility in which workers have stopped work or been locked out, and where replacement workers might be sought.
A license under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-2 that would be needed to charge employee fees.

procedures: The Administrator reviews every employment application, offer letter, employment agreement, handbook, and training or orientation form before use. The review confirms that none contains a fee, deduction, liquidated damages clause, repayment obligation for training or placement, or restriction on outside work. The review date is recorded.

Human resources does not collect any fee from an applicant or employee, directly or through a deduction from pay. Costs of orientation, competency evaluation, background checks, ID tags, and required training are paid by the agency.

Human resources does not require an employee to repay costs, or pay damages, if the employee leaves. Any proposed change to employment contracts is sent to the Administrator and legal counsel before use.

Employment agreements permit employees to work for other employers or clients. Agreements may require employees to follow agency conflict-of-interest and confidentiality rules (see CR-03 and PER-08) but must not bar them from working for others.

Recruiting staff do not post job advertisements, interview for placements, or make job offers for the agency until registration with the Division of Consumer Affairs is in place. The Administrator confirms registration status in writing before the first recruiting activity (see GOV-02).
Intake staff do not offer services or sign a contract with a client or facility before registration is in place.
When a request for staffing comes from a facility, the intake staff member asks whether a strike or lockout is in progress. The answer is documented on the intake form.

If a strike or lockout is reported or suspected at a facility that is not under NLRB jurisdiction, no employee is scheduled to work there as a strike replacement. The Administrator is told the same day.

If a strike or lockout begins at a facility already served, the Administrator reviews the situation within one business day and withdraws agency employees from any assignment that would replace strikers. The Administrator documents the decision and tells affected clients and employees.

Staff who are asked to charge a fee, impose a restrictive contract, or staff a strike facility must refuse and report the request to the Administrator or Compliance Officer. Retaliation against them is prohibited.

If the agency ever decides to seek an employment agency license, the governing body must first approve it in writing, and no employee fee may be charged until the license is issued and this policy is revised.
The Compliance Officer reviews payroll records and employee contracts at least annually for any unauthorized deductions, fees or restrictive terms, and records the results.
Violations are corrected immediately. Any improperly collected fee is refunded in full to the employee within [NUMBER] business days, and the Compliance Officer documents the cause and fix.

responsibilities.duty: Approves employment documents, confirms registration before recruiting and decides on strike-related withdrawals.
Collects no employee fees and uses only approved contracts and forms.
Ask about labor disputes before accepting a facility assignment and never staff strike replacements.
Conducts annual audits of payroll and contracts and handles reports of violations.

documentation: Annual contract and forms review record
Payroll deduction audit
Written confirmation of registration status before recruiting or offering services
Intake form entries on strike or lockout status
Administrator decisions on strike-related assignments
Refund records for any improper fee
Employee reports of requests to violate this policy

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All clients (patients/employers) and their representatives, and all staff of [AGENCY NAME], including private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA and MLTSS clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows and can exercise his or her rights, and receives the information the State requires before and during services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats every client with dignity and respect and informs each client and representative of their rights and responsibilities in writing at or before the start of services. New Jersey's rule uses the term patient/employer for the home care consumer. We give the Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides at least 24 hours before services (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(b)-(c)). The client or representative receives a copy of the written plan of care and any revisions (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(h)). Medicaid and MLTSS clients are also told their MCO and State grievance and appeal rights, and we confirm the wording against the MCO contract. Our approach to person-centered planning and respect for the client's choices follows 42 CFR 441.301(c) for home and community-based services, and we do not discriminate on any basis protected by the ADA or other law.

definitions.definition: The term used in N.J.A.C. 13:45B for the home care consumer receiving services from the firm.
A person legally authorized, or designated by the client in writing, to act for the client.
The Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides.
The written plan prepared and signed by an appropriately licensed person after evaluating the client's needs, before placement.

procedures: At the intake visit or call, the intake staff member gives the client or representative the Client Rights and Responsibilities statement in the client's preferred language and in a format the client can understand (see CR-05). The staff member explains it verbally and answers questions.

The statement lists the client's right to: be treated with dignity and respect; be free from abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination; privacy and confidentiality; participate in planning care and to refuse care; receive services safely from qualified, identified caregivers; be told the rates and charges in advance; receive a copy of the plan of care; make a complaint without retaliation; and end services.

The statement lists the client's responsibilities: give accurate health and contact information; tell the agency of changes in condition, hospital admissions or schedule changes; provide a safe home environment; treat caregivers with respect; and pay for private-pay services as agreed.
The agency gives each client or representative the Consumer Guide at least 24 hours before services begin (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(b)-(c)). The delivery date and method are recorded (see CR-07).

If the client waives the 24-hour timing, the client signs a written waiver. The agency still provides the Consumer Guide before services begin and keeps the waiver for at least 2 years (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(d)).

Before placement, the licensed person who evaluates the client prepares and signs the written plan of care with his or her license designation (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(a)). The Health Care Practitioner Supervisor reviews it with the client or representative and gives a copy.
When the plan is revised, the Supervisor gives the client or representative a copy of the revision promptly, and records the date and who received it (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(h)).

The Supervisor tells the client of his or her right to take part in developing and revising the plan, to refuse a service, and to ask for a different caregiver. Refusals and requests are documented and any safety concern is passed to the Supervisor.

Medicaid and MLTSS clients are told in writing that they have grievance and appeal rights through their MCO and the State, and are given the MCO contact number. The intake staff member checks the wording with the current MCO contract and updates it when the contract changes.

The client or representative signs an acknowledgment that he or she received and understood the rights statement, Consumer Guide, plan of care and grievance information. If the client cannot sign, the staff member records the reason and a witness.
Caregivers are trained on client rights at orientation and each year (see PER-04). Caregivers wear the required ID tag while giving care (see CR-07).
Supervisors review client rights with the client at each 30-day contact and 60-day in-home evaluation (see SVC-05) and document any concerns.

Suspected rights violations are reported immediately to the Administrator, and abuse, neglect or exploitation is handled under SAF-01. The agency does not retaliate against a client or staff member who raises a concern.
The Administrator reviews the rights statement each year and after any change in State, MCO or program requirements.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the rights statement is current, delivered and followed, and handles rights violations.
Deliver the rights statement, Consumer Guide and grievance information and obtain acknowledgments.
Review the plan of care with the client, give copies of the plan and revisions, and check rights at each contact.
Respect client rights, wear the ID tag and report concerns.

documentation: Signed Client Rights and Responsibilities acknowledgment
Consumer Guide delivery record with date and method
Written waiver of the 24-hour timing, if any, retained at least 2 years
Plan of care and revisions with record of copies provided
MCO and State grievance and appeal rights notice
Record of rights discussions at 30-day and 60-day contacts

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All clients and representatives, family members and staff who make or receive a complaint at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give clients a clear and safe way to raise complaints and to make sure each one is acknowledged, investigated and resolved.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] welcomes complaints and grievances from clients, representatives and family members, about services, caregivers, billing or any other matter. We give every client our written complaint process at intake. Each complaint is logged with the date, the complaint, the investigation, the resolution and the response sent. We give external contacts: the Division of Consumer Affairs Regulated Business Section at (973) 504-6370, and the NJ Board of Nursing for aide conduct at 973-504-6430. For Medicaid clients, we also provide the MCO contact. No HCSF rule sets a complaint response deadline, so [AGENCY NAME] sets its own standard: a written acknowledgment within 5 business days. We will have our accreditor confirm that standard. No client or employee is retaliated against for making a complaint.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency, its services or its staff, made orally or in writing.
A complaint that is formally filed and requires a documented investigation and written response.
The agency record of all complaints, investigation steps and outcomes.

procedures: At intake, the intake staff member gives the client or representative the written complaint process. It names the person to contact ([COMPLAINT CONTACT NAME], [PHONE]), explains that complaints may be made orally or in writing, and states that there will be no retaliation.

The written process lists the external contacts: DCA Regulated Business Section (973) 504-6370 and regulatedbusiness@dca.njoag.gov; the NJ Board of Nursing (973-504-6430, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) for complaints about a certified aide's conduct; and, for Medicaid and MLTSS clients, the MCO member services number.
Any staff member who receives a complaint records it the same day and passes it to the Administrator or designee within one business day. Staff may not discourage or dismiss a complaint.
The Administrator or designee enters the complaint in the complaint log with the date received, complainant, client, nature of complaint, staff involved, and who received it.

The agency sends a written acknowledgment to the complainant within 5 business days of receipt, and records the date sent. If the complaint is received by phone, the staff member also confirms the details back to the caller.

Immediately, the Administrator reviews whether the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, injury or an immediate safety risk. If so, it is handled under SAF-01 and SAF-02 and the client is protected right away, for example by changing the caregiver.

The Administrator assigns an investigator who is not the person complained about. The investigator interviews the complainant, client, caregiver and Supervisor as appropriate, and reviews the plan of care, schedules, EVV records and notes.

If the complaint concerns a caregiver's conduct, the Administrator decides within 5 business days whether to suspend the caregiver from the client's case while the investigation continues, and documents the decision. Conduct that may violate the certification standards is reported as required (see REC-02 and SAF-01).

If the complaint concerns identification or the ID tag, the Supervisor verifies that the caregiver wore the required photograph tag showing name and certification level, and corrects any lapse (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(a)).
The Administrator finishes the investigation within [NUMBER] business days where possible. If more time is needed, the complainant is told the reason and the new date.

The agency sends the complainant a written response that states the findings, the action taken and how to contact the external agencies listed above if the complainant remains dissatisfied. A copy is placed in the complaint log, not in the personnel file unless discipline results.

If a complaint investigation shows that application information on file with DCA has changed (for example a change in managing agent or ownership), the Administrator reports the change to the DCA registration section in writing within 30 calendar days (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(c)). See GOV-03.

If the complainant is a Medicaid or MLTSS client, the Administrator also tells the client of the right to use the MCO and State grievance and appeal processes, and shares required information with the MCO care manager (see SVC-11).
The Compliance Officer reviews the complaint log quarterly for trends, and results are reported to the governing body and used in quality improvement (see GOV-06).
Complaint records are kept for at least [RETENTION PERIOD] years in a file separate from the clinical record.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees the complaint process, assigns investigators, decides on caregiver suspension and issues written responses.
Give the complaint process and external contacts at intake.
Record and report every complaint the same day and never retaliate.
Help investigate care-related complaints and correct the plan or assignment.
Review the complaint log quarterly for patterns.

Complaint log
Acknowledgment letters and dates
Investigation notes and evidence
Written response to the complainant
Quarterly trend reports
Records of changes reported to DCA, if any

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and business associates of [AGENCY NAME] who create, receive, use or disclose client information
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and security of client health information and to meet HIPAA requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] protects the confidentiality of all client information, whether in paper, electronic or spoken form. The agency is a HIPAA covered entity when it bills Medicaid electronically, and as agency policy we treat ourselves as a covered entity for private-pay clients too. We give each client a Notice of Privacy Practices and keep the signed acknowledgement. The agency names a Privacy Officer and a Security Officer.
