Aides may not post client information or photos on social media. Breaches are handled under the breach notification rules at 45 CFR 164.400-414. Client identity badges required by N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(a) show only the caregiver's name, certification level and photograph and never client information.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information, including name, address, diagnosis, care needs, schedules and payment information, in any form.
A health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard transactions such as Medicaid billing.
A person or company outside the workforce that handles PHI on the agency's behalf, such as a billing service or software vendor.
An impermissible use or disclosure of unsecured PHI that compromises its privacy or security, as defined at 45 CFR 164.400-414.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing a Privacy Officer ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]) and a Security Officer ([SECURITY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]). The same person may hold both roles in a small agency.

At or before the start of services, the intake staff member gives each client or representative the Notice of Privacy Practices, explains it, and asks for a signed acknowledgement. If the client declines or cannot sign, the staff member records the attempt and the reason (45 CFR 164.520).

Staff use or disclose PHI only as permitted by 45 CFR 164.502: for treatment, payment and operations, as the client authorizes in writing, or as required by law. Disclosures use the minimum information necessary.

Disclosures that need the client's written authorization (for example to family members who are not representatives, or for marketing) are made only after the client signs an authorization form. The authorization is kept in the client record.
Within 30 days, the Privacy Officer responds to client requests to see or get copies of their records, to ask for corrections, or to receive an accounting of disclosures, and documents the response.

Every new employee signs a confidentiality agreement and completes HIPAA privacy and security training at orientation, and annually after that. Training covers the Notice of Privacy Practices, minimum necessary use, social media rules and breach reporting (45 CFR 164.530).

Aides may not post, share or message any client information, photographs, videos, locations or care details on social media or personal messaging accounts. Violations lead to discipline up to termination.
Caregivers do not discuss clients in public places, with other clients or with people who do not need the information. Caregivers do not leave care notes or schedules where others can see them.

The Security Officer applies administrative, physical and technical safeguards under 45 CFR 164 Subpart C. These include unique user IDs, passwords and access limited by job role, encrypted devices, locked storage for paper records, automatic log-off, and prompt removal of access when employment ends.
Phones and tablets used for EVV or care documentation must be passcode-protected and may be remotely wiped if lost. Staff report a lost or stolen device to the Security Officer immediately.
The Security Officer conducts and documents a security risk analysis at least once a year and when systems change, and fixes the risks identified.
The agency signs a business associate agreement with every vendor that handles PHI, such as billing, EVV, payroll and software vendors, before any PHI is shared.

Any staff member who suspects a breach or improper disclosure reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the same business day. The Privacy Officer investigates and does a documented risk assessment.

If a breach of unsecured PHI is confirmed, the Privacy Officer notifies affected clients, and notifies HHS and others as required, within the deadlines in 45 CFR 164.400-414, and documents each notice and mitigation step. The Privacy Officer also consults the governing body and counsel.
The Privacy Officer keeps required privacy policies and documentation for at least six years and reviews this policy annually.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees the Notice of Privacy Practices, access and amendment requests, authorizations, breach investigation and notification.
Oversees technical, physical and administrative safeguards, risk analysis and device security.
Provides resources, enforces sanctions and signs business associate agreements.
Protect client information, complete training, avoid social media disclosure and report suspected breaches immediately.

documentation: Privacy and Security Officer designations
Signed Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgements
Client authorization forms
Confidentiality agreements and training rosters
Security risk analysis and corrective actions
Business associate agreements
Breach investigations, risk assessments and notices
Sanction records for violations

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All caregivers (Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides), health care practitioner supervisors, office staff and the Administrator, for private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and PPP clients
policies.purpose: To protect clients' money, belongings and legal affairs from loss, misuse and exploitation, and to keep caregivers within the tasks delegated by the supervisor and the compensation paid by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] prohibits caregivers from accepting gifts, loans, bequests or any add-on compensation from clients or their families. Caregivers are agency employees who perform only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7), and the agency's pay is their only compensation for care. Caregivers do not handle client cash, cards or accounts except under a written, documented errand procedure with receipts. Caregivers may not be named as agent, attorney-in-fact, executor or beneficiary by a client. Suspected financial exploitation is reported under SAF-01. The Medicaid PCA exclusion of family members and live-in aides (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(b) and (d)) is addressed in SVC-14.

definitions.definition: Money, goods, services, favors or anything of value offered to a caregiver by a client or the client's family, regardless of amount.
Any payment to a caregiver outside the agency's payroll, such as tips, cash for extra time or payment to work privately.
The written, supervisor-approved process under which a caregiver may purchase items for a client, with a signed authorization and receipts.
Improper use of a client's funds, property or assets, including theft, coercion, misuse of accounts or cards, and undue influence over wills or financial documents.

procedures: The Administrator or designee reviews this policy with each caregiver at hire (PER-04) and each year, and the caregiver signs an acknowledgment kept in the personnel record (PER-06).

The intake coordinator gives each client or representative a written statement at admission that caregivers cannot accept gifts, tips, loans, or bequests, or handle money except under the errand procedure. The statement is part of the service agreement (CR-06).
A caregiver offered a gift, tip or loan declines politely and tells the supervisor by the end of the shift. The supervisor records the offer in the client record.

If a gift is left behind or cannot be returned at the time, the caregiver reports it to the supervisor within one business day. The supervisor arranges return to the client or representative and documents the return.

A caregiver never accepts payment for extra hours or private work, and never offers to work for a client outside the agency. Any such request is reported to the supervisor, who addresses it under PER-02.
Caregivers do not borrow or lend money, property, vehicles or other items with a client, and do not sell or buy items from a client.
Caregivers do not use or keep client credit, debit or EBT cards, checkbooks, PINs or passwords, and do not access client accounts.

Errands involving client money are done only when the errand is included in the delegated tasks on the plan of care (SVC-04) and the client or representative signs an errand authorization stating the purpose and the amount given.

For each errand, the caregiver counts the cash with the client, buys only the authorized items, obtains an itemized receipt, returns change and receipt to the client, and has the client sign the errand log. Both the caregiver and the client sign.

The supervisor reviews errand logs and receipts at the 30-day contact (SVC-05) and resolves any discrepancy the same day it is found. An unexplained shortage is treated as a possible exploitation report under SAF-01.
The caregiver does not hold keys, valuables or documents of a client except as listed on a written key and property log signed by the client, and returns them at the end of service.

A caregiver does not witness, sign or help prepare wills, powers of attorney, trusts, deeds, beneficiary designations or joint accounts, and does not accept appointment as an agent or beneficiary. If a client mentions naming the caregiver, the caregiver declines and informs the supervisor immediately.
Any lost or damaged client property, or suspected theft, is reported by the caregiver to the supervisor immediately and documented on an incident report (SAF-02) within 24 hours.
A caregiver or other staff member who suspects financial exploitation, by anyone, reports it immediately to the supervisor and follows SAF-01. Reporting in good faith is never a basis for discipline.
The Administrator reviews errand logs, property complaints and exploitation reports quarterly for the QA program (GOV-06).
Violations result in discipline up to termination under PER-08. The Administrator determines whether other reporting is required under SAF-01 or REC-02.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the policy, investigates reports, decides on discipline and reports suspected exploitation under SAF-01.
Approves errand tasks in the plan of care, reviews errand logs and receipts at each 30-day contact, and documents declined gifts and property concerns.
Declines gifts and compensation, follows the errand procedure, never handles accounts or documents, and reports concerns immediately.
Gives clients the written notice at admission and confirms it is in the service agreement.

documentation: Signed caregiver acknowledgment in the personnel record
Client notice and service agreement acknowledgment
Errand authorization and errand log with receipts
Key and property log
Incident reports for lost property, theft or offers of gifts
Supervisor notes of gift declinations in the client record
Quarterly QA review summary

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, clients, applicants for service and job applicants of [AGENCY NAME]
federal: Title VI, Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d)
policies.purpose: To make sure every person is treated equally in access to services, to remove language and disability barriers, and to meet federal civil rights requirements and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in accepting clients, providing services, assigning caregivers or hiring on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, disability, marital or family status, or any other characteristic protected by law. [AGENCY NAME] provides qualified interpreter services and translations of key documents at no cost to the client, and makes reasonable accommodations for clients with disabilities. A nondiscrimination statement is posted in the office and given to clients. No state HCSF rule was located on this topic, so this policy rests on Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (the statute section has not been verified for this manual). Staff should confirm current requirements with counsel.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in care without help.

A person who is fluent in both languages, understands the terminology involved and is impartial. A client's family member or child is not used except at the client's informed request, and never in an emergency when another option exists.
Documents a client must understand to receive services, such as the service agreement, client rights, the grievance process, consent forms, privacy notice and the plan of care summary.
A change in policy, communication or service delivery that lets a person with a disability use the agency's services, unless it would be a fundamental alteration or undue burden.

procedures: The Administrator designates a nondiscrimination and language access coordinator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] unless otherwise named, and posts the coordinator's name and [PHONE] in the office and in client packets.
The agency posts a written nondiscrimination statement in the office and includes it in the admission packet and on the agency website.
At first contact, the intake coordinator asks the client's preferred language for spoken and written communication and any communication or access need, and records both in the client record.
If the client has limited English proficiency, the intake coordinator arranges a qualified interpreter, in person, by phone or by video, at no charge to the client, and records the interpreter used.

Staff do not require clients to supply their own interpreter. A family member may interpret only if the client requests it, understanding that a free interpreter is available, and the request is documented.

The agency provides key documents in the client's preferred language, in translated form or read aloud with an interpreter, and documents that this was done. Written translations are prepared at no charge.
The agency gives the client a notice that language assistance is free in the languages most commonly encountered in its service area.

The intake coordinator asks every applicant whether any disability requires an accommodation, such as large print, reading documents aloud, extra time or alternate formats, and documents the accommodation and who approved it.
The supervisor reviews accommodation requests within two business days. If a request cannot be met, the Administrator reviews it and tells the client in writing what alternative is offered.

The agency assigns caregivers based on qualifications, skills, availability and client needs. A client's language need may be matched with a caregiver who speaks the language only if the caregiver has been shown competent in that language.

The agency does not discriminate against a client based on payer source or diagnosis. If a referral cannot be served, the reason must be a documented capacity, geographic or level-of-care limit under SVC-02, not a protected characteristic.
Staff who observe or receive a discrimination complaint report it to the Administrator the same day. Complaints are handled under CR-02, with no retaliation against the person who complains.
The Administrator trains all staff on this policy at orientation and annually (PER-04), including how to request an interpreter.
The Administrator reviews language service use, accommodation requests and complaints at least annually in the QA program (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the coordinator, ensures interpreter and translation resources, investigates complaints and ensures no retaliation.
Asks about language and accommodation needs at first contact, arranges interpreters and records the needs.
Applies the language and accommodation needs in the plan of care and in supervisory contacts.
Use interpreters when needed, treat all clients with respect and report suspected discrimination.

documentation: Posted nondiscrimination statement and copy in the admission packet
Preferred language and communication needs in the client record
Interpreter use log
Record of translated or interpreted key documents
Accommodation requests and responses
Discrimination complaints and resolutions
Annual training roster
Annual QA review

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, billing staff, health care practitioner supervisors and the Administrator, for private-pay and Medicaid clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or representative receives a clear written agreement stating the rates, services, billing terms and rights before services begin, and that no prohibited fees are charged.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] enters into a written service agreement with each client or representative before services begin. The agreement states the hourly rate, minimum visit length, cancellation terms, services included and excluded, billing terms and the complaint process. It states that the aide is an agency employee and that the client may not hire the aide privately. [AGENCY NAME] does not charge a client or an aide a placement fee or liquidated damages unless it also holds an employment agency license under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-2 (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6). For Medicaid clients, no client payment is collected for authorized PCA hours, and the agency confirms the managed care organization's balance-billing rules in its provider agreement. [AGENCY NAME] does not offer services before it is registered as a health care service firm.

definitions.definition: The written contract between [AGENCY NAME] and the client or representative describing services, rates, billing and rights.
A client who pays [AGENCY NAME] directly rather than through NJ FamilyCare, an MCO or another public program.
Hours of Medicaid personal care assistant services that the State or the managed care organization has prior authorized for the beneficiary (see SVC-12).
A set sum charged to an employee or other party for breaking a contract term. This agency does not charge such sums in connection with employment (GOV-09).

procedures: The Administrator sets private-pay rates, the minimum visit length and cancellation terms in writing, and records the rates on the agency rate schedule dated [DATE]. The rate is set from local market checks. For reference, a 2025 national survey reported a New Jersey median of about $38 per hour for non-medical in-home care, but the agency's own rate is not set by that number.
The intake coordinator reviews the service agreement with the client or representative, using an interpreter if needed (CR-05), at least before the first visit. The client receives a copy.

The agreement lists the hourly rate, minimum visit length, any different rates for nights, weekends or holidays, cancellation terms and notice required, billing frequency, payment methods and late-payment terms.

The agreement lists the services included and excluded, and states that caregivers perform only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor and listed in the plan of care (SVC-01, SVC-04).
The agreement states that the caregiver is an employee of [AGENCY NAME], not of the client, and that the client may not hire or pay the caregiver privately (PER-02).

The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] charges no placement fee or liquidated damages to clients or caregivers and that any change in this policy would require an employment agency license (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6).
The agreement states how the client can raise a complaint, including the agency contact [PHONE], and the Division of Consumer Affairs contact for complaints about firms (CR-02).

For private-pay clients, the agency gives written notice of any rate change at least [NUMBER] days before it takes effect, and the client signs the revised rate schedule. Services continue at the old rate until the client acknowledges.

For Medicaid clients, the agreement states that no client payment is collected for authorized PCA hours. For reference, the fee-for-service PCA rate (T1019, 15-minute unit) is $26.68 per hour effective July 1, 2024 (NJ SPA 24-0013). Managed care rates are contracted and are not given to clients.

Billing staff confirm the balance-billing and client-liability rules in each MCO provider agreement before the first claim. They do not bill a Medicaid client for denied, reduced or unauthorized hours unless the provider agreement and the written agreement permit it.

Medicaid hours billed must not exceed hours authorized. The maximum is 40 hours per calendar work week, prior authorized, and unused units cannot be carried over (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8). Billing staff do not bill for unauthorized or non-covered services (GOV-07).
The client or representative signs and dates the agreement. If the client declines to sign, the intake coordinator documents the reason and the Administrator decides whether services can begin.
Billing staff issue invoices to private-pay clients at the stated interval with dates, hours, rate and total. The invoice is based on verified visit times from the timekeeping record (SVC-08).
Billing staff investigate any invoice dispute within five business days, correct errors and issue a credit or revised invoice, and record the outcome.
The Administrator reviews the service agreement template and rate schedule annually and after any change in law, MCO contract or agency practice (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Sets rates and terms, approves the agreement template, confirms no prohibited fees are charged and reviews billing disputes.
Reviews the agreement with the client or representative before services start and obtains signatures.
Bill only authorized and verified hours, confirm MCO balance-billing rules and handle invoice disputes.
Confirms that services listed in the agreement match the plan of care.

documentation: Signed service agreement and copy given to the client
Agency rate schedule with dates
Rate change notices and client acknowledgments
Invoices and payment records
MCO provider agreement billing rules file
Dispute log and outcomes
Annual agreement template review

policies.title: Consumer Guide Delivery and Caregiver Identification Tag
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, health care practitioner supervisors, scheduling staff and all certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or employer receives the Board of Nursing Consumer Guide before services begin and that every caregiver can be identified in the home.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives each patient or employer the New Jersey Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides at least 24 hours before services begin. The patient may waive the 24-hour timing in writing. The agency keeps the waiver for at least 2 years, and the guide is still given before services begin (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(b)-(d)). Every aide wears an identification tag at all times while giving care in the home. The tag shows first name or initial, full surname, 'Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide' or the equivalent certification or licensure level, and a photograph. Letters are equal in size and at least 1/4 inch, and the tag is at least as large as any other identification worn.

definitions.definition: The Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides that the HCSF must provide to each patient or employer.
A written statement signed by the patient or employer giving up the 24-hour advance delivery period. It does not waive delivery of the guide before services begin.
The photo badge worn by the aide showing name and certification level as required by N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(a).

procedures: The intake coordinator obtains the current Consumer Guide from the Board of Nursing and checks quarterly that the agency is using the current version. Printed copies and an electronic copy are kept ready for delivery.

At admission, the intake coordinator gives the Consumer Guide to the patient or representative, in print or another format the person can use, and notes the date and time of delivery and method. The guide is given at least 24 hours before the first scheduled visit.
The patient or representative signs a receipt stating the date and time the guide was received. The receipt is filed in the client record (REC-01).
Scheduling staff do not confirm a first visit until the intake coordinator has recorded delivery of the guide at least 24 hours in advance or a signed waiver is on file.

If a patient wishes to start sooner than 24 hours after delivery, the intake coordinator explains the guide, offers the full waiting time and, if the patient still wishes to waive, obtains a signed and dated written waiver.
The waiver states that the patient waives the 24-hour timing only, and that the guide will be provided before services begin. The guide is delivered before the aide begins any care.
Waivers are kept for at least 2 years from the date signed. The Administrator reviews the waiver file quarterly to confirm retention and that every waiver has an associated delivery record.

If the patient has limited English proficiency or a disability that affects reading, the intake coordinator follows CR-05 to give the content in a usable form while still providing the Board of Nursing guide.
Before an aide's first assignment, the Administrator or designee issues an identification tag after verifying active Board of Nursing certification (PER-01). A photograph is taken and attached.

The tag shows the aide's first name or initial and full surname, the certification level 'Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide' or equivalent, and the photograph. Letters are equal in size and at least 1/4 inch tall.
If any other agency badge or ID is worn, the aide ensures the certification tag is at least as large as that other ID.
Aides wear the tag in a visible location at all times while giving care in the home and show it when asked. An aide without a tag does not begin or continue a visit and calls the supervisor.
Lost, damaged or outdated tags are reported to the supervisor on the same day. A replacement is issued within [NUMBER] business days and a temporary tag is used meanwhile.
Supervisors check the tag during the in-home evaluation (SVC-05) and record whether it meets requirements. Corrections are made immediately.
Tags are surrendered at separation and are updated when a name or certification status changes. The Administrator keeps a tag log.

responsibilities.duty: Delivers the Consumer Guide at least 24 hours before services, obtains receipts and waivers and keeps the guide current.
Do not schedule a first visit before guide delivery or a waiver is documented.
Issues tags after certification verification, reviews waiver retention and tag compliance.
Checks aide tags during in-home evaluations and corrects non-compliance.
Wears the tag visibly at all times during care and reports a lost or damaged tag immediately.

documentation: Signed receipt for the Consumer Guide with date and time
Signed written waivers, retained at least 2 years
Tag issuance and replacement log with photograph on file
Supervisor in-home evaluation notes on tag compliance
Quarterly waiver file review

policies.title: Scope of Services: What Caregivers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: All certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides, health care practitioner supervisors, RNs, scheduling staff and intake staff
policies.purpose: To define the tasks caregivers may perform, to keep them inside the delegated plan of care and to prevent services that Medicaid PCA does not cover.
policies.policy: Aides perform only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor, and every delegated task is listed in the client's record (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(c) and (e)). For Medicaid PCA clients, [AGENCY NAME] does not provide or bill respite, stand-alone supervision, companionship, child care or babysitting, parenting tasks, services for mental-health-service needs, or needs that are not hands-on (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(c)). PCA services in places of employment or schools must not duplicate services provided under the ADA, IDEA or Section 504 (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(e) and (f)). Nursing tasks are performed only by an RN or under valid RN delegation under the New Jersey Board of Nursing's delegation rules. Aides do not perform tasks outside the plan, and any such request is escalated to the supervisor.

definitions.definition: A task the health care practitioner supervisor assigns to an aide, after confirming the aide is competent to perform it, and documents in the client's record.
Direct physical assistance with activities of daily living, such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, eating and mobility.
A task that requires the judgment or skill of a registered professional nurse and can be done by an aide only if properly delegated.
Watching or monitoring a client without hands-on assistance, which is not a covered PCA service.

procedures: The health care practitioner supervisor lists each delegated task in the plan of care before placement (SVC-04) and documents the delegation in the clinical record (REC-03). The aide receives a written task list for each client.
Before an aide performs a delegated task for the first time, the supervisor confirms and documents that the aide has demonstrated competence in that task (SVC-03).

Aides perform only tasks on the written task list. If a client, family member or other person asks for a task not on the list, the aide declines politely and tells the supervisor the same day. The aide does not decide by themselves.

The supervisor reviews the request within one business day, decides whether to add the task, and if added, delegates, checks competence and updates the plan under SVC-04. If the task is outside the aide's scope or the plan, the supervisor explains this to the client and records it.

Aides do not perform nursing tasks or procedures unless an RN has delegated them under the Board of Nursing's delegation rules and the delegation and competence check are documented. The agency's RN confirms the current rules before delegating.
Aides do not give or change medications except as allowed in SVC-06. Aides do not provide any care they have not been trained and cleared to perform.

For Medicaid PCA clients, intake staff and the RN confirm that the plan lists only covered hands-on tasks and hours. Respite, stand-alone supervision, companionship, child care or babysitting, parenting tasks, mental-health-service needs and non-hands-on-only needs are not provided or billed as PCA (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(c)).

If the client's only needs are among those not covered, intake staff tell the client or representative and refer them to other options, such as private pay or the care manager, and document the referral (SVC-02).

If PCA services will be given at a place of employment or school, the RN confirms that they do not duplicate services under the ADA, IDEA or Section 504 and documents the review (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(e) and (f)).

Light household tasks are provided only when listed in the plan and, for Medicaid clients, only within the authorized hours. Where two or more beneficiaries share a residence, hours are combined as required by N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(h) (SVC-12).
Aides do not perform tasks for other household members unless the plan allows it and the supervisor documents it. Aides do not run personal errands except under the CR-04 errand procedure.
Aides do not provide transportation unless the agency has approved it under SAF-07 and the plan lists it.
Aides report any refusal of a task, unsafe request or request for out-of-scope care to the supervisor right away. The supervisor documents the event and any change in the plan.

If an aide performs a task outside the plan, the supervisor reviews the event within one business day, takes corrective action including retraining or discipline, and decides whether an incident report is needed under SAF-02.
Supervisors check at the 30-day contact and 60-day in-home evaluation (SVC-05) that aides are performing only listed tasks, and record the result.

responsibilities.duty: Delegates tasks, confirms and documents competence, handles requests for new tasks and monitors scope at each contact.
Assesses needs, decides on nursing delegation under Board of Nursing rules and confirms PCA plan content is covered and non-duplicative.
Performs only tasks on the written task list and escalates other requests to the supervisor.
Screen for non-covered PCA needs and do not schedule services outside the plan.
Ensures scope training, reviews violations and approves corrective actions.

documentation: Plan of care with delegated task list
Documentation of each delegated task and competence check in the clinical record
Aide's written task list for each client
Records of out-of-scope requests and supervisor decisions
Nursing delegation documentation, if any
Review of non-duplication for work or school PCA
Supervisory visit notes on scope compliance
Incident reports and corrective actions

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, health care practitioner supervisors, RNs and the Administrator, for private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and PPP referrals
policies.purpose: To make sure each client is accepted only when the agency can safely meet the needs, is assessed by an appropriately licensed person before placement, and, for Medicaid clients, has the required certification and authorization.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts clients only after intake, eligibility screening and an assessment. Before placement, an appropriately licensed person evaluates the patient's needs and writes a plan of care (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(a)). For Medicaid PCA, the agency obtains the written physician or practitioner certification of need at the start of service and annually (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.4). The RN assessment and plan of care are completed at the start of service and no later than 48 hours after it (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5). The agency screens for settings where PCA is not reimbursable, including assisted living, nursing facilities, hospitals and adult day health (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(a)). For MLTSS, adults 21 and over are screened through the county Area Agency on Aging / ADRC, and eligibility is hands-on help with 3 or more ADLs. Income or asset limits are not quoted to families without verification.

definitions.definition: The written statement of a physician or practitioner that the beneficiary needs PCA services, required at the initial application and annually.
Managed Long Term Services and Supports, delivered through NJ FamilyCare managed care organizations.
The county Area Agency on Aging – Aging and Disability Resource Connection, which does intake and screening for adults 21 and over seeking MLTSS.
A licensed professional, such as a registered professional nurse, who is permitted to evaluate the patient's needs and prepare the plan of care under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9.
The assessment completed by a managed care plan for beneficiaries in managed care to set authorized PCA hours.

procedures: The intake coordinator records each referral on the intake form, including name, contact, referral source, payer (private pay, FFS PCA, MCO, MLTSS or PPP), living situation, setting, diagnoses, services requested, language and accommodation needs (CR-05), and requested start date.
The intake coordinator screens for service area and capacity. The coordinator confirms that the agency has an available aide and a health care practitioner supervisor (SVC-03) before accepting.

For Medicaid clients, intake staff screen the setting. If the person lives in or will receive services in an assisted living facility, nursing facility, hospital, adult day health setting or other excluded setting, PCA is not billed, and the intake coordinator explains this to the client and refers to other options (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(a)).

Intake staff check whether the proposed PCA is a family member or would live in the beneficiary's home. If so, the file is referred to the Administrator under SVC-14 before any scheduling. Family members are not covered PCAs, except under the Personal Preference Program (SVC-13).

Intake staff screen for needs that are not covered as PCA, such as respite, supervision only, companionship, child care, parenting tasks, mental-health service needs, non-functional diagnoses, acute short-term conditions or non-hands-on needs (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(c)), and refer or offer private pay under SVC-01.

For MLTSS, the intake coordinator confirms the person is 21 or older and has been screened through the county ADRC. Eligibility is hands-on help with 3 or more ADLs. The coordinator refers unscreened adults to the county ADRC. The coordinator does not quote income or asset limits to families unless verified with DMAHS or the ADRC.

For Medicaid PCA, intake staff obtain the written certification of need from the physician or practitioner before PCA services start and diary the annual renewal date (SVC-12). Services do not start without it.

For beneficiaries in a managed care plan, the intake coordinator confirms that the plan has completed the State PCA Assessment and authorized hours, and records the authorization number, hours, dates and care manager contact (SVC-11).

Before placement, an appropriately licensed person evaluates the patient's needs and writes the plan of care, signing it with their license designation (SVC-04). The level of care in the plan determines the aide placement.

For Medicaid PCA, the RN assesses the beneficiary and prepares the plan of care consistent with the certification of need, at the start of service and no later than 48 hours after it. The plan lists tasks, hours, goals and the beneficiary's strengths and family needs, and is dated and signed by the RN and the PCA (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5).
The first RN supervisory visit is started within 48 hours of the start of PCA service (SVC-05).

The RN also reviews the home setting for safety, equipment, pets, smoking and hazards, and notes risks for the caregiver (SAF-06). If the home cannot be made safe, the RN advises the Administrator before any placement.

If the needs exceed what a home care aide can safely provide, or require skilled care, the RN tells the client or representative and refers to an appropriate provider. The decision and reason are documented. The agency does not accept clients whose needs it cannot meet.
Before services start, the intake coordinator confirms that the client has received the Consumer Guide (CR-07) and signed the service agreement (CR-06) and the client rights notice (CR-01).
Intake staff open the clinical record with the intake form, certification, authorization, assessment and plan of care (REC-01, REC-03), and the Administrator signs off on acceptance.
If the agency declines a referral, the intake coordinator records the reason, which must be capacity, service area, level of care, payer or setting, and helps the person find other resources.

responsibilities.duty: Screens referrals, checks setting, payer and eligibility, obtains certification and authorizations and confirms required documents before start.
Evaluates needs and writes and signs the plan of care before placement. For PCA, completes it at start and no later than 48 hours after.
Confirms the aide placement matches the plan's level of care and arranges delegation.
Approves acceptance, decides on family-member or live-in referrals with SVC-14 and reviews declined referrals.

documentation: Intake form and referral source
Screening results for setting, eligibility and covered needs
Physician or practitioner certification of need and annual renewal date
MCO authorization and State PCA Assessment record
Signed and dated plan of care with license designation
Home safety assessment
Consumer Guide receipt, service agreement and rights notice
Record of declined referrals and reasons

policies.title: Health Care Practitioner Supervisor Designation and Delegation of Tasks
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, scheduling staff and all Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs) employed by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every CHHA placed by [AGENCY NAME] works only under the direction of a qualified New Jersey health care practitioner supervisor, performs only tasks that supervisor has delegated or directed, and has shown competence in each task, with every delegated task recorded in the client's record.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is registered as a Health Care Service Firm (HCSF) and places only actively certified CHHAs whom it employs (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). Each CHHA is supervised by a health care practitioner supervisor who is a New Jersey-licensed registered nurse (RN) or physician, designated to the Division of Consumer Affairs at registration. A New Jersey RN supervises the certified HHA and the program of care delivered (N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.2). An aide performs only tasks that the supervisor has delegated or directed. Before an aide performs a delegated task, the supervisor verifies that the aide has demonstrated competence in it. The supervisor documents every delegated task in the client's record. Delegation follows the nursing delegation rule referenced in N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.2 (N.J.A.C. 13:37-6.2). No task is delegated or directed unless it is within the scope of the aide's certification and the client's written plan of care. The rules set no required supervisor hours or caseload. [AGENCY NAME] sets and documents its own standard, described in this policy, and reviews it at least annually under GOV-06.

definitions.definition: The New Jersey-licensed RN or physician designated by [AGENCY NAME] to direct, delegate tasks to, and supervise CHHAs and the program of care.
The supervisor's assignment of a specific task to a specific aide for a specific client, after confirming the aide is competent to perform it.
A task the supervisor instructs the aide to perform as part of the plan of care.
A Homemaker-Home Health Aide certified by the New Jersey Board of Nursing and employed by [AGENCY NAME].
Observation by the supervisor (or a qualified designee under the supervisor's direction) that the aide can correctly and safely perform a task, documented before the aide performs it unsupervised.

procedures: Before registration is filed and whenever the supervisor changes, the Administrator designates a New Jersey-licensed RN or physician as health care practitioner supervisor and records the designation, name, license number and effective date in the governance file (see GOV-01).

The Administrator verifies the supervisor's license on the Board of Nursing online license lookup at hire, at each license renewal and at least once every 12 months. A dated screen print is kept in the supervisor's personnel file (PER-06).

If the supervisor's license is inactive, suspended, expired or restricted, the supervisor stops delegating immediately. The Administrator designates a qualified replacement the same day, notifies affected clients of any change, and reports the change to the Division of Consumer Affairs within the deadline in GOV-03.

The supervisor and Administrator set a written agency standard for supervisor availability and caseload. It covers the number of active clients and aides per supervisor, on-call availability, and a backup supervisor. The standard is reviewed at each annual policy review under GOV-05 and when client volume changes substantially.
Before assigning an aide to a client, the scheduler confirms through PER-01 that the aide is an agency employee with an active Board of Nursing certification.
The supervisor reviews the client's plan of care (SVC-04) and identifies each task the aide is to perform. The supervisor confirms each task is within the aide's certification and the plan.

For each task, the supervisor checks the aide's competence evaluation file (PER-04). If competence in a task has not been demonstrated, the supervisor observes the aide perform it, either in a skills lab or in the home, before the aide performs it unsupervised.
The supervisor records each competence demonstration on the Competence Verification Form, with the task, date, method of observation, result and supervisor's signature with license designation.

The supervisor delegates or directs tasks in writing on the Delegation of Tasks Record for the client. The record names the aide, the client, each task, any client-specific instructions, precautions and the date of delegation.
The supervisor reviews the delegated tasks with the aide before the first shift. The aide signs to acknowledge understanding and receives a copy of the task list for the home.

Delegations follow the nursing delegation rule referenced in N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.2 (N.J.A.C. 13:37-6.2). Before relying on any task delegation not already on the approved task list, the supervisor reviews the current text of that rule and Board of Nursing guidance and records the decision in the record.
The supervisor adds the delegated tasks to the client's clinical record the same day the delegation is made and never later than the first day of service (REC-03).

Aides must not perform any task that has not been delegated or directed and recorded. An aide asked by a client, family member or other person to do an undelegated task declines, explains that the task is outside the plan of care, and reports the request to the supervisor within 24 hours.

When the client's condition changes, the plan is revised, or a new aide is assigned, the supervisor re-reviews each delegated task, re-verifies competence as needed, and updates the Delegation of Tasks Record before the changed task is performed.
The supervisor may withdraw a delegation at any time for safety or competence reasons. The supervisor documents the reason, informs the aide and client, and arranges retraining or reassignment.

The Administrator audits a sample of client records at least quarterly to confirm that every task performed is delegated, that competence is documented, and that supervisor licensure is current. Findings go to the QAPI committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Designates and verifies the supervisor, sets the supervisor availability and caseload standard, and reports supervisor changes to the State.
Delegates and directs tasks, verifies aide competence before performance, documents each delegated task, and withdraws delegation when needed.
Performs only delegated or directed tasks, declines others, and reports requests for undelegated tasks and any difficulty performing a task.
Assigns only certified agency employees and confirms a current Delegation of Tasks Record exists before the first shift.
Reviews audit findings on delegation and competence documentation.

documentation: Supervisor designation record and license verification (dated screen print)
Written supervisor availability and caseload standard
Competence Verification Form for each aide and task
Delegation of Tasks Record in each client's clinical record
Aide acknowledgment of task list
Quarterly delegation audit results

policies.title: Plan of Care Before Placement and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, intake staff, scheduling staff and CHHAs of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that no client receives aide services before a licensed person has evaluated the client's needs and written a signed plan of care, that placements match the level of care in the plan, and that the plan is kept current and shared with the client.
policies.policy: Before placing a CHHA, [AGENCY NAME] has an appropriately licensed person evaluate the client's needs and write a plan of care. The preparer signs it with his or her license designation (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9). Placement matches the level of care in the plan. If the supervisor's inquiry shows the plan needs revision, a licensed person reassesses it immediately. The agency keeps the original and every revision and gives copies to the client or representative. For clients receiving Medicaid personal care assistant (PCA) services, the RN assesses the beneficiary and prepares a plan consistent with the physician or practitioner certification, at the start of service and never later than 48 hours after it begins (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5). The agency plan is also aligned with the managed care organization (MCO) plan of care for MLTSS clients.

definitions.definition: The written document, prepared by an appropriately licensed person after an evaluation of the client's needs, that states the services, tasks and level of care.
The type and intensity of care identified in the plan, to which the aide placement must correspond.
For Medicaid PCA, the RN's plan listing tasks, hours, goals and the beneficiary's strengths and family needs, dated and signed by the PCA and RN.
A Medicaid managed care organization that, for enrolled beneficiaries, completes the State PCA Assessment tool and authorizes hours.
A person legally authorized to act for the client or designated by the client to receive plan information.

procedures: At intake (SVC-02), the intake coordinator identifies the payer (private pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS or Personal Preference Program) and schedules the licensed evaluation before any aide is assigned.

A licensed person evaluates the client's needs at the client's residence and records the findings. For Medicaid PCA the evaluator is the agency RN. For clients in other programs, the evaluator is the supervisor or another person licensed to evaluate under state law.
The licensed evaluator writes the plan of care, which includes the client's needs, services and tasks, frequency and hours, level of care, safety precautions and client goals.
The preparer signs and dates the plan with his or her license designation (for example, RN). An unsigned plan is incomplete, and no aide is placed under it.
The scheduler confirms the plan exists, is signed, and states a level of care that matches the aide's certification and delegated tasks (SVC-03) before assigning any aide.

The scheduler places the aide only at the level of care in the plan. If the client needs a higher level of care than the plan or the aide's scope allows, the supervisor is notified immediately and services do not begin or continue until the plan is revised or the client is referred elsewhere (SVC-10).

For Medicaid PCA, the RN completes the assessment and plan at the start of service and never later than 48 hours after service begins. The plan lists tasks, hours, goals, and the beneficiary's strengths and family needs. The RN adds short- and long-term nursing goals. The plan is dated and signed by the PCA and the RN, and the RN reviews it with the PCA.

For MLTSS clients, the MCO completes the State PCA Assessment tool and authorizes hours. The RN obtains the MCO care plan and authorization, compares them to the agency plan, and resolves any difference with the MCO care manager before service begins. Contacts are documented (SVC-11, SVC-12).
The supervisor gives a copy of the original plan to the client or representative at or before the start of service. The client or representative acknowledges receipt in writing.

At each 30-day supervisory contact and 60-day in-home evaluation (SVC-05), the supervisor asks whether the plan is adequate. If the answer or any other information suggests the plan needs revision, the supervisor requests reassessment by a licensed person immediately.

A change in condition, hospitalization, new diagnosis, a change in authorized hours, a change in client goals, or a request for different tasks also triggers an immediate reassessment by a licensed person (see SVC-09).

The licensed person revises the plan, signs and dates it with license designation, and the supervisor informs the aide of changes and updates the Delegation of Tasks Record (SVC-03) before the aide performs any new task.
The agency gives a copy of every revised plan to the client or representative within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days of revision and documents the date and method of delivery.
The original plan and every revision are kept in the client's clinical record and are never discarded or overwritten (REC-01, REC-03).

If the plan is not being carried out properly, the supervisor takes corrective action immediately, including aide coaching, retraining, reassignment or revising the plan, and documents the action (SVC-05).

The Administrator audits a sample of new admissions each quarter to confirm that a signed plan existed before the first shift, placement matched the level of care, and copies were delivered. Findings go to QAPI (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Identifies the payer, schedules the licensed evaluation, and does not release a client for scheduling until a signed plan exists.
Evaluates the client, writes and signs the plan with license designation, and reassesses promptly when revision is needed. For Medicaid PCA, meets the 48-hour requirement.
Reviews plan adequacy at each contact, orders corrective action, and ensures aides are informed of plan changes.
Verifies the plan and level of care before placement.
Ensures copies are delivered to clients and audits plan compliance.

documentation: Original signed and dated plan of care with preparer's license designation
Each revision, signed and dated
Medicaid PCA plan signed by the PCA and RN
MCO care plan and State PCA Assessment tool results for MLTSS clients
Receipt acknowledgment for plan copies given to client or representative
Reassessment requests and corrective action notes
Quarterly plan audit results

policies.title: Supervision of Caregivers, 30-Day Contacts and 60-Day In-Home Evaluations
policies.applies_to: Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, agency RNs, Administrator and CHHAs of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To establish required supervisory contacts and in-home evaluations so that each client's plan is adequate and being carried out, and that problems are corrected immediately.
policies.policy: At least once in every 30-day period of service, the supervisor inquires whether the plan of care is adequate and whether it is being carried out, and records the responses (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9). At least once in every 60-day period of service, the supervisor makes an on-site, in-home evaluation of the plan. If the plan is not being carried out properly, [AGENCY NAME] takes corrective action immediately. For Medicaid PCA clients, the RN directly supervises the PCA in the home during the PCA's assigned time at least once every 60 days. The first visit is initiated within 48 hours of the start of service (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5). Additional visits are made for a new PCA, nurse delegation or changed needs. When more than one aide serves a client, the RN rotates visits until all aides have been assessed on each covered shift.

definitions.definition: A supervisor inquiry, made at least once in each 30-day period of service, into whether the plan is adequate and being carried out, with responses recorded.
An on-site visit to the client's home by the supervisor at least once in each 60-day period of service to evaluate the plan.
The RN's in-person supervision of the PCA in the home during the PCA's assigned time.
The span of days counted from the start of service, or the date of the last required contact, as set by the agency's tracking system.
Steps taken to bring service delivery into line with the plan, such as coaching, retraining, reassignment or plan revision.

procedures: On the start-of-service date, the scheduler enters the client in the supervision tracking log. The log calculates due dates for the 30-day contact, 60-day in-home evaluation and, for Medicaid PCA, the 48-hour first visit.

For Medicaid PCA clients, the RN initiates the first in-home supervisory visit within 48 hours of the start of service and observes the PCA during assigned time. The RN documents the date, time, observations and PCA competence.

The supervisor makes the required 30-day contact at least once in every 30-day period of service. The supervisor sets a target of [NUMBER OF DAYS] days after the prior contact so that the requirement is not missed.

During each 30-day contact, the supervisor contacts the client or representative and asks, at minimum: whether the plan is adequate, whether the aide is carrying out the plan and arrives on time, whether the client has any concerns or changes in condition, and whether the client wants any change in services.
The supervisor also asks the aide about the plan, the client's condition, and difficulties in performing the delegated tasks.
The supervisor writes down the responses on the 30-Day Supervisory Contact Form, signs and dates it with license designation, and files it in the clinical record the same day (REC-03).
If the 30-day contact shows the plan needs revision, the supervisor requests immediate reassessment by a licensed person (SVC-04).

The supervisor makes an on-site, in-home evaluation of the plan at least once in every 60-day period of service. During the visit the supervisor reviews the plan with the client, observes the home environment and aide performance when the aide is on duty, and reviews the aide's task records.

For Medicaid PCA clients, the RN's 60-day direct supervision visit occurs during the PCA's assigned hours so that the PCA is observed delivering care. The RN may combine this visit with the in-home evaluation of the plan if timing allows.
The RN adds visits beyond the 60-day minimum when a new PCA starts, when nurse delegation begins or changes, or when the client's needs change. The RN documents the reason for each added visit.
When more than one PCA serves a client, the RN builds a rotation schedule so that every PCA is observed on each covered shift, and records which PCAs and shifts remain to be assessed.

The RN or supervisor records the evaluation findings on the 60-Day In-Home Evaluation Form, including the plan's adequacy, whether it is being carried out, safety concerns, and follow-up actions, and signs it with license designation.

If the plan is not being carried out properly, the supervisor takes corrective action immediately, for example by coaching the aide at once, retraining, reassigning the aide, or revising the plan. The action, date and result are recorded.

If a client or representative cannot be reached for the 30-day contact, the supervisor makes at least three documented attempts on different days and times, tries an alternate contact, and informs the Administrator. Attempts do not replace the contact. The supervisor continues until it is completed.
The supervisor sends a weekly list of overdue or soon-due contacts and visits to the Administrator. The Administrator resolves any overdue item within 2 business days.
Supervision compliance rates, including timeliness of 30-day contacts, 60-day evaluations and Medicaid PCA RN visits, are reported to the QAPI committee at least quarterly (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Makes 30-day contacts and 60-day in-home evaluations, records responses and takes corrective action immediately.
Provides direct in-home supervision, meets the 48-hour first visit, adds visits as needed and rotates visits among multiple aides.
Maintains the supervision tracking log and alerts the supervisor to due dates.
Reviews the weekly overdue list and resolves lapses.
Cooperates with supervisory visits and reports plan concerns.

documentation: Supervision tracking log
30-Day Supervisory Contact Forms with recorded responses
60-Day In-Home Evaluation Forms
Medicaid PCA RN supervisory visit notes, including the first visit within 48 hours
Rotation schedules for multi-aide cases
Corrective action records
Quarterly supervision compliance reports

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, CHHAs, scheduling staff and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To limit aide involvement with medications to tasks that the supervisor has delegated and documented, to protect clients from medication errors, and to ensure that errors and refusals are reported promptly.
policies.policy: Aides at [AGENCY NAME] perform medication-related tasks only when the supervisor has delegated or directed them and recorded them in the client's record (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). The supervisor verifies the aide's competence before the aide performs the task. Permitted assistance is limited to reminders, opening containers, and reporting refusals or errors, unless a specific RN delegation under N.J.A.C. 13:37-6.2, referenced in N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.2, applies. Before any further medication task is delegated, the supervisor reviews the current text of that rule and Board of Nursing guidance. Aides do not set up, adjust or administer medications on their own initiative. The client keeps responsibility for his or her own medications. Medication errors and refusals are reported to the supervisor the same day and logged under SAF-02.

definitions.definition: The client takes his or her own medication, with the aide providing only the permitted support.
Verbally prompting a client to take medication at the time the client's prescriber has ordered, without selecting, measuring or giving the medication.
Any deviation from the prescriber's order that the aide observes or learns of, such as a missed or doubled dose, wrong medication or wrong time.
The client's decision not to take a medication.

A written delegation by the supervisor, for a named aide and client, of a medication-related task that is permitted under the nursing delegation rule referenced in N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.2 (N.J.A.C. 13:37-6.2).

procedures: At assessment (SVC-02), the supervisor asks the client what help, if any, he or she wants with medications, and records the client's medication list, prescriber and level of independence.
The supervisor decides whether any medication-related task is appropriate for delegation. If none is, the plan states that the aide does not assist with medications except to report concerns.
If a task is appropriate, the supervisor reviews the current text of N.J.A.C. 13:37-6.2 and Board of Nursing guidance, and confirms the task is within the delegation permitted for the aide.
The supervisor verifies the aide's competence for the specific task by observation before the aide performs it, and records the competence on the Competence Verification Form (SVC-03).
The supervisor documents each medication-related task in the Delegation of Tasks Record, naming the aide, client, task, medication-specific precautions and the date.
The aide may remind the client to take medications at the times prescribed, but may not choose which medications to take or how much.

The aide may open a container, such as a bottle, blister pack or pill organizer, only when the task is listed in the Delegation of Tasks Record. The client takes the medication and the aide does not place it in the client's mouth or hand unless the delegation specifically permits.
The aide does not fill, set up or adjust a pill organizer, change a dose or time, crush or split medications, administer injections, or apply or give any medication on the aide's own initiative.

The aide does not give advice on medications, does not give over-the-counter products, supplements or the aide's own medication, and does not accept a request from a family member or another person to do any of these.
If the client refuses a medication, the aide does not force or coax it, and tells the client that the supervisor will be informed. The aide calls the supervisor the same day.

If the aide notices or suspects a medication error, an adverse reaction, or a wrong or missed dose, the aide calls the supervisor immediately. If the client appears seriously ill, the aide follows SVC-09 and calls 911.
The supervisor assesses the situation and notifies the client's prescriber, representative or MCO care manager as needed, and records the response.
The aide enters the refusal, error or concern on the visit record and completes an incident report under SAF-02 before the end of the shift or by the next business day if the shift ends after hours.
The supervisor reviews the aide's medication-related activities at each 30-day contact and 60-day visit (SVC-05), and withdraws the delegation if the aide cannot perform the task correctly.
The Administrator reviews medication incident reports at least quarterly and refers trends to QAPI (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Decides what, if anything, may be delegated, verifies competence, documents each delegated task and responds to errors and refusals.
Performs only delegated tasks, never sets up, adjusts or administers medications independently, and reports errors and refusals the same day.
Ensures incidents are logged and reviewed, and that this policy reflects current Board guidance.
Routes after-hours medication calls to the on-call supervisor.

documentation: Client medication list and level-of-independence notes
Delegation of Tasks Record entries for medication-related tasks
Competence Verification Form
Visit record entries on refusals, errors and concerns
Incident reports (SAF-02)
Supervisor follow-up notes and prescriber or MCO contacts

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Scheduling staff, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, Administrator and CHHAs of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure that visits are staffed only by actively certified agency-employed aides, that Medicaid PCA hours stay within authorized limits, and that missed visits are handled quickly so clients do not go without care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] schedules only actively certified aides whom it employs (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). Certification status is verified before an aide's first shift and at each renewal. For Medicaid PCA, the maximum is 40 hours per calendar work week, prior authorized, and unused units cannot be carried over (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8). Medicaid PCA is also not reimbursable in certain settings and is not authorized for needs such as respite, stand-alone supervision or companionship (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8). The agency does not schedule such services under PCA billing. When a visit is missed, the agency notifies the client and the supervisor, sends a replacement aide, and escalates to the MCO if the client is in MLTSS. No rule sets a notice period, so [AGENCY NAME] applies the standard in this policy.

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that does not occur, or that starts more than [NUMBER OF MINUTES] minutes after the scheduled start without the client's agreement.
An actively certified, agency-employed aide who is delegated the client's tasks and assigned to cover a missed visit.
The recurring seven-day period defined by the agency for Medicaid PCA hours and payroll, applied consistently.
Approval of PCA hours from the State or the MCO before services are delivered.
Assigning consistent aides and ensuring there are no unplanned gaps in care.

procedures: Before the first shift and at each certification renewal, the scheduler or HR verifies the aide's Board of Nursing certification online and records the date and result (PER-01). The scheduler does not assign an aide whose certification is inactive, expired or unverified.
The scheduler confirms that the aide is an agency employee on the payroll, not an independent contractor or privately arranged worker (PER-02).
The scheduler confirms a signed plan of care (SVC-04) and a current Delegation of Tasks Record (SVC-03) exist before scheduling the client's first shift.
For Medicaid PCA clients, the scheduler enters the authorized hours and authorization dates from the State or MCO authorization and schedules no more than authorized.

The scheduler builds schedules so that no aide is scheduled for more than 40 PCA hours per calendar work week for a Medicaid PCA client. Any exception must be approved in writing by DMAHS or the Division of Developmental Disabilities, as applicable, before hours are scheduled. If unsure, the scheduler asks the Administrator before scheduling.
The scheduler tracks authorized units used each week and does not schedule or bill unused units in a later week, because unused units cannot be carried over.

The scheduler does not schedule PCA hours for settings that are not reimbursable, or for services PCA does not cover. The scheduler refers questions about unallowed services to the Administrator and the supervisor (SVC-12).
Where possible, the scheduler assigns a primary aide and a named backup aide who has been introduced to the client and has delegated tasks in place, to support continuity of care.

An aide who cannot make a shift calls the scheduler or on-call line at [PHONE] as soon as possible and at least [NUMBER OF HOURS] hours before the shift, except in an emergency, so a replacement can be found.
If the aide has not arrived or checked in by [NUMBER OF MINUTES] minutes after the scheduled start (or by the EVV exception alert, SVC-08), the scheduler calls the aide and the client.
If the visit will be missed, the scheduler tells the client or representative immediately and no later than [NUMBER OF MINUTES] minutes after discovery, and tells the supervisor.

The scheduler sends a replacement aide from the backup list. The replacement must be certified, agency-employed and, for clients with delegated tasks, cleared by the supervisor for the client's tasks.

If no replacement is available, the supervisor reviews the client's risk. If the client has urgent needs, the supervisor arranges alternative help, contacts the family or representative, and follows SVC-09 if there is danger to the client.
For MLTSS clients, the scheduler or supervisor notifies the MCO care manager of any missed visit not covered by a replacement, and of any pattern of missed visits, on the same business day.
The scheduler logs every missed visit with the reason, who was notified, the time of notification, whether a replacement was sent, and the outcome. The Administrator reviews the log weekly.
Missed-visit rates and causes are reported to the QAPI committee at least quarterly (GOV-06). The Administrator reviews the notice standard annually.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies certification and employment, schedules within authorization and the 40-hour limit, handles missed visits and logs them.
Clears replacement aides for delegated tasks and evaluates client risk when a visit cannot be covered.
Approves exceptions, reviews the missed-visit log and sets the notice standard.
Reports absence or delay promptly and follows the schedule.

documentation: Certification verification record for each aide
Client schedules and authorization tracking sheets (authorized hours, units used)
Written approvals for any weekly hours over 40
Missed-visit log
Notifications to clients, supervisors and MCO care managers
QAPI reports on missed visits

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: CHHAs, scheduling and billing staff, payroll staff, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that every Medicaid personal care visit is verified electronically as required by federal law, that billing and payroll rely on accurate time records, and that every correction to a time record is approved and documented.
policies.policy: Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) is required for Medicaid personal care and home health services delivered in the home (21st Century Cures Act §12006(a); 42 USC 1396b(l)). New Jersey's EVV aggregator is HHAeXchange. [AGENCY NAME] records the start and end of every Medicaid personal care visit through an accepted EVV method, which is the mobile app, landline telephone or FOB device. PCA is billed under code T1019 in 15-minute units. EVV also applies to self-directed services, other than live-in caregivers. The same time records support payroll, and time worked is paid in compliance with wage and hour law (PER-07; 29 CFR 552). Manual edits are allowed only under the exception rules and approval process in this policy.

definitions.definition: Electronic Visit Verification, the electronic capture of the date, time and location of service, the type of service, the client and the aide.
The State system, HHAeXchange, that receives EVV data from providers.
A small device kept in the home that generates a code to verify the visit start and end.
A change to the recorded time, date or other visit data made by agency staff after the visit, rather than captured automatically.
The procedure code used to bill Medicaid personal care assistant services in 15-minute units.

procedures: Before the first shift, the scheduler or EVV coordinator confirms that the client's visit is set up in the EVV system with the correct client, aide, service code (T1019 for PCA), authorized units and payer.

The agency assigns each aide a log-in or device and trains the aide on the accepted EVV methods (mobile app, landline telephone and FOB). Training is recorded in the personnel file during orientation (PER-04).

The aide checks in at the start and checks out at the end of each visit, in the client's home, using the method set up for that client. The aide does not check in or out before arriving or after leaving.
The aide records only time actually worked. The aide does not check in for another aide, does not share a log-in, and does not check in for a visit that did not occur.

If the EVV method fails (for example, no signal, device failure or dead battery), the aide calls the office at [PHONE] immediately and, at minimum, before leaving the home, so the start or end time can be documented.

The EVV coordinator reviews exception reports at least daily. Exceptions include late or missing check-ins, check-outs, duplicate visits, visits outside authorized time and units not matching the schedule.
The coordinator contacts the aide and, where needed, the client or supervisor the next business day to find out why the exception occurred and to confirm the hours actually worked.

Manual edits are made only when the cause is documented, for example device failure, a client's phone problem or an aide's missed check-out. A manual edit requires the aide's written or recorded explanation, a reason code in the system, and approval from the Administrator or designee before the edit is entered.

The coordinator does not make a manual edit to add time that was not worked, to fill gaps in authorized units, or to change times to match the schedule. The Administrator reviews any pattern of manual edits by an aide or a client and reports suspected falsification under GOV-07.
The EVV system retains the original captured data and a record of each edit, including who made it, when, and why. The agency does not delete original records.

Billing staff submit claims only for visits that have a verified EVV record or an approved, documented manual edit, and only within authorization. Staff do not bill units that were not delivered (GOV-07).

Payroll staff use the same visit time records, reconciled to aide time sheets for travel or other compensable time, to calculate pay, including overtime (PER-07). Aides must be paid for all time worked, even if EVV exceptions delay billing.

For self-directed services, the EVV coordinator confirms with the Personal Preference Program and fiscal intermediary which EVV method applies, and does not use EVV for a live-in caregiver where the State has excluded it (SVC-13).
The Administrator confirms with each MCO and with the State whether any EVV fees apply to providers, and records the answer in the payer file. No fee is assumed until confirmed.
The EVV coordinator runs a monthly comparison of EVV visits, billed units, payroll hours and authorizations, and reports discrepancies to the Administrator within 5 business days.
EVV compliance, exception counts and manual edit rates are reported to the QAPI committee at least quarterly (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Checks in and out accurately at the client's home, reports EVV failures immediately and never falsifies times.
Sets up visits, reviews exceptions daily, documents reasons and prepares manual edit requests.
Approves manual edits, investigates patterns, and confirms payer rules on EVV fees.
Bill only verified or approved visits within authorization.
Pay all time worked using reconciled time records.

documentation: EVV set-up records and aide training records
Daily exception reports and follow-up notes
Manual edit requests with aide explanation, reason code and approval
EVV system audit trail of original data and edits
Monthly reconciliation of EVV, billing, payroll and authorizations
Payer confirmations on EVV fees
QAPI reports on EVV compliance

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All caregivers (CHHAs), Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, schedulers and administrative staff serving private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and other clients
policies.purpose: To make sure that every emergency and every change in a client's condition is handled promptly and safely, that the right people are notified, and that the plan of care is reassessed and revised immediately when the client's needs change.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] places only actively certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides whom it employs, and those aides act only on tasks delegated or directed by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). In an emergency, the aide calls 911 first. After that, the aide notifies the supervisor, the client's representative and, for Medicaid clients, the MCO care manager. An aide reports any change in a client's condition to the supervisor the same day. The supervisor decides whether the plan of care needs reassessment. If it does, a licensed person reassesses it and the plan is revised immediately (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(e)). Aides do not diagnose, treat or perform tasks that have not been delegated, even in an emergency, except for calling for help and giving basic comfort and safety measures within their training. Every event is documented in the client record, and an incident report is filed under SAF-02.

definitions.definition: A situation that appears to threaten life, health or safety and needs immediate medical or public safety response, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, difficulty breathing, stroke signs, serious injury, a fall with suspected injury, a fire, or an intruder.

Any noticeable difference from the client's usual physical, mental, emotional or functional status, or in the client's home environment, that could affect the client's safety or the adequacy of the plan of care.
The licensed person designated by the agency to delegate tasks to aides, supervise them and oversee plans of care (see SVC-03).
The person the client has identified, or who is legally authorized, to receive information and make decisions for the client.

procedures: The aide's first action in any emergency is to call 911. The aide does not delay the call to contact the agency or the family.

While waiting for emergency responders, the aide stays with the client and gives only the basic comfort and safety measures covered in orientation (for example, staying calm, keeping the client from further harm, and following the dispatcher's instructions). The aide does not perform tasks that were not delegated.
The aide unlocks or opens the door for responders and gives them the client's medication list and emergency information sheet if available in the home.
As soon as the client is safe or care has been handed to responders, the aide calls the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, or the on-call supervisor after hours at [PHONE], to report what happened.
