The supervisor or designee notifies the client's representative and any emergency contact on file immediately after the emergency, unless the client has restricted that contact in writing.

For clients with NJ FamilyCare MLTSS or other managed care coverage, the supervisor or designee notifies the MCO care manager by the next business day, or sooner if the MCO requires, and records the call.

The aide reports every change in a client's condition to the supervisor the same day it is noticed. Examples include new confusion, falls, skin breakdown, a change in eating, drinking or toileting, new pain, medication concerns, signs of abuse or neglect, or unsafe conditions in the home. Reports that cannot be called in may be left by phone message and confirmed by the supervisor.
The supervisor documents each report in the client record on the day it is received, including who reported, what was observed, and when.
The supervisor reviews the report the same day and decides whether the client's plan of care needs reassessment. Where there is doubt, the supervisor reassesses.

If reassessment is needed, a licensed person evaluates the client's needs immediately and revises the plan of care, signed with the preparer's license designation (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(e)). The supervisor documents the reason for the revision.

For Medicaid PCA clients, the registered professional nurse notifies the physician or practitioner and the MCO care manager when the change may require a new certification of need or a change in authorized hours (see SVC-11 and SVC-12).
The supervisor re-delegates, changes or withdraws delegated tasks as needed, confirms that the aide is competent in any new or changed task, and records the delegation (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(d),(e)).
The supervisor gives copies of any revised plan of care to the client or representative and tells the aide and scheduler of the changes before the next visit (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(h)).
If the change in condition suggests abuse, neglect or exploitation, the supervisor follows SAF-01 in addition to this policy.
The aide or supervisor completes an incident report under SAF-02 for every emergency, fall, injury or other reportable event within the timeframe in that policy.
If the client is taken to a hospital, the supervisor notes the date and facility, holds services until a return-to-home plan is in place, and reassesses the plan of care before services resume.
The Administrator reviews emergency and change-in-condition events at least quarterly as part of the quality program (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Call 911 first in an emergency, stay with the client, report any change in condition to the supervisor the same day, and not perform tasks that were not delegated.

Receive reports, decide on reassessment, ensure a licensed person revises the plan immediately when needed, re-delegate tasks, notify the client representative and care manager, and document all actions.
Reassess and revise the PCA plan of care and notify the physician or practitioner and the MCO as needed.
Answer calls after hours, reach the on-call supervisor, and relay plan changes to the aide before the next visit.
Make sure on-call coverage exists, review events for trends, and ensure that incident reports are filed.

documentation: Dated, signed note of the emergency or change in condition in the client record
Record of notifications to the supervisor, client representative, MCO care manager and physician or practitioner, with date and time
Reassessment and revised plan of care signed with license designation, and proof copies were given to the client or representative
Delegation records for any new or changed tasks
Incident report (SAF-02)
On-call log

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, schedulers, intake and billing staff, and caregivers serving all clients
policies.purpose: To make sure services end in an orderly, safe and respectful way, that clients are never abandoned, and that the plan of care, records and referral information move with the client when care is transferred.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] discontinues or transfers services only for a documented reason and with written notice to the client or representative that states the reason and gives a transfer plan. The plan includes referral options and coordination of the transfer of the plan of care and records. The agency does not abandon a client. No New Jersey HCSF rule specifying a notice period was located, so the notice period in this policy is an agency standard. For Medicaid PCA clients, a transfer to a different provider agency also follows the Medicaid PCA transfer requirements in the NJ FamilyCare rules, which the Administrator confirms before any transfer is completed.

definitions.definition: The end of all services by the agency to a client.
The move of a client's services from the agency to another provider agency or setting.
Ending or reducing services at the request of the client, for loss of eligibility or payment, or because the agency can no longer safely serve the client.
Ending services without notice or a reasonable transfer plan, leaving a client without needed care.
The minimum written notice [AGENCY NAME] gives before ending services: 14 calendar days, except where an immediate safety threat requires a shorter period.

procedures: Any staff member who learns that a client wishes to end services, or that the agency may need to end them, tells the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor the same day.

The supervisor and Administrator review the reason. Reasons may include the client's choice, a move or hospitalization, goals met, change to a level of care the agency cannot provide, loss of authorization or payment, non-payment of private fees after notice, or a serious safety risk to the client or staff.
For client-initiated discharge, the supervisor confirms the request, the end date and the client's plans for ongoing care, and records them in the client record.

For agency-initiated discontinuation, the Administrator approves the decision in writing after the supervisor has documented the reason and the efforts made to resolve the problem, where resolution is possible.

The agency gives written notice to the client or representative at least 14 calendar days before the end date. A shorter notice may be given only where there is an immediate threat to the safety of the client or staff, and the reason is documented.
The notice states the reason, the last date of service, how to reach the agency, the client's right to file a grievance (CR-02), and the transfer plan.

The transfer plan lists referral options, including other registered HCSFs, the MCO care manager or county ADRC for Medicaid clients, and other community resources, and the supervisor reviews it with the client or representative.

For Medicaid clients, the supervisor notifies the MCO care manager and, where applicable, the physician or practitioner, before the end date so that authorized services can be moved to another provider with minimal gap.

Before any Medicaid PCA client is transferred to a different provider agency, the Administrator confirms the current Medicaid PCA transfer requirements with DMAHS or the MCO and the supervisor follows them. The date and source of the confirmation are recorded.

With the client's or representative's written authorization, the supervisor sends the receiving provider the current plan of care, relevant assessments and delegation information, medication and emergency information, and a summary of services, in line with CR-03.
Aides continue to provide services as scheduled until the end date unless safety requires otherwise. The scheduler confirms that no visits are cancelled without client notice.
The supervisor makes a final contact with the client or representative on or just before the end date to confirm that arrangements are in place and records any open concerns.
The agency gives the client or representative copies of the plan of care and any records they request, and returns any client property held (CR-04).
The billing office completes final billing, refunds any prepaid private-pay balances owed, and notifies the payer of the discharge date.
The supervisor writes a discharge summary in the client record stating the reason, date, condition at discharge, referrals made and records transferred.
The record is closed and retained according to REC-01. The Administrator reviews discharges and transfers quarterly as part of GOV-06.

responsibilities.duty: Approve agency-initiated discontinuations, confirm Medicaid transfer requirements, ensure notice is given and clients are not abandoned.
Prepare the transfer plan, coordinate with other providers and the MCO, send records with authorization, complete the discharge summary.
Keep visits in place through the end date and update the schedule after discharge.
Complete final billing, notify payers, and process refunds.
Report any client statement about ending services and continue care until the end date.

documentation: Written notice of discontinuation or transfer with reason and transfer plan, and proof of delivery
Documentation of the reason and any attempts to resolve the problem
Records release authorization and a list of items sent to the receiving provider
Notice to the MCO care manager and physician or practitioner where applicable
Confirmation of Medicaid PCA transfer requirements
Discharge summary signed by the supervisor
Final billing and refund record

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs and Payers (NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, registered professional nurses, intake, scheduling and billing staff, and caregivers serving Medicaid clients
policies.purpose: To make sure that services for NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS clients are authorized, delivered, supervised and billed according to program rules and the client's person-centered needs, and that the agency works with managed care organizations and the State in a coordinated and compliant way.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides Medicaid personal care assistant (PCA) services only with required physician or practitioner certification, a registered professional nurse (RN) assessment and plan of care, and prior authorization. MLTSS services are delivered through managed care organizations (MCOs). The agency obtains each MCO authorization and contracted rate in writing before services begin. The fee-for-service state plan rate for PCA is $26.68 per hour (code T1019, 15-minute unit), under NJ SPA 24-0013, effective July 1, 2024. MCO rates are contracted and are those in the written agreement. Once a client is enrolled in a managed care plan, the MCO completes the State PCA Assessment tool and authorizes hours (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5). Medicaid participation is optional and is not required for private-pay care. The agency follows federal home- and community-based services (HCBS) requirements for MLTSS, respecting client choice, privacy and community integration. The agency bills only for services actually delivered and documented, as required by federal law and GOV-07.

definitions.definition: New Jersey's Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program, administered by the Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services (DMAHS).
Managed Long Term Services and Supports, delivered through MCOs to eligible NJ FamilyCare members.
Managed care organization contracted with the State to administer NJ FamilyCare benefits.
Personal care assistant services: hands-on assistance with activities of daily living and related household tasks, delivered under a certification of need, plan of care and authorization.
The State's assessment instrument that the MCO completes for enrolled members to determine authorized PCA hours.
The county Aging and Disability Resource Connection, the Area Agency on Aging office that screens adults 21 and older for MLTSS.

procedures: Intake staff identify the client's payer at first contact (private pay, NJ FamilyCare fee-for-service, an MCO, or MLTSS) and record it in the intake file (SVC-02).
For a person who may qualify for MLTSS but is not yet enrolled, intake staff refer the person to the county ADRC and do not promise eligibility or hours.

Before accepting a Medicaid client, the Administrator confirms in writing that the agency is enrolled or contracted with the client's MCO or with the State as needed. Provider enrollment steps and fees are confirmed directly with the MCOs and the State, since these may change. The date and name of the contact are recorded.

Intake staff obtain the MCO authorization in writing, showing the service, number of hours or units, dates and the contracted rate, before the first visit. For fee-for-service clients, the agency uses the state plan rate of $26.68 per hour.
For fee-for-service PCA, the agency confirms that there is a current written physician or practitioner certification of need (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.4) before services begin (see SVC-12).
Where the client is enrolled in a managed care plan, the agency asks the MCO care manager to complete the State PCA Assessment tool and does not set authorized hours itself (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5).

The RN assesses the client and prepares the plan of care, consistent with the physician or practitioner certification, at the start of service and no later than 48 hours after it begins. The plan lists tasks, hours, goals and the client's strengths and family needs, and is dated and signed by the RN and the PCA (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5).

The RN directly supervises the PCA in the home during the PCA's assigned time, at least once every 60 days, with the first visit starting within 48 hours of the start of service. Extra visits are made for a new PCA, nurse delegation or changed needs. Where more than one PCA serves a client, visits rotate until each has been assessed on each covered shift (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5; see SVC-05).
The supervisor makes sure that aides are certified HHAs employed by the agency and that tasks are delegated and documented (SVC-03, PER-01).
The agency applies the service limits in SVC-12 and does not provide or bill services that exceed authorization.

The scheduler and billing staff compare each visit, as shown in electronic visit verification (SVC-08), against the authorization before billing. Visits outside the authorization are not billed to Medicaid.

The supervisor reports to the MCO care manager any change in condition, hospitalization, need for more or fewer hours, or inability to staff authorized hours, within one business day, and records the contact.
Clients are given their rights and the agency's grievance process, and are told they may contact their MCO or DMAHS with concerns (CR-01, CR-02).

The agency respects HCBS settings requirements for MLTSS clients by supporting the client's choice of services and daily routines, privacy in their home, visitors, and participation in the community, and does not restrict these without a documented, client-agreed plan.
Billing staff submit claims only for services delivered and documented, using correct codes and units, and do not bill both a private payer and Medicaid for the same service (GOV-07).
The Administrator reviews Medicaid authorizations, denials and billing corrections monthly, and refunds any overpayment promptly through the proper payer process.

responsibilities.duty: Confirm payer enrollment and contracts, approve acceptance of Medicaid clients, oversee billing compliance and refund overpayments.
Assess clients, prepare the PCA plan of care within 48 hours of start, and supervise PCAs in the home.
Coordinate with MCO care managers, ensure delegation and documentation, and report changes.
Identify payer, collect authorizations and certifications, and refer to ADRC or MCO as appropriate.
Schedule within authorization, verify visits through EVV, and bill only for documented, authorized services.
Provide only authorized, delegated services and record visits accurately.

documentation: Written MCO authorization with units, dates and rate; fee-for-service authorization where applicable
Physician or practitioner certification of need
State PCA Assessment tool results received from the MCO
RN plan of care dated and signed by the RN and PCA
RN supervisory visit records
MCO care manager communication log
EVV records and claims reconciliation
Provider enrollment and contract confirmation

policies.title: Medicaid PCA Certification of Need, Authorization and Service Limits
policies.applies_to: Administrator, registered professional nurses, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, intake, scheduling and billing staff, and caregivers serving NJ FamilyCare PCA clients
policies.purpose: To make sure Medicaid PCA services are provided only with a current certification of need and prior authorization and within the service limits set by NJ FamilyCare rules, so that clients receive covered care and the agency bills correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not begin Medicaid PCA services without a written physician or practitioner certification of need at initial application and again annually (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.4) and a prior authorization. Services are limited to a maximum of 40 hours per calendar work week, prior authorized. More hours are provided only where DMAHS or the Division of Disability Services (DDS) has approved an exception. Unused units cannot be carried over (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8). Where two or more beneficiaries live in one residence, the agency bills a combination of individual hands-on hours and group hours for household tasks. The agency does not provide or bill PCA services in excluded settings or for excluded purposes. Before finalizing task lists and authorization steps, the Administrator reads the current text of the other Medicaid PCA rules and confirms them with DMAHS or the MCO.

definitions.definition: A written statement by a physician or practitioner that the beneficiary needs PCA services, required at initial application and annually.
Approval of PCA hours by DMAHS or the MCO before the services are delivered.
The weekly period used to apply the 40-hour PCA limit.
Hours billed for household tasks that benefit two or more beneficiaries living in the same residence, as opposed to individual hands-on hours.
Settings in which PCA is not reimbursed, including assisted living, nursing facilities, hospitals and adult day health.

procedures: At intake, the intake staff member confirms that the client is a NJ FamilyCare beneficiary and requests the physician or practitioner certification of need. Services do not start until a written certification is in the file.
The intake staff member checks that the certification is signed and dated, and enters its expiration date (12 months from certification) in the tracking system with reminders at 90, 60 and 30 days.

The supervisor contacts the client, family and physician or practitioner at least 60 days before expiration to obtain a new certification. If the certification will lapse, the Administrator informs the MCO care manager and the client and services are not billed for any period without a current certification.
Intake staff obtain the written prior authorization before services start and record the authorized hours, effective dates and weekly limit in the client's scheduling profile.
The scheduler may schedule only up to the authorized weekly hours, and never more than 40 hours in a calendar work week for a client without a written DMAHS or DDS exception on file.

If a client needs more than 40 hours in a calendar work week, the supervisor refers the matter to the MCO care manager or DMAHS to request an exception and does not schedule the extra hours until the exception is approved in writing.

The scheduler does not carry unused authorized units from one period to another. If visits are missed, the supervisor reports the missed hours and cause to the care manager (SVC-07) and does not make up hours by billing for time not provided.

Where two or more beneficiaries live in the same residence, the supervisor identifies which tasks are individual hands-on tasks for each person and which are household tasks that benefit the group. Billing staff bill individual hands-on hours separately for each person and bill household tasks as group hours, and do not bill the same household time to more than one person.

Before starting care, the supervisor confirms that the client does not live in an excluded setting such as an assisted living facility, a nursing facility or a hospital, or attend adult day health during the hours to be billed. Hours are not billed for time the client is in an excluded setting.

The supervisor makes sure the plan of care contains only covered PCA tasks and does not include respite, stand-alone supervision, companionship, child care, parenting tasks, mental-health service needs, non-functional diagnoses, acute short-term conditions, or needs that do not involve hands-on care.

If a client or family asks for an excluded service, the aide declines, the supervisor explains that Medicaid PCA does not cover it, and offers private-pay or other referral options under SVC-01 and CR-06.
Billing staff do not bill any PCA service for a PCA who lives in the beneficiary's home, except as allowed under SVC-14.

Billing staff match each visit in electronic visit verification (SVC-08) against the authorization and the weekly limit before claims are released. Any visit outside the authorization is held for review by the Administrator.
The supervisor reviews each client's authorized hours against hours delivered every month and reports significant differences to the care manager.

Before finalizing the PCA task list and authorization steps, the Administrator reads the current text of the other Medicaid PCA rules on covered services and prior authorization, and updates this policy through GOV-05. The date of review is recorded.
The Administrator audits a sample of Medicaid PCA records each quarter for certification, authorization, limits and billing, and reports results to the quality committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure compliance with certification, authorization and limit rules, approve held claims, and keep this policy current.
Make sure plans contain only covered tasks, request exceptions through the care manager, and monitor hours.
Obtain and track certifications and authorizations.
Schedule within authorized hours and the 40-hour weekly limit, and flag excluded settings.
Bill only authorized, documented hours, apply individual and group hours correctly, and hold non-conforming claims.

documentation: Signed physician or practitioner certifications of need with expiration tracking
Prior authorizations and any written exception from DMAHS or DDS
Plan of care showing covered tasks and authorized hours
Records of individual and group hour allocation for shared residences
Weekly hours reports and claim reconciliation
Records of review of current Medicaid PCA rule text
Quarterly audit reports

policies.title: Personal Preference Program and Self-Directed Services Interface
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, intake and scheduling staff, and billing staff
policies.purpose: To explain how [AGENCY NAME] relates to the Personal Preference Program (PPP), in which the participant directs their own care, so that clients are given accurate information and a real choice and agency services are not confused with self-directed services.
policies.policy: In the Personal Preference Program, the participant hires and directs their own personal care assistant, and the participant, not the agency, is the employer. [AGENCY NAME] does not place aides for PPP and does not act as the employer, supervisor or payer of PPP workers. Unlike agency PCA, family members may be paid under PPP (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(b) makes this exception for PPP). Self-directed PCA is paid under the 1915(j) methodology described in NJ SPA 22-0005. The agency refers clients to the MCO care manager for PPP information and does not discourage any client from choosing PPP. Clients keep the right to choose between agency services and self-direction under federal HCBS rules.

definitions.definition: A New Jersey Medicaid self-directed option in which the participant hires, directs and manages their own PCA, supported by a fiscal intermediary and a care manager.
A model in which the participant, not an agency, is responsible for choosing, scheduling, training and supervising the worker.
The entity that handles payroll and related employer financial functions for self-directed workers. The research indicates that the fiscal intermediary is assigned by the MCO.
PCA services delivered by an agency employee, such as a CHHA employed by [AGENCY NAME], under an RN plan of care and agency supervision.

procedures: When a client or family member asks about self-directed care, or when intake finds a client who may prefer to hire their own worker, intake staff tell the client in plain language that PPP exists and that the MCO care manager can explain it.
Intake staff give the client the name and phone number of the MCO care manager, or help the client contact the care manager, and record that a referral was made.
No staff member discourages, delays or conditions agency services on a client's decision about PPP. Staff do not make statements that suggest PPP is worse, riskier or unavailable.
Staff explain the main difference accurately: under PPP the participant is the employer and directs the worker, while under agency PCA the agency employs, schedules, supervises and pays the aide.
Staff explain that family members may be paid under PPP, whereas agency PCA by family members is not covered except through the limited process in SVC-14.
The agency does not place, refer, recruit or schedule aides for PPP participants, and does not accept PPP funds as the employer of record.

If a client chooses PPP, the supervisor coordinates a safe transition with the MCO care manager, including an agreed end date for agency services, so that there is no gap in care. Discharge follows SVC-10.
With the client's written authorization, the supervisor shares the plan of care and relevant information with the care manager to support the transition.
If a client who is in PPP wishes to return to agency services, intake staff confirm the authorization and certification requirements in SVC-11 and SVC-12 with the care manager before services begin.

If a client uses both agency services and PPP for different hours, the supervisor confirms with the care manager how hours are authorized, and billing staff confirm that agency hours do not duplicate or overlap those of the PPP worker.
Billing staff do not bill the agency's PCA rate for any PPP service. Payments under the 1915(j) methodology are made through the self-directed program and not through the agency.
The agency respects each client's choice, and records the client's stated preference and the information given in the intake or supervision file.
Administrative staff are trained on this policy at orientation and when it is revised.
The Administrator reviews the policy annually, including for any change in PPP rules or the fiscal intermediary arrangements, and updates it through GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure that staff do not discourage PPP, that the agency does not act as a PPP employer, and that this policy stays current.
Give accurate information, refer clients to the MCO care manager, and record the referral.
Coordinate transitions to and from PPP with the care manager and share records with authorization.
Avoid scheduling or billing for PPP workers, and prevent duplication of hours.

documentation: Record of PPP information given and referral to the MCO care manager
Client's stated choice of service model
Transition plan and end date for agency services where applicable
Client authorization for sharing records
Staff orientation records on this policy

policies.title: Family Member and Live-In Caregivers under Medicaid PCA
policies.applies_to: Administrator, registered professional nurses, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, intake, scheduling and billing staff, and caregivers
policies.purpose: To prevent billing for non-covered family member and live-in PCA services, and to set out the narrow process by which the agency may ask for a case-by-case exception for a relative other than a spouse, legal guardian or parent of a minor.
policies.policy: Under N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(b), PCA services provided by a family member are not covered under agency PCA. There are no exceptions for a spouse, legal guardian or parent of a minor. For other relatives, an exception may be considered case by case, at the discretion of the DDS Director, when the agency requests it. If an exception is granted, the PCA must be a currently certified HHA, an employee of the requesting agency, and directly supervised by that agency's RN. The exception is renewed annually. Under N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(d), there is no reimbursement if the PCA lives in the beneficiary's home, except as provided in subsection (b) and in other applicable Medicaid PCA rules. [AGENCY NAME] does not bill Medicaid for services that are not covered under this policy. Family members remain free to use PPP, where the participant may hire family (see SVC-13).

definitions.definition: A relative of the beneficiary by blood, marriage or legal relationship. For this policy, spouses, legal guardians and parents of minors can never be paid PCAs under agency PCA.
A PCA who resides in the beneficiary's home.
Written approval, at the discretion of the DDS Director and on the agency's request, to use a relative other than a spouse, legal guardian or parent of a minor as a PCA.
Supervised in the home by the agency's registered professional nurse under N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.5 (see SVC-05 and SVC-11).

procedures: At intake, intake staff ask whether any person who wishes to provide care, or is already providing care, is a relative of the beneficiary or lives in the beneficiary's home. The answers are recorded in the intake file.

The agency does not hire a spouse, legal guardian or parent of a minor beneficiary to provide agency PCA services to that beneficiary. If asked, staff explain that these persons cannot be paid for PCA under any exception and offer information on PPP through the MCO care manager (SVC-13).

The agency does not assign any aide who is a family member of a Medicaid PCA beneficiary to that beneficiary, and does not bill Medicaid for such services, unless a written exception under this policy is in effect.

When another relative wishes to serve as the PCA, the Administrator and the RN review whether the relative is a currently certified HHA (PER-01), would be an agency employee (PER-02), would complete background checks and training (PER-03, PER-04), and can be directly supervised by the agency's RN.

If the requirements can be met, the Administrator prepares a written exception request, with the supporting information needed for the DDS Director, and sends it through the channel the State or MCO directs. A copy is kept in the client record.
The agency does not schedule or bill the relative as the PCA until the written exception is received. The scheduler records the exception dates and conditions in the scheduling profile.

If an exception is granted, the relative is hired as an agency employee and is subject to the same rules as other aides, including delegation, competency evaluation, supervision, EVV and payroll (SVC-03, SVC-05, SVC-08, PER-07).

The RN directly supervises the relative in the home at least once every 60 days, with the first visit within 48 hours of the start of service, and more often if needs change (SVC-05, SVC-11). The RN records each visit.

The Administrator tracks each exception's renewal date and submits a renewal request annually in advance of expiration. If renewal is not approved, the relative's PCA assignment for that beneficiary ends on the expiration date and the supervisor arranges another aide and notifies the client and the MCO care manager (SVC-10).

The agency does not bill Medicaid PCA for any PCA who resides in the beneficiary's home, except where a written exception under subsection (b) or another applicable Medicaid PCA rule allows it. The Administrator confirms the applicable rule in writing before billing in any such case.
The scheduler flags any aide whose address matches a client's address, and the Administrator reviews it before the aide is scheduled.
Billing staff review each claim for a Medicaid PCA client for any family or live-in indicator and hold it for the Administrator's review if one is found.

For private-pay clients, a family member who is an agency employee is subject to the same delegation, supervision and documentation rules as any other aide, and the agency does not bill Medicaid for those services.
The Administrator reviews all exceptions and any held claims quarterly and reports to the quality committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Decide whether to request an exception, submit and renew requests, and review all family and live-in billing questions.
Directly supervise any relative PCA in the home and document visits.
Screen for family and live-in relationships and record the answers.
Prevent assignment of family members or live-in aides without a written exception, and track expiration dates.
Hold and review any claim with a family or live-in indicator.

documentation: Intake screening record of family and live-in relationships
Written exception request and DDS Director's decision
Annual renewal requests and decisions
HHA certification verification and employment records for any relative PCA
RN supervisory visit records
Billing review notes for family and live-in claims

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, including Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs), health care practitioner supervisors, office staff, administrators and contractors, and all clients served under private pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and the Personal Preference Program (PPP)
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect and exploitation. To make sure every suspected incident is reported promptly to the correct authority. To make sure aides who are suspected of misconduct are removed from client contact, reported to the Board of Nursing and investigated.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, exploitation or mistreatment of any client. Every employee is a reporter. Any employee who suspects or witnesses abuse, neglect or exploitation of an adult must report it to the county Adult Protective Services (APS) program, as required by the New Jersey Adult Protective Services Act, and must call 911 if the client is in immediate danger. Suspected abuse or neglect of a child must be reported to the NJ Department of Children and Families (DCF) hotline. Employees do not need proof before reporting, and they do not need supervisor approval. Informing a supervisor never replaces the employee's own duty to report. The agency prohibits retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith. Suspected aide misconduct is also reported to the NJ Board of Nursing at 973-504-6430. The aide is removed from the client pending investigation. For Medicaid clients, the client's managed care organization (MCO) is notified. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7, an aide performs only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor. Any act outside delegated tasks that harms or exploits a client is treated as a possible incident of misconduct under this policy.

definitions.definition: Willful infliction of physical harm, pain, injury, unreasonable confinement, sexual contact without consent, verbal or emotional mistreatment, or intimidation of a client.
Failure by a caregiver to provide the care, supervision, food, hygiene, medication support or protection that a client needs and that the caregiver is responsible for providing.
Improper use of a client's money, property, benefits, identity or resources for the benefit of someone other than the client, including by an employee or family member.

The county program that receives and investigates reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults. County intake numbers are listed in the agency's Emergency and Reporting Contact List.
The managed care organization that coordinates a client's NJ FamilyCare or MLTSS benefits.

procedures: At hire and at orientation (see PER-04), each employee receives this policy, signs an acknowledgment that they are a mandatory reporter for this agency, and is trained on recognizing signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation. The training is repeated at least annually and documented in the personnel record.

The Administrator posts and distributes a current Reporting Contact List to every employee. It includes 911, the county APS intake number for each county served ([COUNTY APS INTAKE PHONE]), the DCF hotline ([DCF CHILD ABUSE HOTLINE NUMBER]), the Board of Nursing line (973-504-6430), and the on-call supervisor ([PHONE]).

Before publishing this manual and at least once each year, the Administrator confirms the Adult Protective Services Act citation, each county APS intake number and the DCF hotline number. The Administrator records the date and the person who verified them in the policy review log (GOV-05).

An employee who sees or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation of an adult calls 911 first if the client is in immediate danger. Otherwise, the employee reports to the county APS program as soon as possible and no later than the end of the shift.
An employee who suspects abuse or neglect of a child in the home reports it directly to the DCF hotline immediately.

After making an external report, the employee notifies the health care practitioner supervisor or on-call supervisor immediately, and no later than one hour after the report. The employee does not wait for a decision before reporting externally.

The supervisor makes sure the client is safe. This may include arranging a replacement aide, contacting the client's representative, and calling emergency services. The client is not left alone if unsafe.

If an aide is the suspected person, the supervisor removes the aide from the client's schedule immediately and keeps the aide off all client assignments pending investigation. The aide is told only what is necessary and is told not to contact the client about the allegation.

The Administrator reports suspected aide misconduct to the NJ Board of Nursing at 973-504-6430 and documents the date, time, person spoken to and any reference number. If the aide is an employee of another firm, the agency still makes the report on what it knows.

For a Medicaid client, the Administrator notifies the MCO care manager (or, for PPP, the program's designated contact) as the provider agreement requires. The Administrator confirms the MCO's notice timelines in the provider agreement and records them in the Reporting Contact List.

The Administrator, with the health care practitioner supervisor, opens an investigation file within one business day. The investigation includes interviews, review of EVV and timekeeping records (SVC-08), review of the plan of care and delegated tasks, and review of the aide's work history and background file (PER-03).
The agency cooperates fully with APS, law enforcement, the Board of Nursing and the MCO. Employees give truthful information and preserve records. No employee destroys, alters or withholds evidence.

The Administrator decides the outcome of the internal investigation, which may include retraining, discipline, termination, or a return to duty only if the allegation is unfounded and external authorities have not objected. The decision is documented in the investigation file.

The agency notifies the client or representative of the report and the outcome as appropriate to the client's privacy and the status of the outside investigation. It also makes sure the plan of care is reviewed by a licensed person if the client's needs have changed (SVC-04).
All reports, outcomes and corrective actions are logged in the incident log (SAF-02). Trends and repeat concerns are reviewed quarterly by the quality committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the proper authority directly, report immediate danger to 911, notify the supervisor, and cooperate with investigations.
Respond to reports, secure client safety, remove a suspected aide from assignments, document delegation and plan changes, and support the investigation.
Make Board of Nursing and MCO notifications, run investigations, verify contact numbers and statutes annually, ensure training and prevent retaliation.
Review investigation summaries and trends and make sure the agency has resources to protect clients.

documentation: Signed employee acknowledgment of mandatory reporter duty and annual training records
Reporting Contact List with annual verification dates
Written record of each external report (date, time, agency, person contacted, reference number)
Investigation file with interviews, findings and corrective actions
Record of Board of Nursing and MCO notifications
Entry in the incident log (SAF-02)

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees and all clients, including private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and PPP clients
policies.purpose: To make sure incidents involving clients, caregivers or the agency are reported quickly, reviewed, followed up and used to improve care and safety.
policies.policy: No state HCSF rule was located that sets incident categories or report deadlines. [AGENCY NAME] therefore sets its own standard. Any incident is reported verbally to the health care practitioner supervisor or on-call supervisor immediately and in writing within 24 hours. The client's representative is notified. For Medicaid clients, the MCO is notified as its contract requires. Every incident and its follow-up is recorded in the incident log and reviewed for trends under the Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement program (GOV-06). Where an incident shows that a plan of care is not being carried out properly, the agency takes corrective action immediately under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9, and where it shows a need to revise the plan, a licensed person reassesses it immediately.

definitions.definition: Any unplanned event that harms or could have harmed a client, caregiver or other person, or that affects the safety, rights, property or services of a client.
An event that did not cause harm but could have, such as noticing a hazard or catching an error before it affected the client.
An incident the agency is required by this policy to report to a person or agency outside the agency, in addition to internal reporting.
The agency's running record of incident reports, notifications, follow-up and closure.

procedures: Employees are trained at orientation (PER-04) and annually to recognize and report incidents. Training includes falls, injuries, medication errors or concerns, client behavior changes, hospitalization, missing client, unsafe home, property loss or damage, suspected abuse or neglect, caregiver injury, infection exposure, vehicle accidents, threats or violence, privacy breaches, and missed visits that cause risk.
Any employee who witnesses or learns of an incident first makes sure the client and others are safe and calls 911 if there is a medical emergency or danger (see SVC-09).
The employee reports verbally to the supervisor or on-call supervisor at [PHONE] immediately. The employee never delays a verbal report until the shift ends.
The employee completes the written Incident Report form within 24 hours. The form records who, what, when, where, witnesses, actions taken, who was notified and the client's condition.
The supervisor reviews the written report within one business day, confirms the client is safe, and decides whether a licensed person must reassess the client or revise the plan of care (SVC-04).

If the incident suggests the plan of care is not being carried out properly, the supervisor takes corrective action immediately. This may include retraining the aide, changing the assignment or revisiting delegation, and the supervisor documents it in the clinical record (REC-03).

The supervisor notifies the client's representative as soon as possible and in any case on the same day for incidents involving injury, medical treatment, abuse, neglect or exploitation, a missing client or property loss. The notification is documented.

For Medicaid clients, the supervisor or Administrator notifies the MCO care manager as the provider agreement requires. The Administrator confirms MCO timelines in each provider agreement and keeps them on the Reporting Contact List. For PPP clients, the supervisor notifies the program contact as applicable.

Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01. Aide misconduct is reported to the Board of Nursing at 973-504-6430 under SAF-01. Caregiver injuries are reported under PER-09. Privacy breaches are reported under CR-03.
The Administrator enters every incident in the incident log within two business days with its category, date, client and caregiver identifiers, notifications and follow-up actions.
The supervisor follows up on each incident until closure, and records the root cause and the corrective action. Serious incidents get a documented review within five business days.
The Administrator reports the incident log to the quality committee quarterly, including counts by category, trends by caregiver, client or location, and the status of corrective actions (GOV-06).
The quality committee makes recommendations for training, policy change or staffing, and the Administrator tracks them to completion.
Incident reports are kept apart from the personnel file and the client file, but a summary is placed in the clinical record if the incident affects care. Reports are retained under REC-01.
No employee is punished for reporting an incident in good faith.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure safety, report verbally at once, submit a written report within 24 hours, and cooperate with follow-up.
Review reports, take corrective action, notify the client's representative and MCO, request reassessment and document follow-up.
Maintain the incident log, make external notifications, confirm MCO timelines and report trends to the quality committee.
Analyze incident trends and recommend improvements under GOV-06.

documentation: Written Incident Report form
Incident log with category, notifications and closure
Record of client representative and MCO notification
Corrective action and reassessment documentation in the clinical record
Quarterly quality committee minutes showing incident trend review

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervisors and office staff who have contact with clients or client environments
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of infection for clients and employees by applying standard precautions, providing personal protective equipment (PPE), and responding to exposures and outbreaks.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] applies standard precautions in every client home. Standard precautions are part of the Board-approved aide training curriculum under N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.4 (2.00 hours in the recommended curriculum outline). The agency reinforces them at orientation and annually. The agency supplies PPE, trains employees on hand hygiene, and sets a glove and sharps procedure. Aides report any exposure to the supervisor at once. The agency follows current NJ Department of Health and CDC guidance for outbreaks and communicable disease. No HCSF-specific rule on infection control was found, so the agency uses these sources and its accreditor's standards. Occupational exposure to blood and other potentially infectious material is governed by the federal bloodborne pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, and by SAF-04.

definitions.definition: Basic infection control practices used for every client, including hand hygiene, PPE, safe handling of sharps and waste, cleaning, and respiratory etiquette.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection.
Contact with blood, body fluids or an infectious agent through the eyes, mouth, mucous membrane, broken skin, or a sharps injury.
An increase in cases of an infection that public health authorities identify as an outbreak or alert.

procedures: At orientation, the health care practitioner supervisor or designated RN trains each aide on standard precautions, hand hygiene, glove use, PPE selection, cleaning and disinfection, laundry, waste handling and sharps safety. Competency is observed and documented before the aide works alone (PER-04).
Training is repeated annually and whenever guidance changes. The Administrator records dates and content in the personnel record.

The agency supplies PPE at no cost to employees. Aides pick up supplies at [ADDRESS] or the supervisor arranges delivery. Aides tell the supervisor when supplies run low so the aide is not left without them.
Aides wash hands or use alcohol-based sanitizer when arriving, before and after glove use, before and after meals or personal care, after toileting care, and when leaving the home.

Aides wear gloves for contact with body fluids, wounds, soiled linen or non-intact skin, and change gloves between tasks and between clients. They wear masks, gowns or eye protection when splashes or respiratory illness make them necessary.

Aides place soiled disposable items in sealed bags. Aides do not recap, bend or break needles and do not reach into sharps containers. If the client uses sharps for self-administration, the aide only points out safe disposal and does not handle sharps beyond safe cleanup of a container and surrounding area, consistent with delegated tasks (SVC-01).
Aides clean and disinfect shared equipment and high-touch surfaces used in care with products appropriate for the surface.

Employees with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash or other symptoms of communicable illness must call the supervisor before the shift and not work until cleared under the agency's illness and return-to-work rules. The supervisor arranges coverage so the client is not left without services (SVC-07).
Employee health screening and TB requirements are handled under PER-05.
An aide who has an exposure washes the area immediately, reports it to the supervisor right away, and follows SAF-04 for evaluation and follow-up.
An aide who notices signs of infection in a client reports them to the supervisor the same day, and the supervisor follows SVC-09.

When the NJ Department of Health or CDC issues outbreak guidance, the Administrator reviews it within one business day. The Administrator communicates any changes in PPE, screening or visit procedures to employees and clients and documents the date.
The Administrator tracks infection-related incidents and exposures in the incident log (SAF-02) and reports them to the quality committee under GOV-06.

responsibilities.duty: Follow standard precautions, use PPE, report exposures and symptoms of illness, and keep supply needs known to the supervisor.
Train and observe competency, respond to exposures and infection concerns, and coordinate coverage.
Provide PPE, keep current with NJ Department of Health and CDC guidance, maintain training records and report trends under GOV-06.

documentation: Orientation and annual training records with competency checklist
PPE supply and distribution records
Exposure and illness reports
Record of guidance reviews and communications during outbreaks
Incident log entries for infection-related events

policies.title: Bloodborne Pathogens Exposure Control Plan
policies.applies_to: All employees with reasonably anticipated occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, including aides, supervisors and any staff who enter client homes
policies.purpose: To protect employees from occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens through a written exposure control plan, vaccination, training, and post-exposure follow-up that meets the federal OSHA standard.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written Exposure Control Plan, reviews it at least annually and updates it when tasks, procedures or technology change. The federal OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, governs the agency as a private employer. New Jersey's public-employee state-plan coverage does not extend to private agencies. The agency offers hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to employees with occupational exposure, provides confidential post-exposure evaluation and follow-up, trains employees at hire and annually, and keeps a sharps injury log.

definitions.definition: Reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials resulting from an employee's duties.
The written plan that identifies job classifications and tasks with exposure, the methods of protection, and the procedures for vaccination, training and post-exposure follow-up.
A cut or puncture from a contaminated sharp object such as a needle, lancet or broken glass.
Confidential medical evaluation and follow-up by a licensed health care professional after an exposure incident.

procedures: The Administrator and health care practitioner supervisor prepare the written Exposure Control Plan. It lists job classifications with exposure, tasks that cause exposure, methods of control (standard precautions, PPE, safe sharps handling, cleanup, laundry and waste), and the schedule for implementation.

The Administrator reviews the plan at least annually and whenever tasks change. The review includes asking employees who do the work for input about safer devices and methods, and the review is documented with the date.
Employees can read the plan at any time. The Administrator gives a copy within 15 days of an employee's request.

Before assignment, each exposed employee is offered the hepatitis B vaccine series at no cost, at a reasonable time and place, and within 10 working days of initial assignment unless the employee is already immune or it is medically contraindicated.
An employee who declines the vaccine signs the hepatitis B declination statement. The employee can change their mind later and receive the vaccine at no cost.

At hire and at least annually, the supervisor trains each exposed employee on the standard, bloodborne diseases, modes of transmission, the plan, PPE, vaccination, emergency response and the post-exposure process. Trainees can ask questions of a knowledgeable person. Training is documented with dates, content, trainer and attendees.

Employees use standard precautions as set out in SAF-03. They do not recap or bend needles, and they place sharps only in puncture-resistant, labeled containers. Contaminated laundry and waste are bagged and labeled or handled according to the plan.
After an exposure incident, the employee washes the site with soap and water or flushes eyes or mucous membranes right away. The employee reports to the supervisor immediately.

The supervisor sends the employee for confidential medical evaluation at no cost and as soon as possible, and records the route of exposure and circumstances. The supervisor gives the evaluating health care professional a copy of 29 CFR 1910.1030, the employee's job duties, exposure details and vaccination records.
With consent, the source individual is identified and tested for HIV and hepatitis B and C where legally permitted, and results are shared with the exposed employee according to law.

The agency obtains the health care professional's written opinion within 15 days of the evaluation and gives a copy to the employee. The written opinion states only whether hepatitis B vaccination is indicated and whether the employee received it, and that the employee was informed of results and need for follow-up.

The Administrator records every sharps injury in the sharps injury log, protecting the employee's privacy. The log notes the type and brand of device, the work area and how the incident occurred. The log is kept for five years.

The Administrator keeps confidential medical records for each exposed employee for the length of employment plus 30 years, and training records for three years. Records are kept separate from the general personnel file (PER-06).
The Administrator reports the exposure to the workers' compensation carrier and handles any claim under PER-09. The exposure is entered in the incident log (SAF-02).
The quality committee reviews exposure incidents at least annually and recommends safer devices or practices (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Follow the plan, use PPE and safe sharps practice, accept or decline vaccination in writing, and report exposures immediately.
Train employees, respond to exposures and arrange medical evaluation.
Maintain and annually review the plan, offer the vaccine, keep the sharps injury log and confidential records, and report to the insurer.
Provide vaccination, post-exposure evaluation and the written opinion.

documentation: Written Exposure Control Plan with annual review dates
Hepatitis B vaccination or signed declination for each exposed employee
Training records
Exposure incident report and post-exposure evaluation records
Healthcare professional's written opinion
Sharps injury log
Confidential medical records kept separate from the personnel file

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All clients, supervisors, caregivers and office and on-call staff
policies.purpose: To prepare for emergencies and disasters so that clients at risk continue to receive needed care or are safely connected to help, and so that staff know what to do.
policies.policy: No HCSF rule on emergency preparedness was located. [AGENCY NAME] therefore builds its plan to the standards of its accrediting body (GOV-04). At intake the agency ranks every client by risk, keeps an emergency contact list and a backup staffing plan, and plans for New Jersey hazards such as hurricanes and tropical storms, flooding, winter storms, extreme heat and power outages. MLTSS clients may have emergency requirements in the MCO contract, and the agency confirms those requirements in the provider agreement. The agency has a documented call-out procedure for clients and aides.

definitions.definition: An event that threatens the health or safety of clients or staff or the ability of the agency to deliver services, such as a severe storm, flood, power outage, fire or public health emergency.
A level assigned to each client (high, medium or low) based on how much the client depends on services, equipment or help to stay safe.
The steps used to contact clients, aides and supervisors during an emergency or when an aide cannot report.
The agency's method of finding substitute aides or other coverage when scheduled staff cannot work.

procedures: The Administrator and health care practitioner supervisor prepare a written Emergency and Disaster Plan based on the accrediting body's standards and the agency's service area. The plan lists hazards likely in the area and the steps for each.

At intake and assessment (SVC-02), the supervisor ranks each client high, medium or low risk. High risk includes clients who are bed-bound, dependent on electricity-powered equipment such as oxygen or a hospital bed, live alone with cognitive impairment, or have no one available to help.

The supervisor records the ranking, emergency contacts, medical conditions, equipment, medications list, evacuation needs, pets and preferred hospital in the client's record. The client or representative receives a copy of the emergency instructions.

The Administrator keeps a current client emergency contact list, sorted by risk, available to on-call staff at all times, including off-site, and updates it whenever clients start, stop or change risk.

The Administrator keeps a current aide contact list and a backup staffing plan. The plan identifies substitute aides by area and a process for assigning them. Aides who cannot reach a client must not leave the client unsafe.

For MLTSS clients, the supervisor reviews the MCO contract and any care management emergency plan and follows any MCO requirement. The Administrator documents the requirements and who the contacts are.

Before a forecast storm or other predictable event, the Administrator reviews the plan with the supervisors within 24 hours of the warning. Supervisors call high-risk clients to confirm needs, equipment, supplies and where the client will shelter, and document the contact.

The agency tells clients and aides how to reach the on-call supervisor at [PHONE]. Aides report to the supervisor when they are unable to work or travel because of conditions, and they do so before the shift starts if possible.

During an emergency, the on-call supervisor contacts high-risk clients first, then medium and low. The supervisor uses the backup staffing plan to cover visits and records any missed visit and the steps taken to protect the client (SVC-07).

Aides who are with a client during an emergency follow the client's emergency instructions, call 911 when needed, help the client move to safety only as their training allows, and stay with the client until the representative or emergency personnel take over if it is safe to do so.

If an aide cannot get to a client, the supervisor tries to reach the client or representative, tries a neighbor, family member or the MCO care manager, and requests a welfare check from local authorities for a high-risk client who cannot be reached.
After an emergency, the supervisor contacts every affected client, checks their condition, reassesses the plan of care if the client's needs have changed (SVC-04) and documents the contact.
The Administrator holds a debrief within 30 days after an actual emergency and an annual drill or tabletop exercise. The Administrator records the lessons learned and updates the plan.
The plan is reviewed at least annually and reported to the quality committee (GOV-06). Staff are trained on the plan at orientation and annually (PER-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the plan, contact lists and backup staffing plan, confirm MCO requirements, run drills and update the plan.
Rank client risk at intake, keep client emergency information current, contact clients before and after events and reassess plans when needs change.
Run the call-out procedure, coordinate coverage and document actions.
Follow emergency instructions, report availability, protect the client and call 911 when necessary.

documentation: Written Emergency and Disaster Plan with annual review dates
Client risk ranking and emergency information in each client record
Client and aide contact lists and backup staffing plan
Records of calls made before, during and after an event
Drill or debrief records
MCO emergency requirement notes

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervisors and office staff, and all client homes where services are provided
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from hazards in client homes, from violence and harassment, and from injury, and to ensure unsafe situations are reported and addressed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses home safety at intake and gives caregivers the right to leave an unsafe situation. A caregiver who leaves must report it to the supervisor immediately. The agency does not tolerate violence, threats or harassment against employees. Employees must report workplace violence and harassment, and the agency will not retaliate against anyone who reports. The agency trains aides in safe lifting and body mechanics (0.50 hours in the recommended curriculum outline). Workers' compensation applies to work injuries and is covered in PER-09. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7, aides perform only tasks delegated or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor, and aides do not have to perform any task that is not delegated or that they have not been shown to be competent to perform. Exposure to blood or body fluids is handled under SAF-03 and SAF-04 and 29 CFR 1910.1030.

definitions.definition: A review at intake of hazards in the home such as clutter, tripping hazards, lighting, stairs, smoke detectors, weapons, pests, unsafe pets, smoking and oxygen use, and household members who may pose a risk.
Any physical assault, threat, intimidation or abusive behavior directed at an employee while working, including by clients, family members, visitors or other employees.
Unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic or of a sexual nature that creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive environment.
Body mechanics, equipment and team methods used to move or position clients without injury to the client or the caregiver.

procedures: During intake and assessment (SVC-02), the health care practitioner supervisor completes a home safety assessment, including a review of hazards, equipment, pets, smoking, weapons, who lives in the home and any history of aggression. The supervisor documents it in the clinical record.

The supervisor tells the assigned aide about relevant hazards before the first visit and records the instructions in the plan of care or the caregiver assignment sheet. The supervisor asks the client or family to correct hazards where possible and records their response.

At orientation and annually, the agency trains aides on safe lifting and body mechanics, use of transfer aids, personal safety, de-escalation, recognizing aggression and sexual harassment, and how to report. The training is recorded (PER-04).

If an aide is asked to lift or transfer a client in a way that is beyond the aide's training, the plan of care or the available equipment, the aide declines that task and calls the supervisor. The supervisor reviews the delegation, ensures the aide is competent for each delegated task (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7), arranges equipment or additional help and updates the plan of care.

An aide who feels unsafe at any time may leave the home. An aide who leaves first makes sure the client is not in immediate danger and calls 911 if there is a medical emergency, and then reports to the supervisor or on-call supervisor at [PHONE] immediately.

The supervisor decides next steps right away, including arranging care for the client so there is no abandonment, reassigning the aide, contacting the client's representative, and requesting help from emergency services or APS when needed (SAF-01, SVC-09).

Employees report any workplace violence, threat, harassment or discrimination to the supervisor or Administrator immediately, verbally and then in writing within 24 hours. Employees may report directly to the Administrator, or the governing body if the Administrator is the subject of the report.

The Administrator investigates each report promptly, interviews those involved, takes action to prevent further harm (such as changing assignments, setting visit conditions or ending services under SVC-10 if needed) and documents the outcome. The agency does not retaliate against reporters.

If a client's or family member's behavior continues to be a risk, the supervisor reviews the plan of care, may require a second caregiver or changes in visit conditions, and may discharge the client under SVC-10 with proper notice and transition steps.

An employee injured on the job reports it to the supervisor immediately. The supervisor arranges medical care, completes an incident report (SAF-02) and notifies the Administrator, who files the workers' compensation claim under PER-09.
For exposure to blood or body fluids, the aide follows SAF-04. For vehicle use, SAF-07 applies.
Supervisors check in with aides who work alone in high-risk settings and, where needed, set up scheduled check-in calls or end-of-visit confirmations.

The Administrator reviews workplace violence and injury reports quarterly and reports trends to the quality committee (GOV-06). The committee recommends changes in training, equipment, staffing or client criteria.

responsibilities.duty: Follow safe work practices, decline tasks beyond their training or delegation, leave unsafe situations, and report hazards, violence, harassment and injuries immediately.
Complete the home safety assessment, brief aides, adjust plans, respond to reports and ensure client safety when an aide leaves.
Investigate reports, prevent retaliation, provide training and equipment, file workers' compensation claims and report trends.
Ensure resources for caregiver safety and review serious events.

documentation: Home safety assessment in the client record
Hazard briefing and plan-of-care or assignment sheet notes
Training records for safe lifting, personal safety and harassment prevention
Incident reports and investigation files for violence, harassment or injury
Workers' compensation first report of injury
Quarterly trend report to the quality committee

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All caregivers (Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides), Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, scheduling staff and the Administrator; private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and PPP-interface clients
policies.purpose: To protect clients and caregivers from the risks of vehicle transport, to keep the agency within the placement role it is registered for as a health care service firm, and to prevent billing for transportation that no payer has authorized.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is registered with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs as a health care service firm under N.J.S.A. 34:8-45.1 to place personnel for health care, companion or personal care services. Our default rule is that caregivers do NOT transport clients in any vehicle. Caregivers may not drive a client's vehicle, and may not use their own vehicle to carry a client, unless the Administrator has approved a written exception for that client and caregiver under this policy. Escorting a client on foot, on public transit, by medical transport arranged by the client or family, or in a taxi or ride-share is not 'transport' by the agency. Escort time is allowed only when it is a task in the client's plan of care and, for Medicaid clients, is authorized by the payer. The agency never bills a payer for transportation or travel time unless it is a covered, authorized service. Medicaid PCA services are limited by N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8, and the PCA tasks reimbursable under NJ FamilyCare are defined in the Medicaid rules for personal care assistant services. When the plan of care and authorization do not clearly cover a task, the caregiver does not perform it, and the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor decides.

definitions.definition: A caregiver driving a vehicle in which a client is a passenger, or a client being driven in a vehicle owned or controlled by the caregiver or the agency.
A caregiver accompanying a client who is traveling by another means (walking, public transit, taxi or ride-share, family or medical transport), where the plan of care includes accompaniment.
Liability coverage for the agency when employees drive their own or rented vehicles for agency business.
A written approval by the Administrator, after supervisor recommendation, allowing a named caregiver to transport a named client in a named vehicle for stated purposes.

procedures: Orientation (PER-04): The Health Care Practitioner Supervisor tells every new caregiver that transporting clients is prohibited unless a written exception exists. The caregiver signs an acknowledgment, which is filed in the personnel file.
Service agreement (CR-06): At intake, the intake coordinator tells the client and family that caregivers do not provide transportation, and records any request for transport in the intake record.
If a client, family member or referral source asks for transport, the caregiver does not agree. The caregiver reports the request to the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor the same day.

The supervisor reviews the request. If a need for escort or accompaniment is identified, the supervisor updates the plan of care (SVC-04) and, for Medicaid clients, checks whether the task is authorized (SVC-12). If it is not authorized, the supervisor tells the client what the client may do instead, such as other transport resources or care manager involvement under SVC-11.

If transport by a caregiver is requested as an exception, the supervisor sends the Administrator a written recommendation. It states the client, the caregiver, the purpose of each trip, the vehicle, and why no safer alternative exists.

The Administrator may approve an exception only after confirming that the driver has a valid, unsuspended New Jersey or otherwise valid driver's license, that the vehicle is currently registered, inspected as required and covered by liability insurance, and that the driver's motor vehicle record is acceptable under agency standards.

Before approving, the Administrator confirms in writing with the agency's insurer that hired and non-owned auto coverage applies to the proposed trips, and keeps the insurer's written confirmation. Without this confirmation, no exception is granted.

The client (or legal representative) signs a written consent to transport that identifies the driver, the purposes, the risks, and the client's right to decline at any time. The consent is filed in the client record. Verbal consent is not accepted.

The caregiver may not transport more than the persons named in the exception, may not make personal stops, and must make sure the client is seated and belted. Wheelchair transfers into a vehicle are performed only if the caregiver was trained and delegated that task under SVC-03.
Caregivers never drive a client's own vehicle and never lend, sell or rent a vehicle to a client or accept a vehicle from one (CR-04).

Transport is recorded in the visit note with date, start and end times, destination and purpose. No separate billing line, mileage charge or fee is charged to a private-pay client unless it is disclosed in the signed service agreement and rate schedule (CR-06).

The agency does not bill NJ FamilyCare, a managed care organization or any other payer for transportation or for time spent in a vehicle unless the Medicaid rules and the client's authorization cover it. Billing staff check the authorization before any claim is submitted (GOV-07).

Any vehicle crash, injury, or unsafe driving event involving a client is handled as follows: the caregiver calls 911 if anyone is injured, notifies the supervisor immediately, and the supervisor files an incident report under SAF-02 and notifies the insurer.

The Administrator reviews each approved exception every 90 days and ends it if the caregiver's license, the vehicle's registration or insurance lapses, if the need ends, or if any safety concern arises. Insurance confirmation is repeated at each policy renewal.

Violations of this policy are handled under PER-08 and may lead to discipline up to termination. The quality assurance committee reviews all transport requests, exceptions and incidents quarterly (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Approves or denies exceptions, confirms hired and non-owned auto coverage with the insurer, reviews exceptions every 90 days, and keeps insurer confirmations.
Teaches this policy, receives transport requests, updates plans of care for escort tasks, checks Medicaid authorization, and recommends exceptions in writing.
Does not transport clients without a written exception, refuses requests, reports them the same day, and reports crashes or unsafe events immediately.
Do not bill or schedule transportation unless it is authorized and documented.

documentation: Caregiver acknowledgment of the no-transport rule (personnel file)
Written exception request, recommendation and Administrator decision
Insurer's written confirmation of hired and non-owned auto coverage
Driver's license, registration and insurance proof for exception drivers
Signed client consent to transport
Visit notes recording any escort or transport
Incident reports for vehicle events (SAF-02)

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications, Board of Nursing Certification Verification
policies.applies_to: Human resources staff, the Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, scheduling staff and all Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs)
policies.purpose: To make sure that every caregiver placed with a client is a currently certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide, employed by [AGENCY NAME], and that no person with a lapsed, inactive or unverified certificate is scheduled for client care.
policies.policy: Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7, a health care service firm may refer or place only actively certified homemaker-home health aides whom it employs. [AGENCY NAME] places only aides who hold an active certificate issued by the New Jersey Board of Nursing and who are our employees. We verify the certificate directly with the Board before the first shift, track every expiration date, and remove an aide from the schedule on the day the certificate lapses or becomes inactive. An aide with an inactive certificate may not be scheduled until the Board has reactivated it and we have re-verified it. A person who is not certified, or whose certification is pending, is never placed, scheduled for client care, described to clients as certified, or given a caregiver ID tag as an aide. Certification requires completion of a Board-approved training program of at least 76 hours (60 classroom and 16 clinical) and clearance of the criminal history check required by N.J.S.A. 45:11-24.3 et seq. and N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.4. The agency relies on the Board's certification and verifies it. The agency does not certify aides itself.

definitions.definition: A Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide, certified by the New Jersey Board of Nursing.
A certificate that is current on the Board's records, not expired, inactive, suspended or revoked.
Checking certificate status directly on the Board of Nursing's online verification or by contacting the Board, not relying on a copy the applicant provides.
The agency's list of every aide with certificate number, issue and expiration dates, last verification date and employment status.

procedures: Recruiting: Job postings for caregiver positions state that an active New Jersey CHHA certificate is required for client placement. Recruiting and advertising begin only after the agency's HCSF registration is in place (GOV-02).
At application, HR collects the applicant's name as it appears on the certificate, the certificate number, the issue and expiration dates, and a copy of the certificate and a government photo ID.

Before any offer of placement, HR verifies the certificate on the Board of Nursing's online verification, confirming that the name matches, the status is active, and there is no discipline. HR prints or saves a dated screenshot to the personnel file. If the lookup is unclear, HR calls the Board Call Center at 973-504-6430 (Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.).

HR confirms that the applicant completed a Board-approved training program of at least 76 hours (60 classroom and 16 clinical) and keeps the training certificate or transcript. The Board's clearance of the criminal history check is evidenced by the issued certificate. The agency also runs its own checks under PER-03.
