The applicant is not scheduled for any client visit until the verification is complete, the criminal history and registry checks under PER-03 are complete, and orientation and competency evaluation under PER-04 are complete.

A person who completed training but has not yet been certified, or whose application to the Board is pending, may not be placed with clients. The agency does not describe such a person as a certified aide to clients or payers.
The aide must be hired as the agency's employee before placement (PER-02). HR does not place an individual who is working as an independent contractor.
HR adds each aide to the aide roster with certificate number and expiration date. The roster is the controlling record for scheduling.
Certificates are renewed every two years. HR sends the aide written reminders at 90, 60 and 30 days before expiration and notes the dates on the roster.

The aide must provide proof of renewal to HR before the expiration date. HR re-verifies directly with the Board and files the new verification. An aide may not work on or after the expiration date without verified renewal.

If a certificate lapses or becomes inactive, HR notifies scheduling the same day, and scheduling removes the aide from every client assignment. The supervisor arranges replacement coverage for affected clients (SVC-07). The aide may return only after the Board has reactivated the certificate and HR has re-verified it.
HR re-verifies the status of every aide on the Board lookup at least every six months and whenever the agency receives a complaint or report about an aide. Results are recorded on the roster.
Aides must tell HR within one business day of any Board notice, discipline, complaint, suspension or change in certificate status.

The Board application fee for initial HHA certification is listed in N.J.A.C. 13:37-5.5 (currently reported as $50, nonrefundable; HR confirms the current amount on the Board's website). The agency does not charge employees any fee in connection with employment (GOV-09). If the agency chooses to pay an aide's Board fee, it does so as an agency expense and does not recoup it from the aide.

If the agency operates its own training program, the program may not begin until the Board has approved it in writing, with no more than 30 students per instructor and clinical supervision by an RN at no more than 10 aides per RN. The Administrator confirms this requirement with the Board before any class starts.
The Administrator reviews the roster and the verification records monthly and reports exceptions to the quality assurance committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Collects certificate information, performs primary-source verification, maintains the roster and reminders, and notifies scheduling of lapses.
Schedules only aides shown as active on the roster and removes any aide on the day of lapse.
Arranges replacement coverage on lapse and confirms that verification is complete before delegating tasks (SVC-03).
Keeps the certificate current, gives proof of renewal before expiration, and reports Board actions within one business day.
Ensures verification is done before placement, reviews the roster monthly, and confirms current Board requirements.

documentation: Copy of certificate and photo ID
Dated Board verification printout for each aide, at hire and at each re-verification
Training program certificate or transcript showing at least 76 hours
Aide roster with certificate number, expiration date and last verification date
Renewal reminder log and proof of renewal
Record of removal from the schedule and reactivation, if any

policies.title: Aides Must Be Agency Employees; No Private Arrangements
policies.applies_to: Administrator, human resources, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, scheduling and payroll staff, and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To ensure that every aide placed by [AGENCY NAME] is the agency's own employee, that aides do not enter private side arrangements with agency clients, and that the agency never imposes fees or restrictive covenants prohibited for health care service firms.
policies.policy: Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7, we refer or place only actively certified aides that we employ. We do not use independent contractors, other staffing agencies or registries to supply aides. Every aide is an agency employee who is paid through agency payroll with required withholdings. Under the Board of Nursing's guidance, aides may not work privately for agency clients. Aides may not accept payment from a client or family for care, offer to work for a client outside the agency, or arrange for a client to leave the agency in order to hire the aide directly. Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6, the agency does not charge any fee or liquidated damages to an employee or in connection with employment, and does not use contracts that prevent employees from working for others. Because the agency is a third-party employer, it does not rely on the federal companionship or live-in exemptions, as 29 CFR Part 552 does not allow third-party employers to claim them. The agency's rule about private arrangements is a workplace conduct rule enforced through discipline. It is not a contract restriction.

definitions.definition: Any agreement, paid or unpaid, between an agency aide and an agency client, family member or representative for care or services outside the agency, or for services that bypass the agency's schedule, billing and supervision.
A worker engaged outside the employment relationship. The agency does not engage aides in this way.
A contract term that prevents an employee from working for another person or business.
An employer other than the individual or family receiving services, such as a home care agency.

procedures: Hiring: HR hires every aide as an employee on agency payroll. HR completes Form I-9, federal and state tax withholding forms and the employment documentation required under PER-09 before the first shift. The agency does not issue Form 1099 to aides.

The agency does not subcontract aide staffing to any other agency, registry or individual. If coverage cannot be provided by agency employees, the supervisor notifies the client and follows SVC-07 and SVC-10.

At orientation, each aide receives and signs this policy, which states that aides may not work privately for agency clients, may not accept payment from clients for care, and must report any request to do so.

The service agreement (CR-06) tells clients and families that agency aides cannot be hired privately while assigned by the agency and that payment goes only to the agency. This statement is also given in the Consumer Guide process (CR-07).

The agency does not require any employee to sign a non-compete or other contract that prevents working for others. HR checks every employment form, handbook provision and offer letter against this policy, and removes any such term.

The agency does not charge employees any fee, deposit or liquidated damages, including for training, background checks, uniforms, ID tags, orientation or termination. Payroll does not deduct such charges.

If an aide wants to work for another employer, the aide may do so. The aide may not serve an agency client privately, may not use agency client information for other employment (CR-03), and must not allow outside work to interfere with scheduled agency shifts.
Supervisors ask clients about private arrangements during the 30-day contacts and 60-day in-home evaluations (SVC-05), including whether the aide has asked for payment or offered private work.
Any employee, client or family member who learns of a possible side arrangement reports it to the Administrator immediately. The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports in good faith.
The Administrator opens an investigation within one business day. The Administrator interviews the aide, the client and the supervisor and reviews schedules, visit notes and payments.
While the matter is investigated, the Administrator may reassign the aide away from the client to protect the client and the agency.

If a side arrangement is confirmed, it is treated as a disciplinary matter under PER-08. Discipline is based on violation of this conduct policy and may include a written warning, suspension or termination.

The Administrator tells the affected client that services must continue through the agency or the agency will help with an orderly transition (SVC-10), and tells the client that private arrangements place the client outside the agency's supervision, insurance and Medicaid billing. The agency does not threaten the client.

If the agency suspects the aide took payment from a Medicaid client or billed a payer for private hours, the Administrator refers the matter to the compliance officer (GOV-07) and follows exploitation reporting in SAF-01 if needed.

Quarterly, the Administrator reviews payroll to confirm that all aides are paid as employees, that no contractor payments exist, and that no prohibited deductions are made (PER-07). Results go to the quality assurance committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures all aides are employees, investigates side arrangements, decides discipline, and removes any prohibited contract terms.
Hire all aides as employees, do not issue contractor payments or make prohibited charges, and keep signed acknowledgments.
Screens for private arrangements during client contacts and evaluations and reports concerns.
Does not accept private work from agency clients, does not accept payment from clients, and reports any request immediately.

documentation: Signed aide acknowledgment of this policy
Employment documents showing employee status for each aide
Review of offer letters and handbook confirming no restrictive covenants or fees
Client service agreement language on private hire (CR-06)
Side-arrangement reports, investigation notes and discipline records
Quarterly payroll review results

policies.title: Background Checks, Work-History Verification and Credential Registries
policies.applies_to: Human resources staff, the Administrator, the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor and every applicant or employee, including caregivers, office staff and supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure that no person with a disqualifying criminal history, an exclusion from Medicaid, or an unverified credential or work history provides care to our clients or has access to their records.
policies.policy: Under N.J.S.A. 45:11-24.3 et seq., all initial HHA applicants must undergo a criminal history background check, and the Board of Nursing will not certify an applicant until it determines that no disqualifying criminal history record exists in FBI or New Jersey State Police files. [AGENCY NAME] relies on that Board process for certified aides, but it also performs its own screening. The agency runs its own criminal history check for non-certified office staff and for the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, verifies each license or certificate status with the issuing Board before the first shift, checks Medicaid and federal exclusion lists for all staff before hire and monthly after that, and verifies work history. No person works with clients or has access to client records until these steps are complete and the Administrator has documented a decision to hire. Screening is applied consistently to all applicants and is carried out in line with applicable consumer reporting, anti-discrimination and fair hiring laws. The Administrator consults legal counsel on questions about how to evaluate a record.

definitions.definition: A criminal history record that, under the Board's determination for certified aides or the agency's written standard for other staff, bars the person from working in the position.

A list of persons barred from federal or state health care programs, including the HHS Office of Inspector General List of Excluded Individuals and Entities, the federal System for Award Management, and the State of New Jersey Medicaid exclusion and debarment lists.
Checking a license, certificate or exclusion status directly with the issuing source.
Contacting prior employers, schools or references to confirm the information on an application.

procedures: Application: Every applicant completes a written application that lists work history for at least the last five years (or all of it if less), explains any gaps, and includes a signed authorization for background checks and reference contact.
HR gives the applicant any disclosures and obtains any consent that applicable consumer reporting law requires before ordering a third-party report.

Certified aides: HR verifies on the Board of Nursing lookup that the CHHA certificate is active (PER-01). Because the Board does not certify until the criminal history check clears, an active certificate is evidence that the Board's check was completed. HR files the verification but does not treat it as the only check; the agency's exclusion and reference checks below still apply.

Non-certified staff and the supervisor: Before the first day of work, HR obtains a criminal history check for office staff, schedulers and the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor through a lawful method approved by the Administrator and agency counsel. HR keeps the result in a confidential file.

Practitioner supervisor license: HR verifies the supervisor's professional license or certificate on the issuing Board's lookup before the first shift, and re-verifies it at each renewal date and at least every six months (GOV-01, SVC-03).

Exclusion checks: Before hire, HR searches the HHS-OIG exclusion list, SAM.gov and the State of New Jersey Medicaid exclusion and debarment listings for every employee and applicable contractor. HR saves a dated printout. HR repeats this check monthly for all staff.

Any exclusion match stops hiring or, for current staff, removes the person from client contact and from billing the same day. The Administrator reviews it with the compliance officer (GOV-07). The agency does not bill any payer for services by an excluded person.

Work history: HR contacts at least two prior employers or references, preferably the most recent employer in health care or home care, and records dates, positions, reason for leaving and eligibility for rehire. If an employer will not respond, HR documents the attempts and obtains another reference.
HR reviews gaps in work history and any unexplained discrepancies with the applicant and documents the explanation.
HR confirms identity and the right to work in the United States (Form I-9) and checks that the name on the ID matches the Board verification.

HR records each completed check on a hiring checklist. The Administrator reviews the checklist, evaluates any adverse finding under the written standard, and signs approval before a start date is assigned. If a finding is adverse, the Administrator documents the reasoning, notes any individualized assessment performed under applicable law, and gives the applicant any notice the law requires.
The agency never lets a person start 'provisionally' while checks are pending. Scheduling is blocked until HR confirms completion.

After hire, an employee must tell HR within one business day of any arrest or charge, conviction, exclusion, Board action or license action. The agency may re-run checks at any time that law allows, and after a client complaint or a report of abuse, neglect or exploitation (SAF-01).
Background-check results are kept confidential, in a file separate from the general personnel file with access limited to HR and the Administrator (PER-06).
The Administrator reports completion rates for background checks, verifications and exclusion screening to the quality assurance committee quarterly (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Collects authorizations, runs and records all checks, completes the hiring checklist, repeats exclusion checks monthly, and blocks scheduling until clearance.
Sets the written screening standard with counsel, reviews results, makes and documents hiring decisions, and handles adverse findings.
Handles exclusion matches and any billing consequences (GOV-07).
Provide accurate information, consent to checks, and report arrests, convictions, exclusions or Board actions within one business day.

documentation: Signed application, authorization and disclosure forms
Board of Nursing verification printouts for aides and licensed staff
Criminal history check results (confidential file)
Dated exclusion list printouts at hire and monthly
Reference and work-history verification notes
Hiring checklist signed by the Administrator
Adverse-finding assessment and notices, if any

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual Training
policies.applies_to: Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, human resources, the Administrator and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure every aide is oriented to agency policies, has demonstrated competence in each task before performing it, and receives ongoing training and supervision.
policies.policy: Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7, an aide may perform only tasks delegated by or directed by the health care practitioner supervisor, and the supervisor must make sure that the aide demonstrates competence in each delegated task. [AGENCY NAME] therefore provides orientation to every new employee before the first client shift, and the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor evaluates and documents each aide's competence in each task before it is delegated. Completion of a Board-approved training program of at least 76 hours (60 classroom and 16 clinical) under N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.4 is a requirement for certification. It does not replace our orientation or competency evaluation. The Board's Training Book describes aide training as continuing through regularly scheduled agency in-services and RN supervision. No health care service firm rule fixes a number of annual training hours, so the agency sets its annual in-service standard at the level required by its accrediting body (GOV-04), and never below [ANNUAL IN-SERVICE HOURS] per aide per year. Training required by federal law, including bloodborne pathogens training under 29 CFR 1910.1030 and workforce HIPAA training under 45 CFR 164.530(b), is provided regardless of hours.

definitions.definition: Agency-specific instruction given before the first client shift.
Observed demonstration by the aide of a specific task, evaluated by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor against a written checklist.
Regularly scheduled agency training for current aides.
A task the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor has assigned to an aide for a specific client in the plan of care.

procedures: Before orientation starts, HR confirms that the aide's certificate has been verified (PER-01) and background checks are complete (PER-03).
Orientation is conducted before the first client shift and is led by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor or a designee. The content is documented on an orientation checklist.

Orientation includes at minimum: client rights and responsibilities (CR-01), grievances (CR-02), privacy and HIPAA (CR-03), abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting (SAF-01), incident reporting (SAF-02), infection control (SAF-03), bloodborne pathogens (SAF-04), emergencies and disaster plans (SAF-05, SAF-09's related content in SVC-09), electronic visit verification and timekeeping (SVC-08), scope of services and delegation (SVC-01, SVC-03), professional boundaries (PER-08), the caregiver ID tag and Consumer Guide (CR-07), and workplace safety (SAF-06).
Workforce HIPAA training required by 45 CFR 164.530(b) is completed and documented before the aide has access to protected health information.
Bloodborne pathogens training required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 is provided at the time of initial assignment, at no cost and during working hours, and repeated at least annually (SAF-04).

Competency: The supervisor evaluates each aide on a written skills checklist covering the tasks the agency expects aides to perform, such as personal care, transfers and positioning, hand hygiene, glove use, and safety. The supervisor observes the aide in a skills lab or in the home and rates each task as competent or not yet competent.

An aide is delegated only those tasks for which the aide has been rated competent. If the aide is not competent, the supervisor provides retraining and re-evaluates before delegation. The aide does not perform the task in the meantime.

Task-specific competency is repeated when a client's plan of care adds a task the aide has not been evaluated on, such as a particular transfer device. The supervisor demonstrates and observes in the home before the aide performs it alone (SVC-03).
The supervisor records every competency evaluation and every delegated task in the client's record (REC-03) and in the aide's personnel file, with the date, task and result, before the first shift.
The aide signs the orientation checklist and competency record. The signed documents go to the personnel file (PER-06).

Annual in-service: The Administrator and supervisor schedule in-services throughout the year. Each aide completes at least the hours set by the accrediting body and no fewer than [ANNUAL IN-SERVICE HOURS] hours per year. Topics include infection control, bloodborne pathogens, client rights, abuse reporting, HIPAA, safe handling, dementia care, emergency response and any topic arising from incidents or quality review.

HR tracks each aide's in-service hours on a training log and notifies the aide and scheduler 60 days before the anniversary date if hours are short. An aide who has not completed required training is not scheduled until the training is complete.
The supervisor re-evaluates each aide's competency at the 60-day in-home evaluation and at least annually thereafter (SVC-05), and whenever a complaint, incident or observation raises a concern.

If the agency runs its own aide training program, it does not start the program until the Board of Nursing has approved it in writing, and it follows the Board's rules on class size (no more than 30 students per instructor) and clinical supervision (an RN for no more than 10 aides) in N.J.A.C. 13:37-14.4. The Administrator confirms current requirements with the Board before starting.
The Administrator reports training completion rates and competency findings to the quality assurance committee each quarter (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Conducts orientation, evaluates and documents competency in every delegated task, retrains where needed, and records delegation in the client record.
Confirms pre-orientation clearances, tracks training hours and deadlines, and keeps training records.
Sets the annual in-service standard from accreditor requirements, ensures resources, and reviews completion rates.
Completes orientation and in-services, performs only delegated tasks for which competence has been shown, and asks for training when unsure.

documentation: Signed orientation checklist
Skills competency checklist for each aide and each delegated task, dated and signed by the supervisor
Task delegation entries in the client record
HIPAA and bloodborne pathogens training records
Annual in-service attendance logs and hours totals
Retraining and re-evaluation records
Board approval letter, if the agency operates a training program

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: Human resources staff, the Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisors and all employees who have contact with clients or client environments
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from communicable disease by screening employees before client contact, offering hepatitis B vaccination, and keeping health information confidential.
policies.policy: No New Jersey health care service firm rule located for this manual sets specific tuberculosis screening or health assessment requirements for home care employees. [AGENCY NAME] therefore adopts the standards of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for health care personnel, the requirements of OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030), and any additional requirement of its accrediting body (GOV-04), whichever is most protective. Every employee who may have client contact completes pre-employment health screening, TB screening and a hepatitis B vaccine offer or documented declination before the first client shift. Employee health information is confidential, kept separate from the personnel file, and used only for the purposes described here. The agency applies this policy consistently and in accordance with disability, medical privacy and leave laws. Employees with signs or symptoms of a communicable illness do not work with clients.

definitions.definition: A review of the employee's ability to perform the essential functions of the job, with or without reasonable accommodation, and of communicable disease risk, completed by a licensed clinician.
A symptom review and a TB test (an interferon-gamma release assay or a tuberculin skin test) as described in current CDC guidance.
A signed statement that the employee was offered the hepatitis B vaccine at no cost and declined it, with the right to accept it later at no cost.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious material during work (SAF-04).

procedures: Before the first client shift, HR gives each new employee the health screening form and TB screening instructions as a condition of assignment to client care, following the same process for all employees in the same job category.

The employee completes a health history and symptom review with a licensed clinician (employee's provider, occupational health clinic or agency-contracted clinic). The clinician states whether the employee can perform the essential functions of the job and whether any communicable disease concerns exist. The agency does not require details of diagnoses.

TB baseline: The employee completes a TB test (IGRA or TST) before client contact, with results documented as a number or reading and the date. An employee with a documented prior positive test provides the result and a clinician's review and symptom screen instead of a repeat test.

If a TB test is positive or the symptom review is concerning, the employee is evaluated by a clinician (including chest imaging as appropriate) and does not work with clients until a clinician documents that the employee is not infectious. The Administrator reports to and follows directions from the local health department as required.

After baseline, the agency follows current CDC guidance: an annual TB risk assessment and symptom review, and testing after a known exposure or when symptoms occur, rather than routine annual testing in the absence of exposure. If the accrediting body requires annual testing, the agency follows the stricter rule.

Hepatitis B: Within 10 working days of initial assignment, and at no cost to the employee, HR offers the hepatitis B vaccine series to every employee with a reasonable expectation of occupational exposure (SAF-04). The offer is made after bloodborne pathogens training.

An employee who declines signs the declination statement. If the employee later chooses to receive the vaccine while still covered, the agency provides it at no cost. The employee's records of vaccine dates are kept in the confidential medical file.

Other immunizations and screening required by CDC guidance or the accreditor (for example, influenza or COVID-19 recommendations, MMR and varicella immunity) are offered or checked according to a written schedule set by the Administrator with a clinician's guidance. Medical and religious exemption requests are handled as required by law.

Employees must not work with clients when they have fever, vomiting, diarrhea, an undiagnosed rash, a draining wound that cannot be covered, or symptoms of an infectious respiratory illness. They must call the scheduler or supervisor before their shift. The supervisor arranges coverage (SVC-07) and decides on return to work with the clinician's guidance. Sick leave rights under the agency's paid leave policy (PER-09) are explained.
Exposure incidents are handled under SAF-04. The employee receives immediate post-exposure evaluation and follow-up at no cost, and the incident is documented under SAF-02.

HR keeps health screening results, TB results, vaccination records and declinations in a confidential medical file separate from the personnel file. Access is limited to HR and the Administrator, and information is shared with supervisors only as needed for work restrictions or accommodations.
Medical records related to OSHA exposure are retained for the length of employment plus 30 years, as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030.
HR keeps a roster that shows only whether each employee is 'cleared' or 'not cleared', with the next due date, so that scheduling can check status without seeing medical details.
The Administrator reviews the roster monthly and reports compliance to the quality assurance committee each quarter (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Collects screening documents, offers hepatitis B vaccine, keeps the confidential medical file and clearance roster, and tracks due dates.
Adopts and updates screening standards from CDC and accreditor requirements, handles exposures and work restrictions, and reviews compliance.
Applies work restrictions and arranges coverage when employees are ill.
Completes screening, reports symptoms and exposures promptly, and stays home when ill.

documentation: Clinician's pre-employment screening clearance (confidential medical file)
TB test results, symptom screens and clinician follow-up
Hepatitis B vaccine offer, vaccination record or signed declination
Clearance roster (status and due dates only)
Work restriction and return-to-work notes
Exposure incident documents (SAF-02, SAF-04)

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME], especially Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs), and the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps a complete, accurate and confidential personnel record for every employee. The record must show that each aide holds active Board of Nursing certification, was screened, was shown to be competent for each delegated task, and was trained. It must be ready for review by a State surveyor, an accreditor or a Medicaid payer.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps one personnel file for each employee, and the file is complete before the employee's first client assignment. [AGENCY NAME] places and refers only actively certified CHHAs whom it employs (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7). The aide's file must therefore show current Board certification, and it must show competence in each task the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor delegates. The file also shows that the background check requirement for certification was met (N.J.S.A. 45:11-24.3 et seq.). Personnel files are confidential, are kept in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system, and are available only to those with a business need to know and to authorized surveyors. Federal Form I-9 documents and payroll records are kept as federal and state law require. No New Jersey HCSF rule was located that sets a personnel-record retention period. [AGENCY NAME] therefore keeps records for the longest period required by its accreditor, its Medicaid and managed care provider agreements, and applicable federal and state law.

definitions.definition: The set of records kept for each employee that documents hiring, qualifications, credentials, screening, training, competency, health clearance, and signed acknowledgments.
The record, signed by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, showing each task delegated to an aide and that the aide demonstrated competence in that task.
A dated copy of the Board of Nursing's online verification showing the aide's certification number, status and expiration date.

procedures: Human Resources ([HR MANAGER NAME]) opens a personnel file for each new hire on the day the offer is accepted and uses the personnel file checklist to track required items.
The file must contain the signed employment application, résumé or work-history information, and the interview or reference-check notes.

For each aide, HR places in the file a copy of the Board of Nursing certificate showing the certification number and expiration date, and a dated verification printout from the Board's online verification, taken before the first assignment (see PER-01).

HR files the criminal history background check results and the registry and work-history verifications described in PER-03, and the aide's attestation of no disqualifying history. These are kept in a restricted section of the file.
The file must contain a photograph of the aide for the identification tag required under CR-07, with a copy of the issued tag specification.

The Health Care Practitioner Supervisor places in the aide's file the signed competency evaluation and the delegation checklist. The checklist lists every task the supervisor has delegated and the date the aide demonstrated competence in it (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(d),(e)). The task delegation is also entered in each client's record (REC-03).
The Director of Training files orientation, in-service and annual training records (dates, hours, topics, instructor, attendance signature) (PER-04).
Employee Health files the TB screening results and other health screening documentation in a separate confidential health section of the file, not in the general personnel section (PER-05).

HR obtains and files signed acknowledgments at hire. These cover the policy manual, client rights, confidentiality, abuse reporting, professional boundaries, the prohibition on private arrangements, and the job description.
HR keeps a copy of the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor's current professional license and verifies its status on each renewal date (GOV-01, SVC-03).

HR keeps Form I-9 and its supporting documents in a separate I-9 binder or system, not in the general personnel file. Payroll keeps time and payroll records under PER-07 and retains them as federal and state wage-hour law require.

HR runs a monthly credential-expiration report. It sends a written 90-day, 60-day and 30-day reminder to each aide whose Board certification, TB clearance or other credential is approaching expiration. An aide whose certification lapses is removed from the schedule until active certification is verified and filed.

HR audits 10% of personnel files, and at least two files per month, against the checklist. It gives deficiencies to the Administrator and records the date each one is corrected. Results are reported to the Quality Assurance committee (GOV-06).

Only HR, the Administrator, the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor (for the staff they supervise), and authorized surveyors, accreditors or payers may view personnel files. Each employee may review their own file by appointment. Requests to copy health or background information are routed to the Administrator.

Before any destruction, the Administrator confirms the longest retention period required by the accreditor, each Medicaid or MCO provider agreement, and applicable federal and state law, and records the confirmation in the retention schedule. Records are destroyed only after that period and are shredded or securely erased. Destruction is logged.
When an employee leaves, HR completes a separation checklist, closes the file, and moves it to secure storage. The file is kept for the period set in step 14 and is not discarded earlier.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures complete personnel files, approves the retention schedule, and authorizes access and destruction.
Creates and maintains files, runs the credential-expiration report, performs file audits, and secures records.
Completes and signs competency and delegation checklists and keeps a current license copy on file.
Provides training records for each employee file.
Provide accurate documents, report credential changes promptly, and sign required acknowledgments.

documentation: Personnel file checklist for each employee
Board certification copy and dated verification printouts
Competency and delegation checklists signed by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor
Training, orientation and in-service records
Health and TB screening records (confidential section)
Signed policy and rights acknowledgments
Aide photo and ID tag record
Supervisor license copy and verification
I-9 and payroll records (separate files)
Credential-expiration report and file audit logs
Retention schedule and record destruction log

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: All hourly and salaried employees, including CHHAs, live-in and overnight caregivers, supervisors, office staff, and payroll personnel
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee at least the New Jersey minimum wage, pays overtime when it is due, pays for all compensable time (including travel between clients and orientation), and keeps accurate time and pay records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] pays all employees in compliance with the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and New Jersey wage and hour law, and applies whichever rule is more protective of the employee. For 2026, the New Jersey statewide minimum wage is $15.92 per hour for most employers and $15.23 per hour for employers with fewer than six employees under the small-employer schedule, as reported by the NJ Department of Labor and Workforce Development. The Administrator confirms which rate applies to [AGENCY NAME] each January and checks for any higher local ordinance. As a third-party employer of home care workers, [AGENCY NAME] may not claim the companionship or live-in overtime exemptions (29 CFR 552). Aides are therefore paid overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek. The agency's treatment of live-in and overnight shifts, including sleep and meal time deductions, must be confirmed with legal counsel before such shifts are offered. Time spent in orientation and required training, and travel time between clients during the workday, is paid working time. Time is tracked through Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) or the agency's timekeeping system. Off-the-clock work is prohibited. [AGENCY NAME] does not charge employees fees or deduct amounts not allowed by law (GOV-09).

definitions.definition: A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour periods) that [AGENCY NAME] designates in writing for overtime calculation: [WORKWEEK START DAY AND TIME].
The hourly rate of pay, including all required pay such as shift differentials and non-discretionary bonuses, used to calculate overtime.
An agency that employs the home care worker and places the worker with clients. Under 29 CFR 552 it cannot use the home care companionship or live-in overtime exemptions.
All time an employee is required or permitted to work, including client visits, orientation, required training, travel between clients during the workday, and administrative tasks.

procedures: Payroll ([PAYROLL MANAGER NAME]) sets each employee's base hourly rate at no less than the current New Jersey minimum wage that applies to [AGENCY NAME]. Payroll documents the applicable rate each January, after reviewing NJDOL guidance and any local ordinance.

The Administrator confirms at least annually, and whenever the minimum wage changes, that all pay rates (including Medicaid PCA, MLTSS and PPP-funded assignments) are at or above the minimum. The Administrator documents the confirmation.
HR classifies every position as hourly non-exempt unless legal counsel has confirmed in writing that an exemption applies. No CHHA or other direct-care aide is classified as exempt.
At hire, HR gives each employee a written notice of pay rate, pay day, and workweek, and an explanation of how to record time and report errors. The employee signs and a copy is filed (PER-06).
Aides record time through EVV or the timekeeping system at the start and end of each visit (SVC-08). Aides may not record time by estimate and may not work before clocking in or after clocking out.

Scheduling ([SCHEDULER NAME]) pays for travel between clients during the workday and tracks it in the timekeeping system. Travel between home and the first client, and from the last client to home, is handled according to the written travel pay rule approved by legal counsel.
Orientation and required training (PER-04), staff meetings, and in-service hours are paid at the employee's rate. Training hours are entered in timekeeping on the day of attendance.

Payroll reviews timekeeping data each pay period for missed punches, visits with no matching clock-in or clock-out, and edits. Payroll corrects errors with the employee and supervisor's written confirmation and keeps an audit trail of edits.

Payroll calculates overtime for all hours over 40 in the workweek at one and one-half times the regular rate. Scheduling reviews projected hours midweek and alerts the Administrator when an aide is approaching 40 hours.

Before any live-in or overnight shift is offered, the Administrator obtains and documents written guidance from legal counsel on how those hours are paid, including sleep time, meal breaks, and the agreement required with the employee. Until then, all hours on such shifts are paid as hours worked.
Payroll issues wage statements with each payment showing hours, rate, gross pay, overtime, and deductions, and pays on the regular pay day in compliance with New Jersey wage payment law.

Payroll makes only deductions required by law or authorized in writing by the employee as law permits. Payroll never deducts fees, liquidated damages, uniform charges or training charges that would violate GOV-09.

Employees who believe they were paid incorrectly report it to Payroll or HR. HR investigates within five business days, pays any amount found due on the next pay date, and documents the finding. Retaliation for raising a wage concern is prohibited.

Payroll keeps payroll and time records for the period required by federal and state wage-hour law and by the Medicaid and accreditor requirements. The Administrator documents the retention period in the retention schedule (PER-06).

Each year, the Administrator compares agency wage rates with the New Jersey median wage for home health and personal care aides (about $17.83 per hour per the O*NET figure used in the research) as a recruitment benchmark and records the comparison. The benchmark is not a legal wage standard.
Each quarter, the Quality Assurance committee reviews a sample of timekeeping and payroll records for compliance and reports findings to the Administrator (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures wage compliance, confirms minimum wage and local ordinances annually, and obtains counsel's guidance on live-in and overnight pay.
Calculates and pays wages and overtime, reviews time records, and keeps payroll records.
Schedules to avoid unplanned overtime, records travel time, and alerts management to overtime risk.
Classifies positions, issues pay notices, and handles pay complaints.
Record all time accurately, never work off the clock, and report pay errors promptly.

documentation: Annual minimum wage and local ordinance confirmation
Signed pay rate and workweek notice for each employee
EVV and timekeeping records, with edit audit trail
Payroll registers and wage statements
Overtime calculations and weekly hours reports
Written legal guidance on live-in and overnight pay
Pay complaint investigation log
Annual wage benchmark comparison

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees of [AGENCY NAME], including CHHAs, supervisors and office staff, and any contractors
policies.purpose: To set clear standards of conduct and professional boundaries so that clients are protected, caregivers work only within delegated tasks, and the agency's legal obligations for employment and placement are met.
policies.policy: All staff of [AGENCY NAME] behave professionally and keep a boundary between their role and the client's personal life. Staff may not accept gifts, loans or financial benefits from clients or their families, may not engage in financial dealings with them, may not contact clients through personal social media, and may not form personal, romantic or business relationships with clients outside the care relationship. Staff may not make private arrangements to work directly for a client (PER-02), because aides must be agency employees. Aides perform only the tasks delegated or directed by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor and listed in the plan of care (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(c)) and do not perform tasks beyond the plan. [AGENCY NAME] does not charge employees a fee or liquidated damages in connection with employment, and does not prevent employees by contract from working for others (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6); staff who raise concerns about such practices are protected from retaliation. Violations lead to discipline up to and including termination and, where applicable, a report to the Board of Nursing.

definitions.definition: The limit that separates the caregiver's professional role from the client's personal, family and financial life.
Any agreement under which an aide provides paid care to an agency client outside the agency's employment, billing and supervision.
Any service not delegated or directed by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor and not listed in the client's plan of care.

procedures: At hire and annually, HR reviews this policy with each employee. The employee signs an acknowledgment that is filed in the personnel file (PER-06).

Staff do not ask for or accept money, gifts, loans, tips, loans of property, or favors from clients or family. If a client or family member offers one, the aide declines politely, tells the client the agency does not allow it, and reports the offer to the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor the same day (CR-04).

Staff do not borrow from, lend to, shop with the money of, or hold, use or manage a client's cards, bank accounts, checks, PINs or passwords. Any errand involving client money follows CR-04 and the plan of care.
Staff do not name themselves as beneficiary, witness, executor or agent in a client's will, power of attorney or other legal or financial document.

Staff do not use personal social media or text messaging to connect with clients or their families, and do not post any client information, photos or care details online (CR-03). Contact goes through agency-approved channels.
Staff do not start romantic, sexual or other personal relationships with clients. Staff do not take part in business dealings with a client or their family.

Staff do not offer, arrange or accept private paid work with an agency client, or refer a client to another caregiver outside the agency, as covered by PER-02. An aide approached by a client with such a request declines and reports it to the supervisor the same day.

An aide performs only the tasks listed in the plan of care that the supervisor has delegated or directed. When asked to do something not on the plan, the aide declines politely, explains that the supervisor must approve it, and calls the supervisor. The supervisor decides whether to revise the plan under SVC-04 (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(c)).
Staff do not discuss personal problems, religion, politics or other matters in a way that pressures the client, and do not use the client's phone, car, home or belongings for personal use.

Staff report to the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor or Administrator any boundary concern, including pressure by a client or family and any concern about another staff member. Reports may be made to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at [PHONE]. Reports of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation follow SAF-01 immediately.

The agency does not charge employees recruitment, placement, training, uniform or similar fees, or liquidated damages, in connection with employment. The agency does not use contract terms that stop employees from working for others (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.6). HR reviews all employment forms against this rule before use (GOV-09).
No staff member is retaliated against for reporting a boundary violation or for refusing to do a task beyond the plan.
The Administrator or designee investigates each reported violation within five business days, interviews the people involved, and documents findings and any action in a confidential conduct file.

Discipline is progressive but may skip steps for serious violations. It ranges from verbal counseling to written warning, suspension, and termination. Financial exploitation, relationship with a client, or a private arrangement ordinarily results in termination.

Where a violation involves a certified aide's conduct that falls under the Board of Nursing's authority, the Administrator, with the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, decides on and files any required report to the Board of Nursing, and keeps a copy of the report. Where a client was harmed, SAF-01 and SAF-02 also apply.
The Quality Assurance committee reviews conduct and boundary reports quarterly for trends and training needs (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, investigates violations, decides on discipline, and files reports to the Board of Nursing when applicable.
Teaches boundaries and task limits, responds to aide questions about tasks, and revises the plan of care when needs change.
Obtains signed acknowledgments, reviews employment forms for prohibited terms, and keeps conduct files.
Maintain boundaries, perform only delegated tasks, and report violations promptly.

documentation: Signed professional boundaries acknowledgment
Gift-offer and boundary concern reports
Investigation notes and outcome
Disciplinary records
Copies of any reports to the Board of Nursing
Quarterly conduct trend review in QA minutes

policies.title: Employer Registrations, Workers' Compensation and Paid Leave
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Human Resources, Payroll, and all employees of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] is properly registered as an employer with the State of New Jersey, carries workers' compensation insurance from the first employee, makes required contributions, and gives employees the paid leave and benefits that the law requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] employs its aides directly, as a third-party employer under 29 CFR 552, and so assumes all employer obligations for them. Before the first employee starts work, the agency registers with the NJ Department of Labor and Workforce Development (NJDOL) for unemployment insurance, temporary disability insurance, family leave insurance, and the Workforce Development and Supplemental Workforce Fund (WF/SWF) contributions, and completes its federal and state tax withholding registrations. The agency keeps workers' compensation insurance in force from the first employee. It withholds and pays contributions correctly, using the wage base and rates in effect each year (the 2026 taxable wage base is $44,800 per the research, and rates are checked each July). It provides paid sick leave as New Jersey's earned sick leave law requires. The Administrator confirms the exact statutory requirements, accrual, usage, carryover, notice and posting rules with legal counsel and writes them into the employee handbook before hiring.

definitions.definition: Enrollment with NJDOL and the tax authorities so that [AGENCY NAME] can report wages and pay required contributions for employees.
Workforce Development Fund and Supplemental Workforce Fund contributions that employers pay to NJDOL.
The maximum amount of each employee's yearly wages on which employer contributions are calculated. It is set each year; $44,800 for 2026 per the research.
Insurance that pays medical care and wage replacement to employees injured or made ill by their work.
Paid leave that employees accrue and may use for the purposes allowed by New Jersey law.

procedures: Before the first employee is hired, the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) completes employer registration with NJDOL for unemployment insurance, temporary disability, family leave insurance and WF/SWF contributions, and completes federal and state withholding registration. The confirmation notices are filed in the corporate compliance file.

Before the first employee starts work, the Administrator binds workers' compensation insurance through [INSURANCE CARRIER], effective on or before the first day of employment. A copy of the policy and certificate is filed. A lapse in coverage is reported to the Administrator immediately and is corrected the same day.
Payroll ([PAYROLL MANAGER NAME]) sets up each contribution account with the current rates and taxable wage base ($44,800 for 2026, to be confirmed each year) in the payroll system.
Each July, Payroll obtains the new NJDOL contribution rates and wage base notices, updates the payroll system, and records the check in the compliance calendar. The Administrator checks the update.
Payroll files required quarterly wage reports and makes contribution payments by their due dates and keeps proof of filing and payment.

HR posts the notices required by New Jersey and federal law in the office and gives employees the required written notices at hire, including notices of rights to temporary disability, family leave, workers' compensation, and earned sick leave.

The Administrator confirms with legal counsel the current earned sick leave requirements (accrual rate, annual cap, permitted uses, notice rules, carryover and payout) and records counsel's written guidance. HR writes the policy into the employee handbook before the first hire and updates it when the law changes.
Payroll tracks each employee's earned sick leave accrual and usage in the payroll system, shows the balance on pay statements or on request, and does not penalize an employee for properly using it.
HR provides information on family leave and temporary disability claim procedures when an employee asks for leave or reports a need, and refers the employee to the state program.

Employees report any work-related injury or illness to the supervisor immediately and no later than the end of the shift. The supervisor completes an incident report the same day (SAF-02, SAF-06) and HR files the workers' compensation first report with the carrier within the time the carrier and state require.
HR provides prompt first-aid direction and medical referral for injured employees and keeps injury records confidential and apart from personnel files.
An employee must not be fired, disciplined or retaliated against for filing a workers' compensation claim, using earned sick leave, or taking protected leave.
Payroll treats aides as employees, not independent contractors, for all payroll purposes. No aide is paid on a 1099 basis (PER-02, PER-07).
The Administrator reviews the employer registration and insurance checklist each quarter and at each registration renewal under GOV-03, and records completion.
Payroll keeps registration notices, contribution filings, insurance policies, claims files and leave records for the retention period set in the agency retention schedule (PER-06).

responsibilities.duty: Completes employer registrations, binds workers' compensation, obtains counsel's guidance on earned sick leave, and reviews compliance quarterly.
Sets up and updates rates, files reports, pays contributions, and tracks leave accruals.
Posts notices, writes the handbook leave policy, handles leave requests, and files workers' compensation first reports.
Take injury reports promptly and do not discourage proper use of leave.
Report injuries immediately and follow leave request procedures.

documentation: NJDOL and tax registration confirmations
Workers' compensation policy and certificate
Annual rate and wage base notices and payroll set-up records
Quarterly wage reports and payment confirmations
Counsel's written guidance on earned sick leave and the handbook policy
Employee notice acknowledgments and posted notice list
Leave accrual and usage records
Workers' compensation first reports and claim files
Quarterly compliance review checklist

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All staff who create, use or maintain client records, including CHHAs, the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, intake, scheduling, billing and records staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps a complete, accurate, secure client record for every client, keeps the specific records New Jersey requires, retains records for the proper period, and gives clients access to their records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for each client that contains the original plan of care and all revisions (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(h)), the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor's delegation entries, the supervisor's 30-day contact responses, and the results of the 60-day in-home evaluations (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(e); 14.9(d),(g)). The record also holds any waiver by which the client gave up the 24-hour advance delivery of the Board of Nursing Consumer Guide, and the agency keeps each such waiver for at least two years (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(d)). For Medicaid PCA clients, the record holds the physician's or practitioner's written certification of need at the initial application and annually (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.4). No HCSF rule setting a general client-record retention period was located. The Administrator therefore confirms the retention periods in each Medicaid and managed care organization (MCO) provider agreement and the accreditor's standards and keeps client records for the longest applicable period. Records on HIPAA policies and procedures and related documentation are kept for six years (45 CFR 164.530(j)). Client records are confidential and secured under CR-03, and clients may access their records under 45 CFR 164.524.

definitions.definition: The paper or electronic file containing the client's identifying and service information, assessments, plans of care, delegation and supervision entries, certifications, agreements, visit documentation, incident reports and correspondence.

The written plan, prepared before placement by an appropriately licensed person and signed with their license designation, that sets the client's needs and the services and level of care to be provided.
The written certification by a physician or practitioner that a Medicaid client needs personal care assistant services, required at the initial application and annually.
The client's signed written waiver of the 24-hour advance delivery of the Board of Nursing's Consumer Guide to Homemaker-Home Health Aides.

procedures: At intake, the Intake Coordinator ([INTAKE COORDINATOR NAME]) opens a client record with a unique client number and files the signed service agreement, rights notice, privacy notice, and consent forms (SVC-02, CR-06, CR-03).

The Health Care Practitioner Supervisor ensures that the original plan of care, signed by the preparer with their license designation, is filed in the record before placement, and that each revision is filed with its date (SVC-04; N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(a),(h)).
The agency gives a copy of the original plan and of each revised plan to the client or representative, and records the date and recipient of each copy in the record (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(h)).

The supervisor records in the client record every task delegated to the aide, with the date and the aide's name, and records that the aide demonstrated competence in the task (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.7(d),(e); REC-03).

At least once in every 30-day period of service, the supervisor contacts the client or representative to ask whether the plan is adequate and is being carried out, and records the responses in the client record (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(c),(d); SVC-05).
At least once in every 60-day period, the supervisor makes an on-site, in-home evaluation of the plan and files the written evaluation in the record (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-14.9(g); SVC-05).

When the Consumer Guide is given at least 24 hours before services, the Intake Coordinator records the date and method of delivery (CR-07). If the client waives the 24-hour period, the Intake Coordinator files the signed written waiver, confirms the guide is still given before services begin, and keeps the waiver for at least two years from its date, or longer if the full record is kept longer (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.7(d)).

For Medicaid PCA clients, the Intake Coordinator files the physician's or practitioner's written certification of need received at the initial application and tracks the annual recertification date. The agency does not begin or continue PCA services without the current certification on file (N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.4; SVC-12).

Aides' visit notes, EVV data, and incident reports are filed in the record in the time set by SVC-08 and SAF-02. Entries are legible, dated, timed, and signed or electronically authenticated, and corrections are made by a single line, with date and initials, without erasure.

Records staff stores paper records in locked, fire-resistant cabinets and electronic records in a password-protected, access-controlled, backed-up system with audit logging. Only staff with a job-related need may open a record.
Staff do not take client records out of the office except as needed for care. Any record taken out is kept secure, returned the same day, and logged.

When a client asks for a copy of the record, Records staff verifies identity and authority, and responds within 30 days of the request, with one 30-day extension allowed with written notice of the reason and date (45 CFR 164.524; CR-03). Any fees follow the written fee policy and HIPAA rules.
Release to anyone else (including Medicaid agencies, MCOs, surveyors and accreditors) is made as permitted by HIPAA and the provider agreement, and each release is logged by Records staff.

Within 30 days of discharge or closure (SVC-10), Records staff completes the closing checklist to confirm the record is complete, adds the discharge summary, marks the record closed, and moves it to secure storage.

The Administrator maintains a written retention schedule that states, for each record type, the retention period and its source. Before the first client is served, the Administrator checks each Medicaid and MCO provider agreement and the accreditor's standards and records the longest applicable period. The schedule shows six years for HIPAA policies and related documentation (45 CFR 164.530(j)), and a minimum of two years for Consumer Guide waivers.

Records may be destroyed only after the retention period ends, with the Administrator's written approval. Destruction is by shredding or secure electronic erasure and is logged with date, record identifiers, and the person responsible.

If the agency closes or changes ownership, the Administrator arranges for secure continued storage and access to client records for the full retention period and reports the arrangement to the State as required by REC-02 and GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the retention schedule, confirms payer and accreditor retention periods, and approves destruction.
Ensures that the plan, delegation entries, 30-day contacts and 60-day evaluations are documented and filed on time.
Opens records, files agreements, Consumer Guide records and waivers, and tracks Medicaid certifications of need.
Maintains secure storage, handles access requests and releases, and logs destruction.
Document visits accurately and timely and protect the confidentiality of client information.

documentation: Client record with index and checklist
Original and revised plans of care and distribution record
Delegation and competency entries
30-day contact responses and 60-day in-home evaluations
Consumer Guide delivery record and signed waivers (kept at least 2 years)
Physician or practitioner certification of need and annual recertifications
Record access and release log
Retention schedule with sources
Record destruction log
Closed-record checklist

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Health Care Practitioner Supervisor, finance and compliance staff, and any staff who prepare or submit reports to the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs, Medicaid or MCOs
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] submits every report and notice required of a registered Health Care Service Firm on time and accurately, and keeps proof of each filing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] files renewal, financial, change-of-information, and accreditation reports with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs, Regulated Business Section, by the required dates. Annual renewal requires evidence of accreditation, and the financial statements and audits required under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A are submitted with the renewal (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5). Registration expiration moved from June 30 to September 30 under P.L. 2026, c.45; the Administrator confirms the date and renewal procedure with DCA before each renewal because DCA implementation guidance was pending and the source is a secondary summary. The agency files its financial statement for the prior calendar year by July 1 each year (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A). It reports in writing any change to application information within 30 calendar days (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(c)). If an officer, director, principal or owner is convicted after filing, [AGENCY NAME] obtains a new affidavit and files it within 30 days of the conviction (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(d)). The agency reports loss of accreditation to DCA within 10 days. Medicaid and MCO reports follow the provider agreement and contract. The Administrator keeps a compliance calendar of every due date.

definitions.definition: The unit of the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs that registers and regulates health care service firms. Contact: (973) 504-6370; regulatedbusiness@dca.njoag.gov; NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal.

The information in the registration package, including firm and trade names, primary locations, officers, directors, principals, owners of 10% or more, managing agents, conviction certifications, and licenses held in other states.
The statement for the prior calendar year that matches the firm's State tax filing and shows assets, liabilities, gross income, operating expenses, and money received for NJ Medicaid PCA services.
The audit, or the report that includes a review by a New Jersey-licensed CPA, that N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A requires of firms at certain revenue levels.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) maintains a compliance calendar listing each State report, its due date, the responsible person, and the date filed. The calendar includes the July 1 financial statement date, the registration expiration date, and Medicaid and MCO report dates.

At least 120 days before the registration expiration date, the Administrator contacts DCA's Regulated Business Section to confirm the current expiration date (September 30 under P.L. 2026, c.45, unless DCA instructs otherwise), the renewal fee, and the portal procedure, and records the answer in the calendar. The Administrator also confirms how DCA treats registrations that had already renewed for 2026-2027.

Not later than 90 days before the expiration date, the Administrator begins the renewal in the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal and assembles the required items, including evidence of current accreditation (GOV-04) and the registration fee for each primary location (GOV-03).

By July 1 each year, the finance lead ([FINANCE LEAD NAME]) files the financial statement for the prior calendar year showing assets, liabilities, gross income, operating expenses, and money received for NJ Medicaid PCA services. The statement must match the firm's State tax filing (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A; GOV-08).

Each year, the finance lead determines which additional report applies: an audit if NJ Medicaid PCA revenue exceeded $250,000 or gross income was $10 million or more, or a report including a review by a New Jersey-licensed CPA if PCA revenue was under $250,000 and gross income was $1 million to under $10 million (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A). The finance lead confirms the current status of these requirements with DCA, because a secondary source reports that some of them are suspended, and records the answer.

The Administrator engages the CPA early enough that any required audit or review is complete and filed with the renewal. An audit must have an unqualified opinion and include compliance and financial components (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A).
Before any change in ownership or management, the Administrator gives DCA the owner and managing-agent information for the new owners or managers (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(b)).

Within 30 calendar days of any change to application information (such as name, address, officers, directors, principals, owners or managing agents), the Administrator sends a written report to the Regulated Business Section, keeps a copy, and records the date sent (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(c); GOV-03).

If any officer, director, principal or owner is convicted after the registration was filed, the person must tell the Administrator at once. The Administrator obtains a new conviction-certification affidavit and files it with DCA within 30 days of the conviction, and the agency reviews the person's role under GOV-01 (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3(d)).
If the agency loses accreditation, the Administrator reports the loss to DCA in writing within 10 days, records the date and method of reporting, and starts corrective action under GOV-04.
Staff who learn of any event that triggers a report (a change in ownership, address, officers, a conviction, or loss of accreditation) tell the Administrator the same business day.

The Administrator tracks each Medicaid and MCO report, notice and data submission required by the provider agreements, assigns an owner and due date for each, and records submission (SVC-11, SVC-12). Required incident and abuse reports are made as described in SAF-01 and SAF-02.

Before submitting any report, a second person (the Administrator or designee) reviews it for accuracy and completeness, and a copy of the submitted report, the portal receipt or confirmation, and proof of payment are filed in the compliance file.
If DCA sends a deficiency notice or request for more information, the Administrator responds in writing within the deadline in the notice and keeps the correspondence.

Each quarter, the Administrator reviews the compliance calendar and the filings with the Quality Assurance committee (GOV-06) and corrects any missed or late items. The corrective action is documented.
Copies of all State reports and filings are kept under REC-01 and the agency retention schedule, and are available for surveyor review.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the compliance calendar, files renewal, change and accreditation notices, confirms deadlines with DCA, and signs reports.
Prepares the financial statement and coordinates any audit or CPA report.
Reports to the Administrator any event that may require a State or payer report.
Reviews the compliance calendar and filing status at least quarterly (GOV-01).
Tell the Administrator immediately of any conviction or change affecting application information.

documentation: Compliance calendar with due dates and filing dates
DCA confirmation of expiration date and renewal procedure
Renewal package, portal receipt and fee payment
Evidence of accreditation
Financial statement, CPA audit or review report, and DCA correspondence on applicability
Written 30-day change reports and proof of delivery
Post-filing conviction affidavits and filing proof
Written notice of accreditation loss and proof of delivery
Medicaid and MCO report tracking log
Quarterly compliance review minutes

policies.title: Clinical Record Content: Plan of Care, Delegation and Supervision Documentation
policies.applies_to: All clients served by [AGENCY NAME] (private-pay, NJ FamilyCare PCA, MLTSS and Personal Preference Program), all Health Care Practitioner Supervisors, supervising registered nurses, intake and scheduling staff, and Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs)
policies.purpose: To make sure every client's clinical record shows, in one place and in a form a surveyor can follow, that care was planned by a licensed person before placement, that every task a caregiver performs was delegated and the caregiver shown competent, and that the plan was reviewed and supervised on the required schedule. The policy also covers the added PCA documents required for Medicaid clients.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a clinical record for every client that contains: (1) the signed, dated plan of care showing the preparer's license designation, and every revision; (2) a record of every task delegated to a caregiver and the supervisor's finding that the caregiver demonstrated competence in that task; (3) the supervisor's documented 30-day inquiry and the responses received; (4) the documented on-site, in-home evaluation of the plan at least once in every 60-day period; (5) documentation of corrective action and plan reassessment when needed; and (6) for Medicaid PCA clients, the physician or practitioner certification, the RN-prepared plan of care signed by the PCA and RN, the managed care plan's PCA Assessment tool and hour authorization where applicable, and RN supervisory visit documentation. Caregivers perform only tasks that are documented as delegated or directed by the Health Care Practitioner Supervisor. A task that is not documented as delegated is not performed. Records are complete, legible, dated, signed with the author's name and credential, and available to the Division of Consumer Affairs, the Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services (DMAHS) and managed care plans on request.

definitions.definition: The appropriately licensed health care professional designated by [AGENCY NAME] to delegate or direct caregiver tasks, confirm caregiver competence, and supervise the plan of care (see SVC-03).
The written plan prepared before placement by an appropriately licensed person after evaluating the client's needs, identifying the tasks to be performed and the level of care required.
A task the CHHA or PCA is permitted to perform because the supervisor assigned or directed it, and for which the supervisor has confirmed the caregiver's competence.
The supervisor's contact, at least once in every 30-day period of service, asking whether the plan of care is adequate and whether it is being carried out, with the responses recorded.
The supervisor's on-site evaluation of the plan of care in the client's home at least once in every 60-day period.

The record of a NJ FamilyCare Personal Care Assistant client, including the physician or practitioner certification, the RN plan of care, the PCA Assessment and authorization where a managed care plan applies, and RN supervisory visit documentation.
A person legally authorized to act for the client or designated by the client to receive the plan of care.

procedures: At intake, Intake staff opens a clinical record for each client and records the payer type (private-pay, PCA, MLTSS or PPP) so the correct documentation checklist is attached. The checklist is [AGENCY NAME]'s Clinical Record Content Checklist.

Before any caregiver is placed, an appropriately licensed person evaluates the client's needs and writes the plan of care. The plan identifies the tasks to be performed and the level of care required. The preparer signs and dates it with his or her license designation. Scheduling staff may not assign a caregiver until a signed plan is in the record.

The Health Care Practitioner Supervisor confirms that the level of care of the caregiver placed matches the level of care in the plan and records this confirmation in the record before the first visit.

For each task on the plan, the supervisor documents the delegation or direction: the task, the date, the caregiver's name and certification, and the supervisor's name and credential. Every task delegated is recorded; a task not recorded may not be performed.

Before the caregiver performs a delegated task independently, the supervisor evaluates and documents that the caregiver demonstrated competence in that task, including the method used (for example, return demonstration) and the date. If competence is not shown, the supervisor documents retraining or reassignment of the task.

For PCA clients, the physician or practitioner certification is filed in the record before service begins. For clients in a managed care plan, the plan's completed State PCA Assessment tool and hour authorization are filed in the record on receipt.

For PCA clients, the supervising RN assesses the beneficiary and prepares the plan of care consistent with the certification at the start of service and never later than 48 hours after it begins. The plan lists tasks, hours, goals, and the beneficiary's strengths and family needs. The RN and the PCA each date and sign it, and the signed plan is filed in the record.

The supervisor records the 30-day inquiry at least once in every 30-day period of service. The entry states the date, the person contacted (client, representative or caregiver), whether the plan is adequate, whether it is being carried out, the responses received and the supervisor's signature and credential.

The supervisor performs the on-site, in-home evaluation of the plan at least once in every 60-day period and documents the date, findings, observations of the caregiver's performance of delegated tasks, and any changes recommended. The entry is signed with the supervisor's credential.

For PCA clients, the supervising RN directly supervises the PCA in the home during the PCA's assigned time. The first visit is initiated within 48 hours of the start of service, and visits occur at least once every 60 days thereafter. The RN documents each visit. Additional visits are made, and documented, when a new PCA is assigned, when nurse delegation occurs or when the beneficiary's needs change. Where multiple PCAs are assigned, the RN rotates visits until all PCAs have been assessed on each covered shift, and the record shows which staff and shifts were observed.

If the 30-day inquiry, the home evaluation, a client report or a caregiver report shows the plan needs revision, the supervisor immediately arranges for a licensed person to reassess it. The revised plan is signed and dated with the preparer's license designation, and the original plan is kept in the record.

If the plan is not being carried out properly, the supervisor takes corrective action immediately and documents the problem, the action taken (for example, retraining, schedule change or caregiver replacement), who was notified and the date resolved.
The agency gives a copy of the original plan, and of each revised plan, to the client or the client's representative and documents the date and manner of delivery in the record.

Clinical entries are made in the record within two business days of the activity they describe, unless a shorter time is required by the payer. Late entries are labeled as such and dated on the day written. Entries are never erased or backdated; corrections are made by a dated, initialed strike-through or an electronic amendment that preserves the original.

The Clinical Record Content Checklist is reviewed by the supervisor at each 30-day contact for contact timeliness, and by the Administrator or designee through a monthly audit of a sample of active records and every record at discharge. Missing items are assigned to a named person with a due date.

The audit results are reported to the quality assurance process (GOV-06). Repeated failures to document delegation, competence, or the 30-day and 60-day contacts result in corrective action for the responsible staff member.

The Administrator reviews this policy and the checklist at least annually against current Board of Nursing, Division of Consumer Affairs and NJ FamilyCare PCA program requirements, including any additional PCA clinical record content required by DMAHS or a managed care plan, and updates the checklist through document control (GOV-05).

Records are stored, secured and retained according to REC-01 and protected under CR-03. Records are produced to surveyors, DMAHS and managed care plan reviewers on request, and the Administrator logs each such release.
